Uniform Title: *Śivastotrāvalī* Author: Utpaladeva Commentator: Kṣemarāja
Editor: Rai Pramadasa Mitra Bahadur Notes: Data entered by the staff of Muktabodha under the direction of Mark S. G. Dyczkowski Revision 0: June 26, 2016
Publisher: Chowkhamba Sanskrit Book Depot Publication Year: 1902 Publication City: Benares
Country of Publication: India, p. 1) Śrī-Śrī-Śiva-Stotrāvalī.
Composed by the venerable teacher Utpaladeva. Om Tatsat.
Om. For one who does not meditate nor recite [the mantra], and for whom it is performed without the prescribed method—
In this very way, Śivābhāsa paid homage to him who was endowed with devotion. || 1 ||
Oṃ tat sat. Salutations to the illustrious remover of obstacles. Salutations to the illustrious Guru, who is Śiva. Oṃ!

She who showers bliss, the one Goddess who is the moonlight of the moon of consciousness, is victorious—she who delivers the entire universe from the blinding darkness. I have been requested many times and in many ways by those possessed of devotion; therefore, I shall explain.
A brief praise of the illustrious author of the *Pratyabhijñā*: The venerable teacher Utpaladeva, whose name is to be revered, the author of the *Īśvarapratyabhijñā*, our supreme preceptor,
who has perpetually realized his own self as the Great Lord, [revealed] his own nature in its true state.
Out of a desire to favor those seeking his aid,

he composed several independent hymns— including the *Saṃgraha-stotra*, *Jaya-stotra*, and *Bhakti-stotra*, as well as daily praises (*āhnika-stuti*) and Vedic hymns (*sūkta*). Then, at one time, Śrī Rāma and Ādityarāja obtained these works interspersed with others.

He established [the hymns] individually upon the beds of praise (*stotra-śayyā*). It is indeed heard that Śrī Viśvāvarta arranged them with twenty hymns using names conceived by himself. Thus, these *saṃgraha* and other hymns are clearly nothing but *sūktas* mounted upon the well-known beds of the Vārtikas.
We shall explain it. To demonstrate that the immersion (*samāveśa*) into the Supreme Lord— which consists of the savoring of the aesthetic delight (*rasa*) of embracing the Fortune of Liberation—
is the supreme object of attainment, he utters this hymn by means of praising the devotees who are immersed in Him and are non-different from His own nature.

"Not by meditating" (p. 2): he who, even without such a means consisting of *māyā*, would have the manifestation of Śiva—the unfolding of his own self as the nature of Śiva—should be honored through devotion alone, which consists of total immersion (*samāveśa*).

This means that we should not be devotees who, while praising [the Lord], are stained by the desire for fruits other than that; rather, through the act of bowing with devotion to the venerable Śiva—who is celebrated as being won over by the wonder of devotion—we should become one with Śiva, who is non-different from Him, through the immersion (*āveśa*) in Śiva who is non-different from Him. This is precisely what is meant by the phrase "in this very way."

He demonstrates the extraordinary sequence indicated [in the previous verse] with the words "he does not meditate," and so forth. For everyone, meditation, recitation, and the like, as well as the essential nature of the object of meditation and the mantra to be recited, manifest only in fixed forms;
however, for one endowed with devotion, they manifest as the very means-less, formless, yet all-formed mass of consciousness and bliss.
The nature of the self as Śiva shines forth at all times; for this very reason, he says "without ritual" (*avidhipūrvakam*).

Ritual (*vidhi*) refers to that which is prescribed, such as sacrifice, study, and so forth, where it serves as a prior cause. By acting in such a manner, because all rituals are limited, they lack the status of being a means toward the unconditioned nature [of the self].

It is through the wealth of immersion in reality (*tattvasamāveśa*) alone that the primary state of the clarity of intuitive insight (*pratibhāprasādana*) is attained. As it is stated in the *Śrīpūrvaśāstra*:
"And nothing is prescribed here," and so forth; "for one who thinks of nothing," and so forth; and in the *Gītā* as well:

"having immersed [the mind] in Me," and so forth. Through meditation (*dhyāna*) and recitation (*japa*), which consist of the nature of light (*prakāśa*) and reflective awareness (*vimarśa*), [this is achieved].
Since worship, oblation, and all other such acts are included therein, only those two have been mentioned here on account of their predominance.
Although my soul is young, having drunk the nectar of devotion to you, it has become grey, as if by the white hairs born from the dust and passion of worldly existence. || 2 ||

"Regarding 'the self': O Maheśvara, my self— the living soul (jīva)— though rendered youthful by drinking the nectar of devotion to you and though its innate vigor has been greatly intensified, is nevertheless made grey and lusterless by the grey hairs of old age, which arise from the passion caused by the dust of worldly activity (*lokavyavahāra*) through the very course of mundane existence."
But in reality, because he has been rendered eternally youthful by drinking the nectar of devotion,
just as a youth appearing gray with dust and seemingly possessed of white hair does not suffer even the slightest internal fading; so it is here.

Rather, it nourishes only diversion, laughter, and aesthetic wonder; thus, through the metaphorical comparison (*rūpaka-upamā*), it suggests that "worldly conduct is mine. Since there was no word of address in the previous verse, [the term] *bhavad-bhakti* (your devotion) does not occur here.

"Since this is indeed entirely appropriate, one must ask Śrī Viśvāvarta himself how this can be called a 'bed of praise' (stotraśayyā); as for us, we are merely intent upon explaining the hymn. || 2 ||
For those devoted ones who dwell in your city and have attained your perfection,
even their movement upon the path of the world occurs through that very same manifestation of yours.
"Because they have attained [it]" means: those who are endowed with the excellence of devotion consisting of immersion (*samāveśa*), and for that very reason have attained your own perfection,

and who dwell in your city— that is, in your own nature which fills the universe— and whose character is such, their movement and worldly activity even on the path of the world is [nothing other than] the unfolding of that very [state] consisting of the bliss of the flavor of immersion.

By virtue of its blossoming, it surely comes to be so; moreover, those devotees of yours who have attained worldly prosperity and dwell within your mandala—all of them are always delighted by their abundance because they are objects of longing—this he conveys through the figure of speech known as *samāsokti* (implied metaphor). || 3 ||
O Lord, since the entire interior of the universe is directly composed of you, what place is not a field for those possessed of devotion? And what mantra would not be accomplished for them? (4)

"Manifesting directly": for those possessed of devotion—meaning those endowed with the form of devotion as previously explained—is there anywhere in the entire world that is not a sacred field (*kṣetra*), a place where a multitude of supreme accomplishments (*siddhi*) arises? And wherein would a mantra, whose nature is to protect through contemplation, not be effective for them? For, from the perspective of direct immersion (*samāveśa*), it is not so.
By the mere mention of their names, this entire world becomes composed of you alone. || 4 ||

O Lord, though You are eternally without a second, those who possess You as their second (Your devotees) triumph— intoxicated by the excellent nectar-wine of the essence of devotion, even though they themselves are always non-dual.

"Victorious are those whose devotion... means: victorious—meaning they exist with supreme excellence—are those who have experienced rising joy through that most excellent drink, the nectar-essence of devotion (*bhakti-pīyūṣa-rasa*). Of what nature are they?
Although they are non-dual and possess a unique nature, they are "with You as their second" (*tvaddvitīyāḥ*), meaning that You alone are their second—that is, their equal form.

Furthermore, because through the immersion of devotion they achieve absolute non-difference, You alone are cultivated as their second in terms of sovereignty; even while being such, they remain non-dual (*advitīyāḥ*), being non-distinct from the universe.

"How can those who are non-dual be Your dual companions, and how can those who are Your dual companions be non-dual?"— O Lord, only those who are drenched in the essence of bliss through intense devotion understand this truth of Yours, which possesses the infinite ocean of such paradoxical splendor. (6)

Those whose dispositions are moistened—overflowing with the essence of the bliss of devotion and the expansion of the bliss of spiritual immersion—are for that very reason "such" ones; because they are like an ocean of the essence of immeasurable bliss, they are identical in form to Your own nature and thus know Your true reality.
For whoever is wise regarding something, he indeed knows it. || 6 ||
"You alone are the self and lord of all, and you are everything within the self, possessing passion.
Knowing that devotion to you is established by your very nature, a person may conquer [the world]. (7)

"You alone are the Lord of the Self. Everyone indeed desires their own self; however, in reality, you alone, whose nature is consciousness (*cidrūpa*), are this self. Therefore, devotion toward you, the self, is inherently established;

one merely recognizes it through the power of immersion (*samāveśa-śakti*). One should conquer that [doubt] and proceed with supreme excellence—this is the sense of the optative suffix (*liṅ*) in the injunction. (7)
O Lord, when the object of knowledge has ceased, by whom would You not be seen standing as the solitary One?
Even amidst the agitation of the known and the knower, You are easily perceived by Your devotees.

"O Lord, when all objects of knowledge have ceased in the state of inward-turned consciousness, whose own essential nature as the Absolute (kevala) would You not manifest? Yet for Your devotees, even amidst the agitation of the known and the knower during the descent into worldly existence, You are easily perceived as Sudarśana."

For by those who are constantly perfumed by the ultimate state of immersion (*samāveśa*), the entire universe is perceived as consisting of Śiva alone, according to the principle that "the enjoyer himself always exists everywhere in the form of the enjoyed. This is for the purpose of abandoning the effort of dissolving the object of knowledge (*vedya*).
It is a good word; for it is stated in the Śrīpūrvaśāstra that the means to liberation is obtainable without effort. || 8 ||
Just as the goddess Anantānandasurāsī is your most beloved and is never separated from you, may I possess devotion toward you that knows this very truth.

"Anantānanda" (Infinite Bliss). By means of this metaphorical expression, he prays for equality with the Supreme Lord. From the perspective of devotion (*bhakti*), the Goddess is radiant, singular, and devoid of desire for fruits; elsewhere, she is the Supreme Power (*parā śakti*) whose nature is play and so forth. While one might say "May I be inseparable from her through devotion," he says "May she be inseparable from me," thus expressing his orientation toward devotion.
The expansion of love has been revealed. || 9 ||
O Lord, for those possessed of devotion, every state of yours is a cause of attainment;
this path of consciousness exists in three ways, through joy, suffering, and delusion.

"Everything indeed is Your attainment. For those characterized by supreme devotion as explained, this path of consciousness— which exists in the world in the form of cognitions of blue, yellow, and so forth, and which is marked by joy, suffering, and delusion— is entirely the cause for attaining You, through the process of submerging the rungs of the ladder of objects of knowledge.
Because of the attainment of the stage of being a supreme experiencer. || 10 ||
O Lord, even that supreme state of awakening which might arise from tasting the nectar of devotion to you would,
for me, be like the acidity of wine.

O Master, for one whose mind is intent on relishing the bliss of devotion consisting of the immersion of Your descent of power (*śaktipāta*), there may arise a supreme state of awakening— the ultimate state of Śiva characterized by peace— which some conceive of as attainable only upon the fall of the body;
yet that state, though conceived by them, appears to me like the sourness of wine.
The meaning is that it appears as if stale. For by those [who do not taste it], the nectar of devotion has been turned into sour gruel (*śukti*) even without being tasted;

whereas for those who do taste it, since it has been made to rest in the bliss of their own wonder, there is no possibility of its being considered sour gruel. The suffix *lyap* is used in the sense of "from tasting" (*āsvādāt*).
The fifth case ending is used after an elided word (lopa). (p.

6) In the phrase "from tasting" (*svādāt*), the suffix *lyap* has been elided, and thus the fifth case is employed. Alternatively, it means "even superior to the tasting of the nectar of devotion to You."

It is possible that some state in the form of liberation exists; however, that does not please me, because the nectar-like taste of devotion alone possesses unsurpassed wonder—this is the ultimate point. || 11 ||
Those in whom the great lore of devotion to you has become firmly established—
whether they possess knowledge or ignorance— they are all knowers of reality.

Regarding the phrase "devotion to you": "of both knowledge and ignorance" means that the reality of both—that which is characterized by knowledge and that which is characterized by ignorance—is present therein.
This includes both the form of knowledge, consisting of Śiva, Mantra-Maheśvara, Mantreśvara, and Mantra;
and the form of ignorance, consisting of the Vijñānākala, Pralayākala, Sakala, and their respective objects of cognition. It is the reality of both of these.

Those who know that devotion to you alone has attained the status of a supreme science (*mahāvidyā*)—by the word "great" (*mahat*), it is indicated that because devotion excels even the science of grammar (*śabdavidyā*), it possesses the quality of making reality known. || 12 ||
May this creeper of speech, which has its root in You and flourishes through gradual expansion, be watered by the nectar of devotion to You and bear for me fruits rich with that very essence. (13)
"From the root, O Speech!"—the "root" is the supreme plane (*parā-bhūmi*); "gradual expansion" is the unfolding of *paśyantī* and the other stages;
its "essence" is the very essence of the bliss of devotion (*bhakti-ānanda-rasa*); and it is "rich," meaning its fruit is characterized by the attainment of identity with Your own self. || 13 ||
"One should worship having become Śiva" is said to mean "having become a devotee.
For you alone are the essence of the body, purified as non-dual by your devotees. (14)

Regarding the statement "having become Śiva": as it is taught in the Āgamas that "having become Śiva, one should worship Śiva," those who believe that Śiva-hood occurs only upon the fall of the body are mistaken; for as long as the body exists, there is an absence of the state of being Śiva, and thus the status of being a sacrificer (*yajamāna*) would be untenable.
The intended meaning is that only one who possesses devotion characterized by immersion into the Śiva of one's own true nature knows how to perform worship.

With this very intention, he says (p. 7): "Since you alone are the essence, the most excellent body, the true nature [of reality], by means of non-duality which cuts down hundreds of spikes of doubt regarding difference."
It has been purified and rendered stainless by the devotees; thus [it is said]. || 14 ||
What arguments are not available for establishing the non-duality of the devotees?
And what veils are not present for those of inferior nature to prevent that realization? (15)

What arguments are there for the devotees who have been explained [in this work] to establish non-dual existence (*bhavadadvaya*), such that even the criticisms of Śiva’s non-duality uttered by the deluded would— by virtue of those very arguments—
be unable to exist without establishing the nature of Śiva as consciousness whose essence is to refute those very criticisms? Thus, by means of reasoning (*yuktyā*).
For devotees, spiritual practices indeed culminate in their goal; but for those who are base and characterized by duality,
what obstacles— despite even the sharpest weapons of logical reasoning— do not arise to prevent the attainment of that [goal], namely the realization of non-dual Śiva?
Even the droplets of the essence of immersion (samāveśa), because they are not recognized due to ignorance, lead only to a fall into great darkness. || 15 ||
"O Lord, it is a deception to say that You are found somewhere by yoga only at some time;
otherwise, how could You manifest in all stages for those possessed of devotion? (16)

"Sometimes" (kadācit): at some time, in a certain state of meditative absorption (*samādhi*), in some place such as the heart-center (*hṛdayacakra*) and so forth, by means of yoga—that is, through the cessation of the fluctuations of the mind—you, O Lord (*īśa*), Master, are "attainable"; this is a deception. Otherwise, how could You manifest to the devoted during other stages, such as those following the emergence from meditation (*vyutthāna*)? || 16 ||
There is this great distinction, untouched by practices such as pratyāhāra:
that those who possess devotion remain concentrated even during the state of emergence (vyutthāna), unlike the yogis.
Pratyāhāra is the withdrawal and restraint of the senses from their objects;

by the word "etcetera," meditation (dhyāna), concentration (dhāraṇā), and so forth are included. Unaffected and untroubled by these, those who possess devotion have a distinction—a great superiority—over yogis established in those practices, such that they [are superior].
p.

8) Even at a time intended for rising from meditative absorption, those who are concentrated—being "ever-disciplined" (nityayukta) according to the principle stated in the Gītā, "those who, having fixed their minds on Me... (Gītā 8.8)—are [the ones referred to]. || 17 ||
Neither yoga, nor austerity, nor any ritual sequence is prescribed here;
in this illusion-free path of Śiva, devotion alone is praised. (18)

"Yoga is not [required]" means that in this supreme Śiva-path, the Śākta plane— which is unsurpassed and has only one witness, namely one's own direct experience— no sequential method of means such as yoga governed by *māyā* is taught;
for since that [method] consists of *māyā*, it is like blinding darkness here.

Since there is no means superior to the radiance of Pure Knowledge (śuddhavidyā), it is devotion alone—which consists in the clarification of intuitive insight (pratibhā) as previously described—that is praised and declared to be the means. || 18 ||
For me, whose obscurations have been destroyed by the splendor of devotion shining forth on all sides and who perceive all things directly, let even the name of "thought" perish.

"Shining everywhere" means that because the veil— namely, non-recognition (*akhyāti*)— has been destroyed by the splendor of devotion, which expands and shines both internally and externally as the light of immersion (*samāveśa*), one thereby forgets the plane of *māyā* through the method of entering the mudrā of manifest Bhairava.

May even the name—that is, the designation—of my thought, which functions as conceptualization, perish for me, for whom all things have become the mere object of pure observation; the meaning is: may I forever enter into the realized nature of Supreme Bhairava. || 19 ||
When the single word "Śiva" dwells forever upon the tip of the tongue, oh, some indescribable savor of all objects of experience belongs only to the devotees! (20)

"Śiva is the one. Among those very devotees mentioned, he who consists of the awareness of his own essential nature—which is the Great Light—is Śiva; he is the one, the extraordinary one, who always exists. Oh, what a wonder! Even for that single object which is a mere word [Śiva], [there is such a state].
Because you bestow the pervasion of supreme bliss, you are a certain, wondrous experience of the joy of the world (*jagadānandacamatkāra*)— the tasting of all objects—
which is established through your own direct experience; and yet, you abide in one place, within the object characterized by sound, right upon the tip of the tongue.
"The tasting of all objects" is an instance of the shadow of contradiction (virodhacchāyā). || 20 ||

In the ocean of the nectar of devotion—which is tranquil, waveless, cool, pure, and sweet—who indeed is not counted among those who are well-established in the tasting of this extraordinary aesthetic flavor? 21.

Regarding the phrase *śāntakallola*: it refers to the ocean of the nectar of devotion, which is a supramundane tasting of aesthetic flavor (*rasa*), wherein the waves consisting of conceptual constructions have subsided; which is cool because it is free from the heat of worldly existence (*saṃsāra*); which is clear and pure because it serves as the substratum for the reflection of the entire universe; and which is sweet because it is blossomed with bliss.

Those who are well-established remain at ease within the wonder of immersion (samāveśa); for them, because differentiation has dissolved, who indeed could be counted? Since nothing whatsoever appears as separate [from themselves], it is entirely appropriate to say that those established in bliss do not take anything into account. || 21 ||
O Blessed One, why should those like me not savor this great medicine of devotion to you, from which the fruit called liberation arises immediately thereafter? 22.

"By those like me" means by those like me who know the essence of devotion (*bhakti*). "Such as that" refers to your very own transcendental devotion; because it bestows desired objects, why would it not be treated as a great medicinal herb? That is to say, why would it not be chewed, why would it not be held, and why would it not be tasted through reflection? Of what nature is it? Immediately after the chewing and contemplation of which—
The immediately following, uninterrupted aesthetic flavor (rasa) known as "liberation while living" is the bliss of relishing. || 22 ||
O Lord, those very prosperities are considered supreme by the virtuous which nourish the confidence of enjoying the flavor of devotion to you.

"Those very ones" means that by the virtuous who possess devotion, those very riches—which consist of the immersion into Your equality—are sought after exclusively, and not powers such as *aṇimā* and the rest. Of what nature are they? Those which provide confidence in the enjoyment of the flavor of devotion to You, that is, in the wonder of the nectar of immersion into You.

(10) They foster their own spontaneous acceptance. Here, there is a suggestion of a simile based on resonance (*anuraṇanavyaṅgyopamādhvani*), wherein the very enjoyment of the beloved nourishes all forms of prosperity according to the principle of seeking wealth. || 23 ||
O Lord, this mind is by nature a wondrous seed of suffering; yet, when sprinkled with the essence of devotion to you, it bears the great fruit of supreme liberation. (24)

"How wonderful is this nature! O Lord, O Master, it is a marvel that this mind—which is the cause of suffering for everyone and is thus to be abandoned—is, when watered by the elixir of devotion to You, transformed into the great fruit of supreme bliss and liberation. Indeed, there is never anything sweet for the world that turns into poison."
Therefore, it is intimated that this sequence is a non-worldly one belonging solely to devotion unto You; may there be auspiciousness. || 24 ||

Thus ends the first [chapter] of the Vivṛti composed by the venerable Kṣemarāja, disciple of the venerable Utpaladeva, the preceptor and sovereign of teachers who authored the illustrious Īśvarapratyabhijñā.
Oṃ tat sat.
Now begins the second hymn, titled "The Contemplation of the Universal Self" (Sarvātmaparibhāvanā).
[Salutations to You] who abide as Agni, Soma, Ravi, Brahmā, and Viṣṇu, and who exist as all that is stationary and moving.
Salutations to you, whose nature is both singular and manifold, who consists of pure consciousness.

[This refers to] the triad of powers (śaktitraya) consisting of burning, nourishing, and illuminating— corresponding respectively to will, action, and knowledge— presided over by the deities Brahmā and Viṣṇu along with Agni, Soma, and Ravi;
and [it refers to] the aggregate of objects of cognition and subjects of cognition presided over by the stationary and the moving.

Because the Universal Self has been accepted as one's own, this address from "O Svarūpa" onwards is directed toward Him. Therefore, O Supreme Lord, whose nature consists of Agni, Soma, Ravi, Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and all things mobile and immobile!
[The five elements are included] because even among mobile beings, they constitute the elemental body. And thus:

[She is] present in fire, moon, and sun, and in all things stationary and moving; she exists as the formless one, and as the presiding deity over all things, characterized by [the forms of] Brahmā and Viṣṇu.

The state of being composed of the universe (*viśvamayatva*). For this very reason, it is said, "to the one of manifold forms" (*bahurūpāya*). Even while possessing such a universal form, he declares his primary essential nature to be "composed of consciousness" (*saṃvinmayāya*). Indeed, this very state of being composed of consciousness consists in being filled with the entire universe as it unfolds through absolute freedom (*svātantrya*). || 1 ||
Salutations to You, the Great Fire, who possess a pure radiance from the application of the great caustic of all-fuel, and who are the sole oblation for the entire universe. || 2 ||
"Viśvendhana" (the fuel of the universe): salutations to You, the Great Fire, the fire of the Supreme Subject.

Of what nature is He? To Him who possesses that great caustic ash—the residual impression (*saṃskāra*) remaining from the withdrawal [of all things]—which is the universal mass of differentiated objects existing in the form of fuel; and who is anointed with that [ash], even through the withdrawal of those impressions.

To Him whose splendor (*varcas*)—that is, His radiant energy (*tejas*)—is pure, stainless, and non-dual; or, according to the terminology of the Āgamas, "to the splendor named *Śuci*," for it is said that the fire named *Śuci* arises from the friction of the Moon and the Sun. By the phrase "He to whom the entire universe is the single oblation" (*viśvamekaṃ haviḥ*), His extreme brilliance is expressed.
Because the meaning of the secret practice (*rahasyacaryā*) is indicated here according to the established tenets of the *Śrīmataṅga* and other Āgamas, there is even the appearance of contradiction.
Salutations to You, the fire of Śiva— dense with the supreme nectar, cool, and yet to some [it is] fierce in its total incineration of the universe.
"Supreme nectar" (paramāmṛta): because it is a mass of consciousness and bliss, it possesses the density of supreme nectar;
because it removes worldly existence, it possesses coolness. How can fire possess moisture and coolness?
This is the shadow of an apparent contradiction (virodhābhāsa). "To whom?"—to that whose nature is supramundane (alaukika). || 3 ||
Salutations to Mahādeva, to Rudra, to Śaṅkara, to Śiva,
and also to Maheśvara— to that certain one whose form is the sacred mantra.

The Lord (*deva*) is intent on the play (*krīḍā*) of creation and so forth; desiring victory through his possession of universal excellence; the initiator of all worldly transactions; shining brightly; worthy of praise by all and the goal to be reached; he "shines" (*dīvyate*) because his purpose is play and the like. And he is "Great" (*mahān*), for even among those beginning with Brahmā, he is the [agent] of creation and so forth.
Because he is the cause of the universe, he is Rudra, so called because of his weeping (*rudana*) and causing to flow (*drāvaṇa*) within the state of consciousness (*citpada*).
Because he consists of the reflective awareness of full I-consciousness (*pūrṇāhaṃtā*), he is the embodiment of mantra (*mantramūrti*). || 4 ||

Homage to the auspicious fire of Śiva, which, though its unevenness is increased by the sprinkling of the blood dripping from the three worlds when they have been entirely cut down, yet leads to well-being.

*Namo nikṛtte* means: that which has been cut (*nikṛttam*) into pieces from its root—characterized by non-apprehension (*akhyāti*)—namely the triple world characterized by *bhava*, *abhava*, and *atibhava*; the marrow (*vasā*) which consists of the essence of internal aesthetic flavor (*rasa*) that kindles the fire of awakening (*bodhānala*) related to that [triple world]; and the sprinkling (*avaseka*), that is, the oblation (*āhuti*), performed with that [marrow]. From that...
Salutations to the auspicious fire of Śiva, which is intensely blazing with terrible [power] and, for that very reason, bestows the avoidance of the inauspiciousness of saṃsāra.
The meaning is that we cause the state of the limited subject— consisting of the body, vital breath, and so forth— to dissolve into that very [fire].
"The fire of the cremation ground, which is incompatible with all consecrations—how can it be auspicious? This is the shadow of a contradiction (virodhacchāyā).
"Salutations to that certain God Śambhu, for whom the very absence of all auspicious marks is the defining characteristic. (6)

Regarding the term *samastalakṣaṇā*: the non-union (*ayoga*), that is, the lack of connection, with all characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*)— both the marks of physical excellence (*abhijñāna*) and the causes for their realization such as recitation, ritual acts, meditation, and so forth— is itself the "characteristic" (*lakṣaṇa*) which is "near" (*upa*), meaning it is brought close to the self, making it penetrate the heart.

Because the very forgetting of all thought is the cause for attaining that [state], it is for this reason that the phrase "to someone" (kasmaicid) suggests, through the indirectness of conventional expression, that it is directed toward the self-manifesting form of one's own Self. || 6 ||
Salutation to the Lord who is contrary to the Vedas and Āgamas, who establishes the Vedas and Āgamas, who is the true essence of the Vedas and Āgamas, and who is the secret one. || 7 ||

Regarding the phrase "Vedic scripture" (*vedāgama*): because it is unattainable through the total shattering of restrictive constraints (*niyamayantraṇā*), that which is contrary to the Veda cannot be enjoined by it.
For how could that which is contradictory to something enjoin it? Furthermore, the object of the mind (*cittārtha*) is of the nature of reality (*satattvarūpa*).
Desiring to cause the world to arise through His own sovereignty, He ordains the Veda; and by the perspective of the Vedānta, He is its ultimate reality.
For this very reason, because He is not an object for anything, He is secret. || 7 ||
Salutations to Śambhu, who has the form of saṃsāra yet is free from saṃsāra, the sole cause of saṃsāra and the sole adversary of saṃsāra.
He alone is the sole cause of the cycle of existence (saṃsāra), from Māyā down to the earth; He alone is its opposite, its destroyer.

Thus, it appears in the form of saṃsāra, yet there is no inherent nature of saṃsāra whatsoever that exists apart from Śiva, who is of the nature of consciousness (cidrūpa). Even so, He has transcended saṃsāra and is free from saṃsāra.
Therefore, "having a form untouched by that" constitutes an apparent contradiction (virodhābhāsa). || 8 ||

Salutations to the one who is the root, the middle, and the tip; to the one whose form is the root, middle, and tip; to the one whose tip, middle, and root are diminished; salutations to the perfect Śambhu.

Regarding the term *mūlāya*: it is the "root" (*mūla*), the "middle," and the "tip" because it is the cause of the universe, its own essential nature, and the locus of rest. Just as it exists separately in the form of root and so forth, so too does it exist simultaneously, because it is the form of the infinite universe without succession. Furthermore, within its own self, there is no such thing as root and so forth, because it consists solely of the single nature of pure consciousness (*cinmātra*).
For this very reason, He is full because He endures everything. The apparent contradiction is as before. || 9 ||
Homage to you, Śiva, who are difficult to attain; even a single utterance of your name is the ripening of a vast accumulation of merit. 10.

"Salutation to the one whose name is well-spoken. Even a single utterance of his name—referring to him as "this one"—is a supramundane ripening of a mass of merit, because it bestows complete rest. To him, who is difficult to attain and accessible only to great yogins, salutation! (10)
Salutations to you alone, the one who consists of pure consciousness, the bearer of the skull-bowl, who eternally sports with hosts of spirits in the form of all that is moving and unmoving.
"Salutations to those who move and do not move. This reveals in its true essence that which is well-known regarding the Lord's observance of the *kapāli* vow:

those "departed ones" (*paretāḥ*) who have gone to the supreme nature consisting of consciousness, appearing in the forms of the moving and the stationary—that is, in the forms of the animate and the inanimate.

They have arrived; and because they are devoid of life, they are likewise departed spirits. To Him who sports eternally and simultaneously with their multitudes, who performs thousands of varieties of joining and separating them, who is composed of consciousness, whose ultimate reality is consciousness, who is the bearer of skulls (Kapālin), who is joined with all skulls without exception, and who sustains the universe which has been reduced to mere bones—to Him, salutation! 11.
Salutations to the master of illusion, to the pure one, to the secret one, to the manifest self, to the subtle one, to the one whose form is the universe, to the wondrous Śambhu. 12.
Regarding the term *māyāvin*: Māyā is the power of absolute freedom (*svātantrya-śakti*) which is the cause of the manifestation of duality.

He who possesses this is pure because his nature is consciousness (*cidrūpatva*). Thus, there is an apparent contradiction: how can one who possesses *māyā*—and is therefore a deceiver (*vyājī*)—be pure?
The same applies elsewhere. "Secret" (*guhya*) means beyond the range of all [ordinary perception]. "Manifest" (*prakaṭa*) means whose form is the very essence of light, dense with radiance.

Subtle, he is unperceivable even by those established in meditative absorption and the like. He possesses universal form (*viśvarūpa*), having assumed all forms through his sovereignty. For this very reason, he is manifold (*citra*), variegated (*vicitra*), and of wondrous nature. || 12 ||
Salutations to you, the one possessed of all powers, who performs the sport of the world’s destruction enacted through Brahmā, Indra, and Viṣṇu, and who is the source of all wonders. 13.

Regarding the term "Brahmendra": the world that has somehow been brought to completion—that is, established, presided over, and maintained by Brahmā, Indra, and Viṣṇu, who are the agents of creation, maintenance, and dissolution—is such that its destruction, while being sustained by all [these gods], is for him merely a pastime. For this very reason, he is the performer of wonders and possesses all powers.

Salutation to Him who is endowed with all powers, since even Brahmā and the other gods must look toward the presence or absence of His desire to withdraw the world as the condition for their own performance of their respective duties. || 13 ||
Salutations to you, the unfathomable ocean of the heart, by those who wander upon its very shores various prosperities have been attained.

"On the very banks" (p. 15) means: by those who have wandered among the very "banks"—namely, the cognitions of mantras, mudrās, maṇḍalas, ritual grounds, and so forth, which are external planes for the flow of the essence of consciousness.
"Those who have exerted themselves in practices such as breath-control, whirling, and the projection of vital energy, and who have wandered among deceptive arts and the like—
they have wandered in vain regarding the supreme state. According to this established tradition of the *Āgama*, those who wander about because they have not attained the inner essence—

those various powers consisting of duality, such as *aṇimā* and the rest— are [compared] to the unfathomable ocean of the *Hara* (Śiva), for they possess an internal reality that can be fully delimited.

The verse suggests through a metaphorical pun (*rūpaka-śleṣa*) that those who wander upon the shores of the ocean of Maheśvara obtain its pearls and such; however, those capable of enduring the inner distractions consume even the nectar that bestows great liberation. || 14 ||
Salutations to the beautiful Śambhu-lotus, which dwells in the midst of the thick mud of the world composed of illusion, yet remains unstained. 15.
Regarding the phrase "consisting of *māyā*": *māyā* is the non-manifestation of [the world] as consisting of consciousness (*cinmaya*). That very thing is the natural form of the universe;

it is itself a thick mire, a dense sludge. To Him who dwells within that [sludge], yet because of His omnipresence pervades it, and who remains untainted—being of the singular nature of pure consciousness—it is Śambhu alone.

Salutations to that lotus, the hundred-petaled one whose petals are infinite powers, possessing the nature of contraction and expansion according to each [state]. Although it stands in the midst of mud, there is "stainlessness" (alepatā) because the Lord, being a mass of consciousness, is untouched by it; thus, there is an apparent contradiction (virodhābhāsa). || 15 ||
Salutations to you, who are auspicious, pure, a treasure-trove, and the very essence of ornament; who are beloved, the supreme reality, and most excellent of all. || 16 ||

Regarding "for the sake of auspiciousness" (*maṅgalāya*): the words beginning with "auspiciousness" (*maṅgala*) and so forth are clear. The phrase "as the most excellent of all" (*sarvotkṛṣṭāya*) is to be applied everywhere.
For by whichever aspect it is examined, it possesses excellence, because it is the most excellent of all. || 16 ||
Salutation to that certain Śambhu who is eternally bound yet eternally liberated, who is devoid of both bondage and liberation. 17.

"Salutation to the one who is eternally... (p. 16). This state [of being both bound and liberated] is understood through the Blessed One himself, by virtue of his being both bound and liberated; yet in reality, because he is a mass of consciousness (*cidghana*), he is independent of that [bondage]. The apparent contradiction is as before. The same applies hereafter. (17)
In this triple world, whose sole essence is mockery,
salutations to you alone, the peerless one who abides in eternal bliss.

"O you who are the sole object of derision!"—salutations indeed unto You alone, who are of such a trivial nature that You are the ultimate object of ridicule; who, though existing within this exceedingly vast triple world consisting of birth, non-existence, and the state beyond existence; who are without a second, possessing a unique and uncommon form; who abide in eternal bliss; who are a mass of pure joy; and who are the most supreme object to be attained. || 18 ||
Salutations to you, the essence of right conduct, who yet desire the left-hand path;
salutations to you, Śarva, who embodies all modes of conduct and is beyond all conduct.

Regarding the term *dakṣiṇācāra*: it refers to one for whom the *Bhairava-tantra*—the practice of the right-hand path (*dakṣiṇācāra*) and its unerring performance—is the essence (*sāra*), that which is held to be the core; whereas he desires the left-hand path (*vāmācāra*), the *Vāma-tantra*, and the inverted sequence. It means one for whom every practice (*ācāra*) is innate, his own natural vibration (*parispanda*). It also means one from whom all conventional practices have departed.

Salutations to him who has transcended conventional conduct such as meditation, ritual worship, and the like; and yet, salutations to him whose nature is both glorious conduct and the transcendence of conduct, who is the embodiment of the reality of the meaning of the scriptures— such as the Matakrama—
and who is worthy of worship in every way.
Wherever he may be worshipped—
whether it be he or whoever else— he is that very God; salutations be unto you!

"In whatever manner" means that by whatever way or in whatever place anything whatsoever is performed, there the worship consisting of resting in one's own self as the deity is accomplished without effort. (p. 17)

The intended meaning is "by those who know reality. The words *yat* and *tat* are used to preclude restrictive rules (*niyama*). One should worship according to the tradition and according to what is available. || 20 ||
Salutations to you, the bestower of boons, who are to be served by those seeking liberation, who remove all suffering,
and who possess an ocean of expansive beauty.

"Desirous of liberation" (mumukṣu): because [this mantra] is the life-force of all mantras for practitioners, it can be served without restraint by those desiring liberation through the reasoning just mentioned. "To the remover"—that is, the destroyer—of all afflictions consisting of duality. The expression "extended" (vitata) is used [to denote its pervasive nature].

Because it is intensely desirable due to its density of supreme bliss; for Amara states: "Vāra means a multitude, a collection, a group, a troop, a host, a cluster, or an accumulation. To the Giver of Boons—that is, to the one who bestows the grace that is the essence of the purity of consciousness. || 21 ||
Salutations to You, the Lord who eternally possesses full-moon phases, and who has entirely filled the three worlds with the essence of uninterrupted bliss. 22.

"Always with uninterrupted bliss" means that, as before, because he fills the three worlds and the entire universe with the essence of his own bliss, the address "to the Lord" is appropriate. "To the one whose festival is eternal" means to him whose form is eternally filling the universe;
for the word *parvan* is used here in the sense of "filling. Indeed, on every festival (*parvan*), he makes everything completely saturated with the essence of bliss.
Salutations to you, that multitude of powers (*śakti-vṛnda*), for the sake of that terrible one who enjoys union with you through experiences characterized primarily by bliss.

That assembly of powers (*śakti-vṛnda*), which is primarily characterized by bliss— the wheel of the goddesses of consciousness (*saṃvid-devī-cakra*)— through its wonder, by resting in the subject who is a mass of bliss, through enjoyments of perceivable objects primarily consisting of happiness,
and through the savoring of swallowing objects whose essence is bliss, worships you alone and offers the entire universe unto you. To that [assembly]...
Salutation to you, who are terrible and the destroyer of all. || 23 ||
Salutations to that certain Being whom even the sages cannot comprehend, yet whom those whose actions are bound by devotion embrace. 24.
"Of the sages" (munīnām): even for those such as Kapila and others who are established in asceticism, yoga, and so forth, [this] is impossible to know.
Their activities are permeated by the essence of immersion (*samāveśa*), consisting of actions connected with devotion (*bhakti*). They embrace [the deity] as well.
Salutations to that which manifests within one's own self, whom they make their own vessel for enjoyment by means of the method of firm resolve. || 24 ||
Homage to you, the treasury of supreme nectar, the mass of supreme nectar, who are attained through the perfection of all perfections. || 25 ||

"Supreme nectar" (*paramāmṛta*) means it is like a treasury or storehouse of the essence of supreme bliss (*paramānanda*); therefore, because it is full of that, it is a "heap" (*rāśi*), and because it consists of that even externally, it is the "supremacy" (*pāramya*)—that is, the state of being supreme (*paramatva*) and the state of being manifest—of everything including *māyā*. The supremacy even of that is the "thick mass of bliss," the wonder (*camatkāra*), the empowered manifestation (*śākta-samullāsa*). [The term refers to that] which is to be attained by means of that.
I bow to your form, which consists of the great mantra, pure and cool,
auspicious with an unprecedented fragrance, and overflowing with the essence of supreme nectar.

"Consisting of the Great Mantra": as before, I bow to Your form, which consists of the Great Mantra—that is, which consists of the unartificial self-reflection (*aham-parāmarśa*). It is "clear" because it holds the reflection of the entire universe; "cool" because it removes the heat of *saṃsāra*; and "delighting" with an unprecedented fragrance—an extraordinary, all-pervading perfume.
In its own nature, it is auspicious and desirable; it is intense and expanded by the essence of supreme nectar, which is supreme bliss. || 26 ||
O Lord, I bow to Your teaching, that great canvas upon which there is no painting whatsoever, because it is the manifestation of oneness with the fullness of the nectar of absolute freedom.

Regarding the word *svātantryā*: that manifestation of oneness with You (*tvadaikyakhyāti*), which is the plenitude of sovereignty (*svatantratā*) through the nectar of autonomy and is a mass of bliss—that very [oneness], by pervading the variegated threads of the universe, is the "Great Cloth" (*mahāpaṭa*).
With respect to that object, the "teaching" (*śāsana*)—so called because one is taught by it—is the scripture (*āgama*) which is Your instruction; [that is what is meant].

I bow [to that] wherein the universe, though its very essence is the manifestation of oneness with You, possesses no diversity of forms at all—being wondrous precisely because it is dedicated solely to establishing the realization of Your oneness.

It is neither variegated nor marvelous, because the scripture is unsurpassed and serves as the ground for all possible conceptions; nevertheless, it is called "variegated" because the teaching resides upon the cloth in a form that is not itself variegated. || 27 ||
We praise the path of Maheśvara, which is a thunderbolt to all doubts, a fire of time to all misfortune, and the end of all inauspiciousness. || 28 ||

"Of all doubts": [it is] the thunderbolt that destroys the very nature of all those doubts—whether they concern the mixing of material offerings, mantras, and so forth, or are otherwise prescribed—which serve as the seeds of the manifold saṃsāra and are the cause for the withering of the mental fluctuations; for even in the sacred tradition (āmnāya), doubt is not [permitted].

One should have no doubt; this has been clearly stated. It is the fire of time (*kālānala*) that burns away all misfortunes (*alakṣmī*), states of lack of bliss, and all inauspiciousness—those things that portend evil—and it is the end of the eon (*kalpānta*) that destroys them without remainder.
We praise the path of Maheśvara and the expansion of Śakti. || 28 ||
Victory to you, O God! Salutations, salutations be unto you;
this entire universe is supported by you;
you are the Supreme Lord of the worlds.
I alone have come to you for refuge as the supreme one. || 29 ||

"O Jayadeva! [He says: "I am the Supreme One," yet through the conceit of the body and so forth—created by the power of Your Māyā—and through the manifold diversity of the universe, I have been made as if separate from You; for this very reason, I have come to You for refuge. And this is fitting, because this entire universe rests upon You, being submerged within Your own nature which consists of consciousness; and therefore, of all worlds...

You alone are the Supreme Lord, superior even to those beginning with Brahmā and ending with Sadāśiva; therefore, O God, whose nature is play and so forth, victory! Cast aside this conceit of the body and other such things, and manifest Yourself in Your true form—as before. || 29 ||
Thus ends the second hymn, titled "The Contemplation of the Universal Self," from the *Stotrāvalī* composed by the venerable teacher Utpaladeva. || 2 ||
Oṃ. To Śambhu, the wondrous one, who transcends that twofold course of existence—consisting of being and non-being—which is logically applicable to all phenomena, I pay homage. (1)

"Oṃ, by way of existence and non-existence. Since those entities— such as objects of cognition (*prameya*) and so forth— are to be meditated upon (*bhāvanīya*), that is, brought about, as possessing a twofold nature through their forms of arising and existence, and through their forms of prior and subsequent non-existence (*prākpradhvaṃsābhāva*), [therefore] that which is a third [nature], having transcended and abandoned that [twofold nature]...

Because it cannot be designated as either existent or non-existent, it remains designated only by its number, like the fourth state (*turya*) and so forth; *salutation to that wonderful one*, the marvel of the universe—*namas* as before. || 1 ||
In these three worlds, which are not independent, those who are dependent upon you alone are truly independent, even among the asuras, rishis, and other beings. (2)

Regarding the term *āsurarṣi*: "the three worlds" is as before. From the *surarṣis*, that is, from the host of divine seers such as Marīci and others—the prefix *ā* here indicates inclusion (*abhividhi*). Their lack of autonomy consists in being within the scope of creation and dissolution. However, Śambhu alone, in his form as the Creator and so forth, is autonomous. And those who are his dependents, who have realized their own selves as being of the same nature as him—they too [are included].
Through immersion in that, they are indeed independent. || 2 ||
Those for whom the constant recollection of your form, which is inlaid with the entirety of the universe, is the sole remedy for the diseases of worldly existence, are truly seated in happiness. (3)
"Without remainder" means: the medicine for the afflictions of existence—the fevers and torments of saṃsāra.
Because it is "pervaded by the universe," the remembrance of your body is capable of performing every kind of assistance;
those who possess that remembrance—which consists of immersion (*samāveśa*)—are those who remember your true nature as the conscious self (*cidātman*) through its pervasive presence.
Seated in bliss: even while the touch of suffering remains inseparable from the body and other such factors, they abide solely in happiness, which is a mass of supreme bliss. || 3 ||
He whose white parasol is the moon, filled with its own radiance,
and whose fly-whisk is the stream of the celestial river— he alone is the Supreme Lord.

(21) Regarding the term *sitātapatra*: the moon, which consists of the form of all objects of knowledge (*meyarūpa*), has attained fullness through its own radiance—the rays of consciousness—during the state of manifestation (*prakāśadaśā*); its [light] is white and pure.

And because it is attached to its own self, it protects from the "sun" (ātapa)—that is, from the heat arising from the conceptualization of what is to be rejected and what is to be accepted by bound souls (paśu); thus, it is an "umbrella" (ātapatra). Likewise, the "celestial river" (svardhunī) is the power of consciousness (cicchakti) flowing through the midst [of existence]; it shakes off (dhunoti) heaven (svaḥ), that is, the celestial realm, and hell as characterized by it—the fruits of merit and demerit. Because it has the nature of spreading forth, it is a "stream" (srotas) for him.
The fly-whisk (*cāmara*) is the cause for the proclamation of his majesty; he alone, and no other, is the Supreme Lord (*parama īśvara*).
From a gross perspective, it is clear that the crescent moon filled with its own rays and the Gaṅgā are his unique parasol and fly-whisk respectively. || 4 ||
O Lord, bestow upon me some indescribable vision— luminous, cool, solitary, and pure like a digit of the moon— that flows with the stream of nectar.

"O Lord, grant me that vision— consciousness— which is luminous, cool, self-manifesting, cooling by removing all torment, pure, dispelling the fear of duality, unique and without a second, some unprecedented stream of nectar, and flowing with immortality."
"Give it! In the case of the "digit of the moon" (śaśikalā), the explicit meaning is clear due to the pun (*śliṣṭokti*). || 5 ||
O Blessed One, how is it that these droplets of consciousness fallen from the ocean of Your consciousness-bliss are so beautiful, like the taste of nectar? (6)

"O Consciousness-Bliss! [This means: From you, the ocean of consciousness-bliss (*cidānanda*), those droplets of awareness (*saṃvittivipruṣaḥ*)—the minute particles of cognition such as [the perception of] blue or pleasure—which, because they are manifest, consist essentially of consciousness-bliss, have fallen forth and issued out;
how is it that these, beautiful as the tasting of nectar, do not become for us simultaneously radiant?
The meaning is that they indeed come into being. || 6 ||
O Lord, O Master, our hearts have not been submerged in the essence of passion for you;
those whose hearts are not so [turned] are indeed heartless, and such as they are become objects of contempt.

"In you, passion" means the essence of passion—that is, the flow of devotion—toward you. Those whose hearts have not sunk into, or been permeated by, that [devotion] are those whose hearts lack the true reality.
"Such as these," being vessels for the afflictions of saṃsāra, are objects of contempt and truly not to be counted among those who possess devotion. (7)
He with whom you, the Lord, have achieved a union of hearts,
is the sole supreme recipient of all sovereign splendors.

"By the Lord," etc. This statement is made as a counterpoint to the previously mentioned view. "Of whom" means of some particular person. The plural number is not used here because those who lack a [receptive] heart are generally many. "Fusion of hearts" (*hṛdayamelana*) is oneness through immersion (*samāveśa*).
"Abundances" (*vibhūtayaḥ*) are the riches of non-dual bliss. And for whom there is a fusion of hearts with a worldly lord—
By means of a pun (śleṣa), it is suggested that he alone, and no other, is the vessel for such powers (vibhūtis). || 8 ||
Then, the flood of the nectar of meditation upon you equally washes away all joys and sorrows, just as water flows down ever-lower ground.
Regarding the phrase "of joys": Your meditation, which consists of absorption and is the very thought of You, is the city of nectar.

Just as it simultaneously floods all levels—whether low or higher—the various grounds of *māyā* and *avidyā*, both pure and impure, thereby bringing about their state of aesthetic equilibrium (*sāmarasya*), so too does it flood worldly sorrow, joy, and the like.
For one who has entered [into that state], everything arises simultaneously as consisting of the pervasion of supreme bliss;
it is like a flood of water which submerges both the lowlands and the highlands of the earth. || 9 ||
O Lord, how could those not possess a state overflowing with an abundance of happiness, for whom there is nowhere any separation from You, who are greater than their own selves? 10.

"What state indeed would not belong to them?"—the meaning is this: for those who are never separated from You, who shine as a mass of consciousness after having submerged the body and so forth within Yourself, who are superior to the self, what kind of state filled with an abundance of happiness and full of supreme bliss would there not be? Indeed, every [state] belongs to them. They are always living and never separated from the Lord.
They become happy. || 10 ||
(23) "I roar indeed, I dance; my heart's desires are fulfilled! For this master of mine has been obtained—one who is exceedingly pleasing. (11)

"I am indeed roaring!"—this is an utterance of one who is reeling with the bliss of the rasa of supreme devotion. "Exceedingly pleasing" means most dear. "This one" refers to that which is established through one's own direct experience and is impossible to describe in words. And thus, because you are exceedingly pleasing, possessing a body of intensely radiant light by virtue of swallowing the universe, you have become my Lord.

Through this immersion, I have attained [the goal]; therefore, I roar with a great sound, I utter [cries], and I dance with an abundance of overflowing joy. I perform a movement of the limbs whose essence is the shaking off of all states of illusion and negligence.
And my desires are fulfilled; the meaning is that I have become free from longing. "Bata" (alas/joy) is used here.
Through the recognition of the nature of the unsurpassed consciousness, it resounds with the entry into the seal of wonder. || 11 ||

Where there is no other object of knowledge and no action, and where there is no other yoga apart from consciousness—therein knowledge arises; rather, the singular, perfect consciousness of the universe unfolds.

"There is no other object of knowledge (*vedya*). The meaning is this: such is my Lord who has been realized, that while that Lord exists, there is no other distinct object of knowledge, no other action, no other yoga, and no other consciousness (*vidā*); nothing at all appears to me apart from the realized Lord. In the phrase "action and consciousness," the word "other" (*anyā*) is to be construed with each. In that state, [the Lord] is full.

He says, "It is indeed so. However, that which is knowledge is the single, complete oblation (*pūrṇāhuti*) for the universe, which kindles the fire of consciousness; this knowledge is, in other words, the very nature of the power of action (*kriyāśakti*) consisting of the reflective awareness of the full "I" (*ahaṃparāmarśa*).
And that which is such knowledge is precisely this manifestation of consciousness (*cittva*), which is the nature of the light of Śiva, and nothing else.

According to the scriptures, yoga is not one thing and action another; for that intellect which is established in reality is called "action" when it brings about the pacification of the latent impressions of one's own mind. (12)
From the hands of those from whose speech the sound of "Śiva" ever resounds, endless and difficult-to-conquer sufferings have suddenly fled away.

Regarding the phrase "of those difficult to conquer" (*durjayānām*): by the expression "fled from the hand," it is intimated that those whose speech is devoid of the resonance of Śiva are overcome by all forms of suffering. Thus it is said: "From Brahmā down to a worm," and so forth.
From Brahmā down to a mere insect, no one is truly happy; everyone, desiring to live, undergoes various transformations. (13)
There is no other Supreme Person distinguished by being a remnant of you;
you alone are the Great Person, the refuge of all persons without exception. (14)

Regarding the phrase "the Supreme Person": Hari is well known as Puruṣottama (the Supreme Person). He is distinguished—that is, rendered specific—by a nature other than that which is obtained through your remnant (*śeṣa*), namely by his own essential nature (*svarūpa*) as the substrate (*adhiṣṭhāna*) within those subjects who are the presiding deities of the non-dual essence-knowledge (*abhedasāravidyā*). Thus says the scripture of the Vaiṣṇavas: *Vaiṣṇavyāstu...* [The Vaiṣṇava [scriptures]...]

"Viṣṇu is remembered. You are the "Great Person" (mahāpuruṣa) because you are the refuge of all persons without exception, from Sakala up to Sadāśiva. The word "anya" has the sense of "some"; "eka" means "without a second. Such is the meaning of one verse. The other [verse], however, [is explained] by way of grammatical derivation (vyākaraṇaprakriyā).

The supreme person (*uttamapuruṣa*), who exists for our sake, has become qualified by being distinguished from the second and first persons (*madhyama* and *prathama*) which belong to "you" (*yuṣmad*); and he is distinct from that first person who is an external referent and oriented toward the object of "you."

This is the distinction regarding the middle person (*madhyama-puruṣa*) and the others: that they have as their locus all persons, and that they are the resting place (*viśrānti-dhāmatva*) for them. This is because everything that is to be reflected upon as "this-ness" (*idantā*) comes to rest precisely within "I-ness" (*ahantā*). Thus, in cases such as the intention to express "he cooks," "you cook," or "I cook," [it is ultimately] we ourselves who cook, and so forth.

Let it suffice to say that this is precisely the intended meaning in the practical application [of the term]. You, however, are the substratum of the unconditioned consciousness (*akalpita-cid-rūpa*) for all the conditioned (kalpita) first, middle, and third persons (*puruṣa*).
As it is stated in the *Pratyabhijñā*: "The two objects—the grasped and the grasper—which are non-different, appear within the subject (*pramātṛ*)."
For this very reason, you alone are the Great Person (Mahāpuruṣa) and Maheśvara, because the word "Great" (Mahat) applies to you just as it does to Mahādeva. || 14 ||
Victorious are those servants of yours, O Lord, who are worthy of worship by the world;
for them, this very ocean of worldly existence is but a great pleasure-lake.
"They are victorious" (p. 25).
They are victorious because they possess the state of being worshipped by the world, which arises solely from immersion into Śiva. O All-pervasive One, those who are Thy servants are victorious;
for them, even this ocean of saṃsāra—which is otherwise exceedingly terrible—is known in its ultimate reality as being of the nature of consciousness.
He is like a great lake for divine play (*krīḍā*). As it has been said: "Or rather, he whose consciousness perceives the entire world as play," and so forth. (15)
Let other forms of wretchedness experienced by those dwelling here be set aside for a moment;
you alone, by manifesting yourself, cause us shame by this very act. (16)

"Let those other [desires] rest for now"—that is, other forms of wretchedness such as the longing for powers like *aṇimā*. For those who delight in Your being (*bhavajjuṣām*), whose own nature is perpetually expanding through constant immersion (*samāveśa*), there is consequently an absence of anything else to be sought; thus, by the very words "may You manifest," [the devotees mean] "may You manifest at some time for those who have attained immersion."
Since one feels shame for that which ought to be prayed for, then by the logic of the "stick and the cake" (the simultaneous implication of both), there is no possibility of any other wretchedness;
there is nothing beyond me, and even in that state, I am a reciter (jāpaka). Because of that unity, you sometimes indicate with a rosary of beads that "recitation" is the ultimate reality.

Regarding the statement "there is nothing higher than Me in this system": some may be deluded into thinking that even for the Great Lord (Maheśvara) there is another deity to be recited due to his connection with the rosary (*akṣamālā*). To enlighten them, [the Lord] says: "There is indeed nothing higher than Me. Nevertheless, I am the reciter;

therefore, through oneness—that is, through identity with consciousness (*cidabheda*)—recitation in the ultimate sense consists of the reflective awareness of full subjectivity (*pūrṇāhantā-vimarśa*).
"He is eternally risen" means that you indicate or declare this by means of a rosary (*akṣamālā*) in certain works such as the *Gaurīśvara*.

Here, the word "that" (*tat*) implies the word "which" (*yat*). Alternatively, it means by means of a rosary—that is, by the sequence of the Mistress (*Karaṇeśvarī*)—for the sake of achieving the succession of creation and dissolution within the entire multitude of objects, which revolves again and again.

Through unity, by means of the method of great significance, and through oneness that is the essence of differentiation, the recitation becomes the essence of supreme reflective awareness; thus, you instruct [the disciple] by means of the rosary itself, according to the logic of the system of phonemes and letters. || 17 ||
O Lord, that which is existent must necessarily be preceded by the supreme non-existent;
and since You are other than both the non-existent and the existent, You are composed of both existence and non-existence. (18)

"Truly, it must be so. Existence and non-existence are mutually distinct. You are different from and characterized differently from non-existent things such as a sky-flower, and from existent things such as blue or pleasure; you are a mass of consciousness and bliss. Therefore, you consist of both existence and non-existence—you are the self of the universe, being of the nature of existence, yet also of the nature of non-existence, and even of the nature of both existence and non-existence, rather than being of the nature of existence alone.

Or rather, it is of a non-existent form, or indeed devoid of both; thus, in the *Śrībhargaśikhā*, beginning with "It is neither existent, nor non-existent, nor both existent and non-existent, nor even devoid of both," it concludes by describing that state as being truly indefinable: "For that state is difficult to know; it is some indescribable Absolute."

By the verse beginning with "viśvottīrṇa," the distinction from the two extremes of existence and non-existence—those which are to be contemplated as the states of being and non-being—is stated; by this [verse], however, its transcendence of all existence and non-existence is expressed. 18.
Possessing a pure radiance exceeding the rays of a thousand suns, though you pervade all the worlds, you are not seen. (19)

He is superior even to the rays of a thousand suns, for He is the light that illumines them as well. His light is pure, consisting solely of consciousness, and is characterized by abundance and excellence. For this very reason, He pervades all worlds.
Though He shines, He is not seen by those deluded by *māyā*; that is to say, He is not recognized. || 19 ||
In this inert world, You are indeed of the nature of consciousness; though an object of knowledge, You are the knower.
Since You are all-pervading even within the limited, therefore, O Lord, You are the supreme among all.

"In the inert world": the connection is that since you are the conscious knower and the all-pervasive one within the inert world—comprising everything from the earth up to Sadāśiva—which is both an object of knowledge and a limited measure, therefore you are the supreme of all. || 20 ||
(27) Enough with other lamentations; O Lord, I shall proclaim only this before you. O Master, though I know it thus, I am utterly bewildered. (21)

"Enough! [Thus he says. Though one is subject to the state of emergence (*vyutthāna*) and, even while knowing the reality of immersion (*samāveśa*), thinks "I am deluded," may I become subject to immersion during that very emergence. May there be auspiciousness! (21)
Thus ends the commentary composed by the venerable Kṣemarāja on the third hymn, titled *Praṇayaprasādana*, within the *Stotrāvalī* (Garland of Hymns) composed by the illustrious teacher Utpaladeva.
Oṃ! Though you are fickle, O mind,
you are nevertheless to be praised because you take refuge even in those who are themselves refuges.
The teacher of the world, the beloved of Ambikā. || 1 ||

"Oṃ, you are fickle. Even if, due to your fickleness, you do not take root in the worship of the Blessed One, nevertheless, you have achieved your purpose; for even a moment's service to Him bestows complete pervasion. For this very reason, the phrase "even of those who have sought refuge" proclaims the extraordinary nature of the Blessed One. Of those who have sought refuge...

He is the refuge and the ultimate resort even for Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and others; the teacher of the universe and the one worthy of worship—the Preceptor of the three worlds. Ambikā is the supreme Śakti. || 1 ||
Having ascended the various steps of the deities and reached the feet of Śiva,
yet having descended to even a lower level, it is a marvel that I have not abandoned [this state] even today.

"Having transcended" (ullaṅghya): having transcended—that is, having made into a state of rest—the very sequence of steps consisting of the various deities in the forms of Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Rudra, Īśvara, Sadāśiva, and so forth; [this refers to] the goal (upeya), that which is to be attained.

Although I have embraced the rays of Śiva’s feet— which are to be attained in one's own proximity— by means of universal immersion (samāveśa), it is a wonder that even now I do not abandon this most inferior state, which has fallen from emergence (vyutthāna) into the subjectivity of the illusory body and so forth. [Of the deities...]

By demonstrating that [other systems] are not to be accepted through the sequence of steps, while the Blessed One’s system is the most worthy of acceptance by taking refuge at his feet, he proclaims his own praiseworthiness through that very refuge. || 2 ||
Reveal your own path and completely shroud the activities of all the worlds,
O Blessed One, so that I may become—
Through this hymn, the servant is instantly and eternally risen. || 3 ||

"Reveal! [He says: "Conceal completely—that is, extinguish entirely—your own path, which is the Śākta way, and my deeds as the knower of the entire world, including the categories of objects of knowledge and subjects of knowledge, ending with Sadāśiva;
until I become your servant, ever risen."
"I shine forth, ever absorbed and intent upon the worship of your feet"—thus far [is the meaning]. || 3 ||
O Śiva, Śiva, Śambhu, Śaṅkara,
you who are affectionate toward those who have come for refuge, quickly show compassion!
[Upon] your pair of lotus feet—
For one who is intent on mindfulness, prosperity is indeed not far off.

"O Śiva, Śiva! Your pair of feet consists of knowledge and action; they are a pair of rays. Prosperities—whose essence is immersion (samāveśa) and which consist of supreme bliss—are not far off, but very near. || 4 ||
Those who, reclining upon the seat of your lotus feet,
fashion the world according to their own desire.
O Lord, they laugh at Viriñci, who is uncontrollable and defiled by the impurity of office.
"O You whose feet... [means: those rays of light, which are intent upon contraction and expansion, rest within Your feet;
from that very source, having tasted sovereignty, they fashion the universe according to their own desire through the method of the unfolding of the Mistress of the Senses (Karaṇeśvarī).
They [fashion] Viriñci—Brahmā—who is completely smeared by the impurity of office (adhikāra-mala), and for this very reason...

Because they are dependent on destiny, they are not self-possessed and lack autonomy; O Lord, O autonomous one! Even the Lotus-Seated One (Brahmā) laughs at them—the meaning is that they become objects of his laughter. || 5 ||
O Blessed One, nothing whatsoever is distinct from Your luminous form, nor can anything fail to manifest; therefore, it is always fully attained by You.
The Lord is even further removed from primordial nature (prakṛti). || 6 ||

Regarding the phrase "tvaprakāśavapuṣaḥ" (whose body is Your own light): O Lord, although You are remote from primordial nature (*prakṛti*) and thus unattainable because of Your self-concealment, You are nevertheless always attained by us—this is the ellipsis. For whatever is capable of appearing or shines forth, that does not exist in reality apart from You, whose body is light and whose nature is consciousness (*cidrūpa*).

The distinction exists only within that which consists of light, because it is that alone which is capable of being manifested. As it has been stated: "Since the individual soul (jīva) consists of everything," and so on, up to the end: "The enjoyer himself always abides everywhere in the form of the enjoyed. (6)
Some have approached the nectar of your lotus feet with a disposition tainted by dualism, while others experience it immediately.
It appeared as two bodies with unimpaired forms, yet devoid of duality.

Regarding the phrase "pādapaṅkaja": some who are established in duality, being exhausted by the sense of difference, [attain] the nectar of Your lotus feet—which consist of the two rays of knowledge and action—suddenly, through the failure to obtain worldly enjoyments. (p. 30)

They have approached— that is, attained— that whose nature is a state of existence reduced almost to the condition of a conch-shell (śukti), yet they do not experience it immediately. However, others, purified by the descent of the supreme power (para-śaktipāta), experience that which has suddenly appeared— flashing forth, presented, possessing an unimpaired form, eternally radiant in its essential nature, free from duality, and a single mass of consciousness-bliss (cidānanda).
"They are amazed. The word "some" (kecit) implies a depreciation, while "even some" (kecana api) suggests an elevation. || 7 ||
O Lord, that splendor of Yours which shines like lightning, which at times appears as if smeared with nectar—
if that were indeed to become perfectly stable, then...
You have been worshipped according to the prescribed rite; what more need be said? || 8 ||

"O Lord, like lightning... O Lord, Your radiance is the supreme vibration of Śakti. Smeared with nectar—that is, augmented by supreme bliss—it occasionally flashes before me for a mere moment when immersion (*samāveśa*) manifests.
If that [radiance], having cast aside powerful emergence (*vyutthāna*), were to become eternally arisen, then [one would attain] according to the rule, in accordance with reality.
"You have been honored. This means: "What else remains to be accomplished? And the state of having fulfilled one's purpose has arisen?"
"Everything else belonging to him is inferior; there is no object whatsoever,
whether real or unreal"— thus has he resolved here with great wisdom, exactly as it is.
May you likewise become clearly manifest to me. || 9 ||

"Thou art all. Thou art all—the other [external] object, whether it be a real entity or a non-entity; for there is nothing whatsoever that exists, since everything is manifested as consisting of light due to its being a mass of consciousness (*cidghana*). Thus, by means of this great wisdom consisting of pure knowledge (*śuddhavidyā*), thou [art present] here in this world.
Just as it has been determined by me, so may You become manifest to me even during the state of emergence (*vyutthāna*), through the power of immersion (*samāveśa*). (9)
O Blessed One, I have been made to set foot upon my own path by the Lord himself through his own will;
how then can I behave like an ordinary person?
I perceive nothing that is worthy of your feet.

"By my own will alone. O Blessed One, I have been made to take my place—made to attain rest—on my own path, the way of the unfolding power (*vikasvara-śakti*), by the Lord himself and not by anyone else, through his own will, that is, by means of the method of the independent descent of power (*nirapekṣa-śaktipāta*). How then am I acting? I act in the state of emergence (*vyutthāna*) just like an ordinary person.
I speak; yet, by the force of absorption, I understand nothing that is worthy of Your feet or appropriate for the intimacy of Your rays. || 10 ||
O Lord, some among them possess that supreme and auspicious state which expands within their hearts;
they are like cātakas for the thundering sound of the cloud of Your stories.
By which even they were made fortunate for a long time. || 11 ||

"Kopi" (something indescribable): O Lord, among those aforementioned devotees, within the hearts of some, a certain supreme (*uttama*) and most excellent (*utkṛṣṭa*) state of blessedness belonging to You unfolds—a certain intensity of the surging essence of bliss—by which even they [become so], their hearts being permeated by immersion (*samāveśa*); and for this very reason...

Your very discourse is like the roar of clouds; and like *cātaka* birds, our hearts—though already gladdened by hearing the unfolding stories of Śiva that inspire such total absorption (*samāveśa*)—have been rendered fortunate for a long time and brought to the ground of such absorption merely by your words. For, by the mere mention of your story...
The meaning is that absorption descends. || 11 ||
In those who delight in you, this passion has reached full maturity through some inscrutable play of yours.
When conversation and remembrance regarding one who is separated bear fruit as a festival of reunion on the ground of separation, that is true love. (12)

Regarding the phrase *tvajjuṣām*: by means of the play (*līlayā*) characterized by unsurpassed immersion (*anuttara-samāveśa*), those who "serve you with affection" (*tvajjuṣām*) are those who worship you with love. "This" (*eṣaḥ*) refers to an extraordinary passion that has reached full maturity. In the state of separation from you—that is, during the period of emergence (*vyutthāna*)—the conversation and the recollection [of you] act as the agents that bring about the festival of union, the state of sexual enjoyment (*sambhoga-daśā*).
By the statement, "It bears fruit as a festival of union in the land of separation," the extraordinary nature of this passion is suggested. || 12 ||
The word "Śaṅkara," which has been nourished by the sprinkling of various aesthetic sentiments and uttered hundreds of times,
enters even the minds of animals.
Even in these [cases], this has ever-new purposes. || 13 ||
Victorious are those who wander within the sphere of bliss, in whom the sound of Śiva is ever present—
like the moon emerging from the ocean of nectar.
And it flows forth as sweet, supreme nectar.

This pair of verses [concludes] with the words "those who wonder are victorious. They are victorious in whom the abode of Śiva exists, wandering having made it certain and fixed within the circle of bliss; which perfectly flows with the supreme, sweet nectar and causes the essence of bliss to surge forth. Of what kind? From the reservoir of nectar.

Emanated from the form of the Supreme Lord, who is the directly realized mass of consciousness, and uttered by His own spontaneous nature—just as the moon, the bearer of nectar, emanates from its reservoir into its orb.
Vibrating intensely, it flows with the supreme, most delicious nectar; nourished by the sprinkling of the essence of the wondrous immersion,
this very word "Śaṅkara," though uttered hundreds of times,
serves ever-new purposes even within the hearts of animals and those dwelling in the state of bound souls (paśus), producing at every moment a corresponding and unprecedented marvel.
It enters and vibrates. || 13 || 14 ||
This formidable world appears as if completely finished;
the dense impurity of the mind has dissolved. Yet, even so, there is no [end] to the gate-towers of your city—
