Not even the slightest rattling of the door or its bolt [should occur]. || 15 ||

"‘As if completely finished’—this statement is made by one who possesses the impression (*saṃskāra*) of a throbbing, fresh immersion (*samāveśa*) and desires to descend to the plane of emergence (*vyutthāna*). ‘Terrible’ means fearsome because it consists of duality.
‘The universe (*jagat*), as if completely finished’: for to one who is immersed, the external universe does not appear; and yet—"

The word "as it were" (iva) is used because he remains as one whose residual impressions (*saṃskāra*) persist. Furthermore, the dense and continuous impurity of the mind, consisting of the subtle portion of ignorance (*avidyā-kalā*), has dissolved. Nevertheless, [he is] composed of the bliss of the world arising from Great Knowledge (*mahā-vidyā*), which is fully blossomed and consists of the entire universe that has been completely pacified without remainder.

Because it fills the city-like body, that which is the gateway—the city-gate—is the form of the Supreme Power (*parāśakti*). In this regard, there is not even the slightest [need for] the opening of the door-panels joined by a bolt, nor the splitting apart of the two very firm leaves of renown; by this, one attains the Supreme State in which all residual impressions (*saṃskāra*) of the body and so forth have completely dissolved away.
It resonates with the very ground as that which is to be grasped. As it is said in the *Śrī-Pratyabhijñā*: "But in every way, it is merged within," and so forth;
and in the earlier scripture: "Śiva is to be known as transcending all; having known Him, one is liberated. (15)
O Lord, perform some slight act for those whose hearts long to behold the interior of your lotus-face, which is perpetually in bloom.
By which [power] you manifest yourself standing before me. || 16 ||

Regarding the word "satata" (p. 34): according to the established principle that "the lotus of your face, which is perpetually blooming and eternally expanded, is here called the mouth of Śiva," the interior of that lotus which is the form of your supreme power (*parā-śakti*)—that is its *udara*.

The "Middle" is Your supreme form, consisting of the aesthetic identity (*sāmarasya*) with the Supreme Power (*paraśakti*), which is the nature of Śambhu; the "beholding" of that is immersion (*samāveśa*). For me, whose mind is intensely longing—that is, possessed of an extraordinary desire—for that, please perform some inconceivable demonstration of means, even if it were merely a slight gesture, by which—
Standing directly before me, you manifest. || 16 ||
What other happiness indeed is there here than the realization of non-difference from you? Or what other prosperity could there be?
Therefore, for one who is your servant in this world, what else is needed?
The mind goes astray, having abandoned her. || 17 ||

Regarding the phrase "of the mind that perceives no difference from You": for one whose non-dual consciousness of You has burst forth through immersion (*samāveśa*), there exists no other pleasure, nor any such thing as supernatural power (*vibhūti*) and so forth; for that very consciousness surpasses all else. What follows from this?
Why does the mind of Your servant turn toward a wrong path, having abandoned that consciousness which is non-different from You?
It rushes toward the very plane of emergence. || 17 ||
I shall certainly not be a vessel for your servitude here even for a moment; rather,
with devotion, [I seek] the wine of the essence of non-difference from you—
If I were not to savor this constantly. || 18 ||

"Even for a moment": if I were not to incessantly taste the wine of the essence of the bliss of Your non-duality, then I would not be a fit vessel for Your servitude even for a single moment, because of my lack of acquaintance with Your own nature, which is a mass of bliss. || 18 ||
Indeed, people do not perceive your body, which consists of truth, because it is defiled by the vision of duality.
Even so, O Knower of All, who is compassionate toward those who take refuge in you, why do you not hear this wailing of mine? 19.

"It is said that 'not [so]'—this person, first of all, because it is defiled by the vision of duality, does not see Your true form, which is a mass of consciousness. Nevertheless, You are all-knowing, omniscient, affectionate toward those who take refuge in You, and favorable to Your devotees;
for this very reason, why do You not hear my wailing and lamentation, even though I myself am crying out for the gift of the vision of Your own appropriate Self?"
First, may there be a sudden vision of You; he thus prays that You might hear even the mere cry of one whose heart is overwhelmed by devotion. || 19 ||
O Lord, do you remember even once that which was desired by me, or rather,
that the pleasure of the sense objects was ever requested by me?
For I have always sought only the constant beholding of your form.
"Give me that beloved one who has died; it is enough. (20)

"Do you remember?"— by this unreserved speech, "O Lord, do you remember even that sensual pleasure which was sought after, acquired through effort, and desired by me at any time," she intimates her deep intimacy with the Master.
"O God, it is only the nectar of beholding your form..."
Grant, bestow, that very elixir which reveals Your true nature, which is most desired. || 20 ||
O Maheśa, it is said that the very moment I was placed by Your will upon Your auspicious path,
hundreds of blessings arose within me at that very instant.
What else, O Lord, shall I seek from you? || 21 ||

*Kileti* means: on the auspicious path (*śivādhvan*) which abounds in hundreds of blessings; on the supreme path of Śakti (*parame śākte mārge*); one who has "set foot" (*kṛtapadaḥ*) there is one who has attained rest (*prāptaviśrāntiḥ*). || 21 ||
When that sun does not set together with all the others, beginning with the moon;
Victorious is that certain Śivarātri, whose form is radiant with the spreading effulgence of its own light.
Regarding the word *yantra*: that is a certain transcendent Śivarātri, the ground of immersion into Śiva.
It is called "night" (*rātri*) because it is like night due to the withdrawal of the entire manifestation of *māyā*. Of what nature is it?
It is that whose form is characterized by luminosity through the expansion of its own radiance—that is, through the unfolding of the light of consciousness (*citprakāśa*).

Such is he. He, the first sprout of the entire phenomenal world (*prapañca*), is Vivasvat, the vital breath (*prāṇa*). Together with the moon and others—representing the downward breath (*apāna*) and so forth—he sets, that is, he subsides. Alternatively, Vivasvat is the light of the means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*); the moon and others are the objects of knowledge (*prameya*) and so forth. || 22 ||
O Lord of the Immortals, I consider even the sovereignty over the three worlds that I have acquired to be entirely tasteless compared to Your feet.
Deprived of the nectar-like essence of touch. || 23 ||
"Even so": I consider even the sovereignty over the three worlds to be tasteless without the touch of your rays. (23)
Alas, O Lord! This firm bond of the self, consisting of the non-recognition of You, was fashioned by You alone;
for this [bond], though it was manifesting itself to me as You—
Without disregarding [the vow], it does not slacken even in the slightest degree. || 24 ||

He says: "It is a marvel! This conceit of being a cognizer (*pramātṛtābhimāna*) regarding the body and so forth—this bond of the self—is of the nature of your non-manifestation. It has been firmly fashioned by you alone, who perform the most difficult of tasks; it is not the power of any other."

The meaning is that because [the mind], having disregarded and subordinated you— who are shining forth even at the very moment of immersion— does not slacken even slightly, it maintains its predominance precisely during the state of emergence. || 24 ||
O Lord of the Immortals, though you are constantly being worshipped by the great ones, you remain as the singular form of the worshipper;
you are perceived here both externally and internally.
You are eternally manifest within the very body of the observer.

Regarding the phrase "of the great ones": at the occasion of external and internal worship and so forth, because [the Lord] manifests precisely through the distinction of the initial encounter (*āpāta*),

O Lord of the Immortals, O God of gods, you— while being worshipped and being perceived— are the singular form of the worshipper for the great ones who possess devotion, and the very body of the beholder.

Through the state of aesthetic fusion (*sāmarasya*) in total immersion (*samāveśa*), you abide and you manifest as the singular form of the subject consisting of pure consciousness; may there be auspiciousness! (25)
Thus ends the commentary composed by Kṣemarāja on the fourth hymn, titled *Surasodbalana*, within the *Stotrāvalī* (Garland of Hymns) composed by the venerable teacher Utpaladeva.

Oṃ! O Lord, grant that I, who am attached solely to the enjoyment of contact with Your lotus feet, may enter Your own abode by means of the *galepādika* [the practice of being smeared with ashes from head to foot]. 1.
Oṃ, thus [it is said]. The "feet" are the rays. "Enjoyment arising from mere contact" is the savoring of immersion (*samāveśa*).

The "application of ointment to the neck and so forth" refers to the process of the descent of power (*śaktipāta*) through forceful means (*haṭha*). One's own abode is the nature of consciousness (*citsvarūpa*), by virtue of its inherent fitness (*aucityāt*). || 1 ||
When shall I have my hair colored by the mass of pollen from the lotus-feet of Your Honor, and perform a dance commenced with boundless impetuosity? (2)

"Bhavat" means: with the dust of your lotus-feet—the pollen of the lotus of the Supreme Power (Para-Śakti) engaged in bestowing grace—one whose hair is colored, that is, whose inner being is perfumed; one in whom the sprouts of the eight upward-radiating powers (ūrdhvāṣṭa-śakti) are burgeoning; and for that very reason...
Through the power of intense joy, he has suddenly commenced and instantly set in motion a dance— an agitation of the limbs that shakes off the state of being a limited subject through illusion—
by means of which he aspires to the blossoming of eternal immersion. || 2 ||
O Blessed One, having you as my sole protector, I always request only this:
may I dwell within you as one who is mute, and never otherwise, even if I am wise. (3)

"Having You alone as my Lord"—this much alone I pray for, and nothing more. That is, one for whom You alone are the Lord, the one being sought after and desired. May I, even though mute, abide within You, fully immersed in Your own nature which is a mass of consciousness;
otherwise, may I not be a wise man, even if I am learned. (3)
"O treasure-house of nectar, O Lord! O delicious one, O Three-eyed One!
O sweet-tasting one, O Virūpākṣa!"—thus crying out, I would dance.
"Aho!"—as before, he expresses his aspiration for eternal immersion. O ocean of nectar, O sea of bliss!
O you who have fallen into words of exquisite wonder! O taste of uninterrupted sweetness! "In the dance"—as before—he exclaims, clearly perceiving [the Lord]. (4)
With my eyes closed by the touch of your lotus feet, may I revel,
reeling from the intoxication of the wine of devotion to you. (5)

"O lotus-feet of yours!"—with the bliss of your power, my senses are turned inward. May I blossom forth by the emergence of the nature of consciousness; may I bend my limbs, that is, may I bring them to a state where consciousness is predominant. Of what kind [is this]?
It is the intoxication of wine, the wonder of *kādambarī*, which is that very devotion (*bhakti*) that arises when You are directly perceived.
By that, he was whirled around and brought to a state of great pervasion. || 5 ||
O Lord, may I dwell somewhere upon the mountain of my own mind, wherever that state exists—
a state consisting of your uninterrupted discourse and filled with the great aesthetic flavor (mahārasa).

Regarding the phrase "the mountain of the mind" (*cittabhūbhṛt*): the mind itself is a mountain by virtue of its being unassailable, its being the substratum for latent impressions (*vāsanā*), and its hardness. May I dwell upon some stage (*bhūmi*) belonging to that [mountain], which bestows discernment (*viveka*), where that aforementioned great aesthetic flavor (*mahārasa*) resides.
Her state or condition is such that her very nature consists of your constant awareness, which is a continuous and dense outpouring of your speech, filled with the bliss of immersion. || 6 ||
Wherever you, accompanied by the Goddess, were stationed— from the palace up to the city gate— there, in that city, I shall remain as a resident, assuming many forms.

"Where," etc.: in that city of yours, which is the filling [pūraka] and whose nature is the Self of Consciousness (cidātman), may I become an inhabitant, fully entered [into it]. From the lofty abode characterized by intuitive insight (pratibhā)—which is like a palace made of nectar within—from the gateway in the form of the objects of the senses up to the city-gate (gopura), you, accompanied by the Goddess, the Supreme Power (paraśakti), are eternally delighted.
"You dwell according to the principle beginning with 'There is no such fraction of life as that,' and so forth; you are the manifold-formed soul of the universe.
Here, by the power of resonance (*anuraṇana-śakti*), the worldly meaning of "to be served" (*paricārya*) is clear.
This should be followed accordingly in what follows as well. (7)
O Blessed One, may the rays of your solar splendor shine forth, so that this lotus of my heart may blossom for your worship. (8)
"May they shine forth" (samullasantu): the rays (*marīcayaḥ*) are the grace-bestowing powers (*anugrāhikāḥ śaktayaḥ*). "May it blossom" (*vikasatu*): may it attain pervasion (*vyāpti*).
For the sake of your worship, for the sake of immersion into your state (*tvatpadasamāveśāya*). || 8 ||
Be gracious, O Blessed One, for my mind, which has fallen forever at your feet,
seems as if it were fainting or as if it were perishing upon tasting each of those [realms].
"Be gracious!"—graciousness (*prasāda*) is the attainment of clarity through the subsiding of turbidity, just as with water.

The same applies to what follows. "Falling and rolling here and there upon Your Śākta path"—by describing how those various eyes [of Yours] are impossible to describe and are so expansive, it resonates with the reality of the experience; one feels as if they are melting or dissolving in the throat.

Thus, by means of the figures of speech *sasandeha* (doubtful), *utprekṣā* (poetic fancy), and the optative suffix (*liṅ*) expressing possibility, [the verse] suggests the hope for a state of being overwhelmed by the essence of unsurpassed bliss, as witnessed by one's own experience. || 9 ||
Whether out of great joy or out of grief, whether from a wall or even from a jar, whether from an external or an internal state, reveal yourself to me, O Lord! 10.

Regarding the phrase "out of great joy" (*praharṣāt*): by means of words such as "starting from" (*vā prabhṛti*), he says that we have no attachment to anything whatsoever, since [reality] manifests clearly from whatever source. O Lord (*prabho*), you whose nature is to manifest everywhere (*sarvataḥ prabhavanaśīla*). 10.
May that nectar of the touch of your lotus feet, which is exceedingly cool, flow for me always, both externally and internally. (11)
"Even outside" means that her lotus-feet are cool, as before. || 11 ||
May this indescribable enjoyment, which plunges one into the nectar-filled lake of contact with your feet and transcends all other worldly pleasures, be mine forever. 12.

"Touching Your feet": touching Your feet is the immersion into the power (*śakti*) of Rudra. That itself is a lake of nectar, an ocean of elixir. May that internal submersion or drowning therein be my extraordinary enjoyment forever. Of what kind? [An enjoyment] that encompasses all enjoyments, from this world up to the state of Sadāśiva.
He leaps over it because of its lack of flavor; one who possesses that character overcomes it. || 12 ||
"O Blessed One, please accept the passion and other afflictions offered by me;
having taken them and transformed them into nectar, partake of them together with your devotees. (13)

"Offered," it is said: O Blessed One, O Self consisting of consciousness! Whatever passion and so forth has been accumulated by me since beginningless saṃsāra—that has been offered to You, having been abandoned through the deceit of wealth; it has been known and understood in its entirety.
Therefore, accept its true nature; take it up, and abiding in Your self-luminous nature, hold it close to Yourself.

"Having made [it] immortal" means having flooded it with the nectar of contact with the Supreme Power (*paraśakti*). By the statement "together with the devotees," he expresses the hope that at the time of the pervasion of one's own immersion, all the devotees as well shall attain identification with that [state]. || 13 ||
O Lord, you who are eternally satisfied by consuming the entirety of all worlds, please accept from us, your servants, this moment of a glance of grace as a comfortable seat. 14.

Regarding the word *aśeṣa*: O Lord, you who are eternally satisfied by the consumption of all worlds (*aśeṣabhuvana*) and are a mass of supreme bliss (*paramānandaghana*), please grant the occasion for the sight of your grace—whose nature has been explained—to us, your servants;
that is, establish in us the fitness for manifestation. Of what kind [is that occasion]? It is that wherein one dwells with ease (*sukha*).
It consists of the pervasion of bliss. || 14 ||
With eyes closed in the savoring of the wonder of internal devotion, may I be satisfied even with blades of grass while worshipping with the words, "Salutation to me, who am Śiva. (15)
Regarding "inner devotion" (*antarbhakti*): as before, it means having one's eyes closed by the wonder of devotion within the fullness of the *ahantā* (I-consciousness).
Having performed the salutation, "Obeisance to Śiva, whose nature is consciousness, for me," may I perceive even blades of grass as Śiva while worshipping them. || 15 ||

May I also, having attained the state of being [your] own being, perceive the world as consisting of the radiance of my own self, and be joined even with the full enjoyment of the rasa of devotion. 16.
"Api" means: having attained "bhavad-bhāva," that is, identity with you; therefore, perceiving the universe—the entire world—whose very nature consists in the manifestation of one's own self as Śiva.

"May I never be separated from the full enjoyment of the aesthetic relish (*bhakti-rasa*) and the powerful wonders of spiritual immersion (*samāveśa*); for, according to the established tradition of the scriptures, obstacles (*vināyakas*) lead one toward transient enjoyments—lest such an obstacle to devotion, namely the obstacle of ego-identification with one's own self, should ever arise for me. (16)
O Protector, since there exists nothing else that could be desired by you,
it is fitting that you, who are without a second, possess complete perfection.
"Desirable" means that because you are free from all longing, you alone are perfectly complete. || 17 ||
May I attain that state where laughter and dance occur, where passion, hatred, and the like are consumed, and where the nectar-essence of devotion is drunk. (18)

"It is laughed at" means that, through the weight of internal exultation, the state of being a subject limited by the body and so forth is made to tremble. "It is enjoyed" means it is swallowed; by this, the subordination of the state of being a subject limited by the *puryaṣṭaka* (the eightfold subtle body) is expressed. "It is drunk" means it is made to marvel—that is, the nectar-like essence of devotion, the outpouring of the bliss of immersion (*samāveśa*). And for everyone...
That activity of eating and drinking, characterized primarily by laughter and dance, is indeed desirable; however, it is described here as being supramundane.
May the fragrance of the mental impressions from the flowers of contemplation on that unprecedented delight attain firmness in my mind, so that the scent of evil tendencies may perish. (18–19)

"Tattaditi" means: that very thought of you, which possesses a diverse, unprecedented, and supermundane fragrance—that is, joy—is itself the "perfume of flowers" because it is so desirable. May its firmness and deep-rooted growth take hold in my mind, so that all evil tendencies such as passion and the like may perish. || 19 ||
Where is passion for worldly desires and the like, and where is devotion to the lotus feet of Hara?
O immortal one, enlighten my heart, which thus relishes such a contradiction, so that it may find its own welfare.
"Where?

[He replies: "My heart is fond of contradiction: it is intent upon You during meditative absorption (*samāveśa*), yet during the state of emergence (*vyutthāna*) it is oriented toward sense objects. Instruct me on what is beneficial and make me discerning, so that during the state of emergence I may abandon the inclination toward passion and the like."
Having abandoned [all else], she remains devoted solely to you. || 20 ||

Even while in the stages of yoga characterized by discursive meditation (*vicāra*), though remaining withdrawn from sense objects, may my heart remain truly intoxicated by the wine of contemplation upon You alone. (21)

"Moving about" refers to the stages of yoga and the knowledges of the levels (*bhūmikās*). "Withdrawals from sense objects" refers to the restraints of the senses (*pratyāhāras*). Abiding therein, the intoxication of wine is simply the thought of you and the attainment of you; by that, he is made unsteady—deprived of the growth established in those various levels—like one who is drunk.

May I become one whose heart descends, even if only slightly, from its own state of wonder into some level of knowledge regarding the stages [of practice], by means of no other [means] than its own inherent marvel. By the word "api" (even), he expresses that this [descent] is not to be disregarded, as it occurs as a matter of course. || 21 ||
May the essence of devotion always be my forerunner in all circumstances—at all times—in speech, mind, and thought, as well as in bodily movements performed through the instruments of action. (22)

Regarding the word "speech" (*vāci*): the mental faculties (*manomatayaḥ*) are cognitions primarily characterized by conceptualization (*kalpanā*). Among those things produced by the instruments—the effects of the organs of intellect and action—since all activities are preceded by seeing, hearing, and so forth, the aesthetic flavor of devotion (*bhaktirasa*) is present everywhere, in all states, as the precursor, manifesting at the very outset.
The wonder of immersion. || 22 ||
O Lord, while this name of yours, "Śiva, Śiva, Śiva," is being recited without end,
may I become one who relishes [this state].
It is some kind of repetition of the great aesthetic flavor (mahārasa). || 23 ||
"Śiva"—when this is being recited, that is, when it is being contemplated as consisting of the supreme mantra; "in this," (p.
44) meaning in the unsurpassed reality whose sole witness is one's own direct experience; the repeated mention of the name indicates the state of being overwhelmed by total immersion (*samāveśa*).

It resounds. "Something" means that which is supramundane. Therefore, this great sound is non-repetitive within the realm whose nature is infinite consciousness, vibrating with ever-new bliss, wherein all dull paths have been completely swallowed up.
O you whose cheeks are composed of consciousness beyond all measure, may I, honored by you, wander about. 24.

Regarding the word *sphurat*: it refers to that which is throbbing, infinite, and undivided—the world (*viṣṭapa*) consisting of consciousness, the realm (*bhuvana*), the place of rest for the universe. Of what nature is it? It is one in which the entire, exhaustive expansion of the path (*adhvan*)—consisting of insentient objects of knowledge such as darkness and so forth—has been completely swallowed up on all sides. Likewise, the other [path], consisting of consciousness, has not been counted.

Where the city of Gaṇḍikā is located—since nothing else exists apart from the nature of consciousness whose essence is Śiva—the refutation of the doctrine of a separate Śiva is stated by this. Therein, may I wander with excellence; may I expand through immersion (*samāveśa*).
Of what sort? One who is intent solely on Your worship, O Lord, being beyond thought due to Your non-dual form. (24)
"Nothing whatsoever is required for that which is established as eternally present and radiantly manifest within one's own body"—
may this conviction become most firm.
For me, who am purified by the dust of your lotus feet... || 25 ||
Regarding the phrase "in one's own body": in one's own [self], which is the imperishable, nourishing essence of the nature of consciousness; which shines clearly as a mass of light;

and which is eternal and constant—nothing such as meditation, recitation, or the like is required to establish a state therein, precisely because it is of the nature already described. Such am I, purified by the dust of the lotus feet of Your Honor.

Through the constant practice of the expansion of the lotus of Your power, for one who is purified, the intellect—characterized by firmness and consisting of unwavering certainty—becomes supreme; that is to say, it becomes a single, dense mass of eternally arisen immersion (*samāveśa*). 25.
O Lord, something [ineffable] flashes forth at some time in the minds of those who touch the soles of Your feet.
Where this entire universe flows into the lake of nectar—there, may you always direct me. 26.

"Something or other": O Lord, for those who touch the soles of Your feet and are graced by the touch of Your power, at some opportune moment, that "something or other"—an extraordinary reality—flashes forth in the mind, wherein this entire universe dissolves into the ocean of supreme bliss and becomes one with it within the lake of the wise man's heart. Such is this [reality].
Always bestow and grant me that reality, so that I may become a mass of bliss through eternal immersion; may there be auspiciousness! 26.

Thus ends the commentary composed by the venerable Kṣemarāja on the fifth hymn, titled "The Instruction on One’s Own Power," within the *Stotrāvalī* (Garland of Hymns) composed by the illustrious teacher Utpaladeva.
Oṃ tat sat. Oṃ!
O Lord, may Your state of being ever-present before my eyes be granted to me, who am scorched by intense suffering even for a mere moment when separated from You. (1)

"Even for a mere moment" means: during a separation of even a single instant from the state of emergence [from meditation]. It refers to one who, due to being overwhelmed by intense passion, is tormented deeply and excessively, experiencing the heat himself, and not one who is merely helpless under the sway of sense objects. "Of my vision" means of my knowledge.
The meaning is that the word should flash forth clearly. || 1 ||
In this cycle of existence whose very essence is separation, may I never be separated from you, my beloved lord, even if I am separated from the entire world. (2)

"Regarding the word *viyoga* (separation): *aviyuktaḥ* means pervaded (*samāviṣṭaḥ*). Even though one is separated—that is, disjoined—from the universe, from the world beginning with the earth and ending with Śiva, in the state of immersion (*samāveśa*), the universe indeed becomes dissolved in reality. || 2 ||
"Whatever I go toward through body, speech, and mind—all that is you alone. May this ultimate reality also be ever-present for me in its full perfection. (3)

Regarding the word *kāya*: in whatever object you yourself are that [very thing], because its sole essence is consciousness (*cidekasāratvāt*). This is the ultimate reality (*paramārtha*), since it is taught in the scripture beginning with "in whatever [object]" and concluding with "because everything consists of Śiva. It is "perfectly full" (*paripūrṇa*) when directly realized through immersion (*samāveśa*). || 3 ||
Just as you are non-conceptual and filled with great bliss,
so may my speech, which offers praise to Bhava, be truly worthy of you.
"Non-conceptual" (nirvikalpa) means having the nature of pure consciousness. "Likewise" (tathā) means both non-conceptual and consisting of great bliss.
For this very reason, she is "congruent," being appropriately suited for praise. (4)
Perceiving every state of being as consisting of Bhava through immersion in Bhava, may I wander free from desire and filled with supreme joy. (5)
"Be!"—by the repetition "each and every state," there is an all-inclusive reference.

"Free from desire" is the reason expressed by means of an adjective, such as "exultation" and so forth. For it is precisely because of being completely filled with exultation, whose nature is supreme great bliss, that one becomes free from desire. || 5 ||
O Blessed One, I would be satisfied with seeing the entire world filled [with you]; therefore, I am not distressed by anything beyond that.

"O Blessed One! [He said. "By virtue of being related to You, who consist of consciousness (*cinmaya*), even a single part of Brahman does not transcend its universal form and is free from conceptual construction (*avikalpa*); thus, by this state of affairs, may I behold the entire world as full.
However, if the reading is *bhavatā pūrṇam*, the meaning is clear. [Thus he spoke,] being satisfied."

(47) From this [state], there arises a joy consisting of supreme bliss; for this reason, O Blessed One, you do not suffer weariness—meaning that you, the Self whose nature is consciousness, are not agitated by prayers for powers such as *aṇimā*. || 6 ||
May all phenomena shine within you alone, like fragments of clouds dissolving into the sky,
constantly tending toward the purity of the sequential stages.

Regarding the phrase "melting away": from the very source from which they emerged, they dissolve back into You alone, step by step, until nothing remains but their latent impressions (*saṃskāra*). It is like fragments of clouds in the sky; for they spread forth from that very place and dissolve back into it.

By the expression "having the nature of going," it is meant that they constantly and perpetually attain purity—the state of being the pure consciousness (*śuddhacidrūpa*)—through this gradual process.
This implies that their true nature is indeed the very essence of consciousness. || 7 ||
May some indescribable jewel of existence shine constantly for me from the midst of worldly life— a jewel whose spreading radiance destroys the continuous succession of darkness at its very borders.

"By Your own radiance": from within existence, that is, from the midst of the universe; "some indescribable one" refers to the pure nature of consciousness. You alone are the jewel; because You fulfill all desires, may You shine continuously by bringing about my state of non-emergence from absorption, manifesting through immersion by the expansion of Your own radiance—that is, by the vibration of Your own rays.
By whom the beginningless continuity of darkness, which proceeds from non-apprehension, has been destroyed. || 8 ||
Upon which stage do you not preside? What could that be which is not your body?
Therefore, without any effort, I shall find you everywhere through weariness [of seeking]. (9)

"Kāmi" means "I am weary"—weary of saṃsāra for a long time because my true nature has not been recognized. "Tvām" (you) refers to the one whose form is consciousness (*cid-rūpa*). "Aprayāsena" means without effort—that is, without the exertion of meditation, worship, and so forth. "Sarvataḥ" means from anywhere whatsoever; "avāpnuyām" means I may attain you through immersion (*samāveśa*) and take you as my own. "Yataḥ" [is used] because [I ask], "Which stage (*bhūmikā*) or state of being?"
You do not rest upon it, nor do you preside over it; therefore, what external or internal object could there be that is not your very body, your essential nature? (9)
O Lord, when this much has been attained, why should the enjoyment of embracing your limbs not be accomplished by my own will? What, then, have I not conquered? (10)

"Bhavad" means the touch of the supreme immersion (*paramasamāveśa*) through the embrace of the limbs. This occurs by one's own will, not merely occasionally. The meaning is: "Has everything not been conquered? I alone remain as the most excellent. || 10 ||
Reveal Yourself; do not cause us distress with other prayers, O Lord. We, though weary, seek You alone. 11.

"Manifest yourself! [The commentary explains: We do not cause any further distress or agitation through other requests or entreaties for you, our own self whose nature is consciousness (*cid-rūpa*), because, being exhausted and overwhelmed by intense passion, we seek and search for none other than you, who are of the nature of consciousness; therefore, manifest yourself.
"May Śiva be manifest! || 11 ||
Thus ends the commentary on the sixth hymn, titled "The Radiance of the Paths," within the *Stotrāvalī* composed by the venerable teacher Utpaladeva, as written by the venerable Kṣemarāja. || 6 ||
Oṃ! O Ānandasarasvatī, when my mind attains a state of equal flavor (samarasatā) with you, O Lord, may it instantly abandon this great calamity rooted in duality. || 1 ||
"In you" means in Ānandasarasvatī, the ocean of joy. "Equanimity" (samarasatām) refers to total absorption.
"Once" (sakṛt) means a single time; the meaning is that he should abandon it so that it does not occur again. This concludes the section ending with "iyantagāryantam. || 1 ||

O Lord, let the axe of the realization of oneness with You fall within me— that realization which cuts through the deeply rooted fetters of passion, hatred, and the like, born from the thought "this is mine" and "this is not mine."

(49) "This"—meaning: "May this happiness, which is the cause of that [bliss], be mine; but may this suffering, which is the cause of that [misery], not be mine. Thus, it refers to the shackles of bondage consisting of passion, hatred, and so forth, which take the form of grasping at distinctions.
Within the firm and solid root—that is, in the midst of one's own being—the conviction of oneness with Bhava is itself the axe, the hatchet for the realization of identity with Consciousness. || 2 ||
May the garland of stains of conceptual construction fall away; may unimpeded freedom shine forth within my heart.
O Blessed One, may my form become composed of consciousness, overflowing with the essence of bliss. (3)
"May it be unimpeded!"—because conceptual constructions (*vikalpa*) are characterized by a predominance of duality, they constitute a "stain.

May my consciousness-natured form (*cinmayī mūrtiḥ*), which is the state of the subject (*pramātṛtā*), be flooded with the essence of bliss (*ānandarasaplutā*), overflowing with the bliss of immersion (*samāveśa*). || 3 ||

May the Mother, who is the cultivation of devotion to You, nourish with her various nectars my body, which has been rolling within the cosmic egg of existence composed of passion and other afflictions.
So that I may become a bird with fully developed wings. || 4 ||

"Rāgādi" means: May Mother Ambikā, through the very contemplation of devotion to You, satiate and nourish me— who am wallowing, falling further and further down— within this egg of existence, this globe of saṃsāra consisting of passion and the like, with those various essences that are the core of supreme bliss, so that I may have my wings fully grown.

Having thoroughly attained the state of my own self, which consists of the knowledge and activity of pervasive [omnipresence], I become a bird moving through the stainless sky of consciousness. And like a chick that has emerged from its egg and, nourished by the fluids of its mother, flies into the air—this is the suggestion of a simile based on double entendre (*śleṣopamā*). || 4 ||
May [this person] attain proficiency in tasting the essence of the nectar-like juice of meditating upon your feet.
This mind of mine has reached its limit, having completely exhausted the latent impressions of attachment to the poison of sense objects. || 5 ||

"Tvaditi": May this mind of mine attain proficiency—that is, skill and discernment—in the savoring of the wonder of that very essence of the nectar of immortality, which is the flow of supreme bliss consisting of the contemplation of Your feet and the thought of devotion to You. Of what nature is it? It is one in which the attachment to the poison of sense-objects and the latent impressions (*vāsanā*) have been entirely exhausted and brought to an end.
By whom the limit or boundary of the latent impressions (*saṃskāra*) of the calamity of the Halāhala poison has been known. || 5 ||
By virtue of contact with the rays of the sun of devotion to you,
may this jewel of my heart cast far away the sparks of fire consisting of passion and other afflictions.

"O You, [the one who says] 'tvad' (from You)!"— my mind-jewel, the *cittasūryakānta* gem, by virtue of its fitness, through the contact with the rays of the sun of devotion to You, and by the union with the solar rays of absorption in You,
perceives those very things such as passion (*rāga*) as glowing sparks of heated fire, [sparks] impossible to behold.
May he release, may he abandon, for the sake of meaning that is far removed from us. || 6 ||
In that state, I would constantly extol you with the highest praise,
wherein even Hari, Haryaśva, and Viriñca wait outside.

"In that" means: in that exceedingly lofty station, on the path of supreme power (*paraśaktimārga*), I would praise you with verses; I would extol you; I would correctly contemplate you. "Haryaśva" refers to Indra. "They wait outside" means, in effect, that even those who desire [to reach him] are ignorant of the way. || 7 ||
Under the influence of the delusion produced by my devotion, may I perceive the entire world as consisting of Śiva with all my senses unimpaired.
And all ritual actions consist of worship. || 8 ||

"Devotion" (*bhakti*): by virtue of that delusion (*vibhrama*), which is a transcendent grace (*vilāsa*) produced by the intoxication of devotion—that is, by the intense joy of immersion (*samāveśa-praharṣa*).
"With the instruments," meaning with the eyes and other senses; "having made them complete," meaning having rendered them undiminished.
Even during the state of emergence (*vyutthāna*), which consists of the expansion of the senses and organs, having become fully absorbed through the method of entering the Śrī-Bhairavī Mudrā,

one perceives the entire world— the whole universe— as consisting of Śiva; and all activities, the operations of speech, mind, and body, as being of the nature of worship and as the manifestation of one's own conscious essence.
Behold this! || 8 ||
Having given birth to sons such as *aṇimā* and others, the virtuous women of your devotees, who have been taken into my heart, possess firmly established roots.
Let them strengthen the notion that "this is mine."

"Mine" (māmaka): this very devotion, grasped by my own mind and accepted as the mistress of my life-breath, is like a noble lady (*kulāṅganā*) because she is exceedingly desirable and beyond the reach of common folk; furthermore, in the language of the scriptures (*āgama*), she is the form of Kuleśvarī. Having given birth to sons such as Āṇa and the others—having brought them to manifestation while they were already situated within her womb—she [remains].

Having clearly perceived [the universe] through the great pervasion (*mahāvyāpti*) with perfect clarity, and having become firmly rooted and fully grown, may it strengthen and bring to full development the conviction that "this entire universe belongs to me and not to another. And here, the powers such as *aṇimā* and so forth, whose essence is non-duality, are intended. For it is thus: in the very state of consciousness...

Aṇimā [the power of atomization] exists because of the capacity for internal inclusion; mahimā [the power of magnitude] because of pervasiveness; laghimā [the power of lightness] because of the absence of the weightiness inherent in duality; prāpti [the power of attainment] because of being the locus of rest;
prākāmya [the power of irresistible will] because of grasping the manifold variety of the universe; and īśitva [the power of lordship] because of being indivisible.

There is the capacity to endure everything (*sarvasahatva*) and the power to resolve [one's will] wherever one desires (*yatrakāmāvasāyitva*). While these exist in reality as complete [powers] elsewhere, here it is intended that they are indeed "complete" only by virtue of being exceedingly limited through your grace; nothing else is meant by "completeness," because there is no further need for it. When it is said, "Let other forms of wretchedness be set aside for now..."
And because it would lead to the consequence of contradiction;
this should likewise be remembered in what follows. May there be auspiciousness. (The clear meaning appears to be exactly as follows:)

Just as a husband’s sense of possessiveness becomes firmer when he has a wife who is a woman of noble family, virtuous, truthful, and possessed of sons, so too may my mind’s sense of possessiveness toward Bhakti— born naturally from the power of *aṇimā* and not by my own will— become very firm.
"May your devotion attain supreme stability in your mind"—this is the extent [of the meaning]. The purport of this verse is the firmness of devotion; may there be auspiciousness. || 9 ||

Thus ends the commentary composed by the illustrious Kṣemarāja on the seventh hymn, titled "The Victory over the Moon," within the *Stotrāvalī* (Garland of Hymns) composed by the venerable teacher Utpala.
Oṃ! When will that small fragment of grace residing in the Lord and that devotion which has come to me be united with one another?
[This] shall attain growth within such a body. || 1 ||
Regarding the word "ya" (who): clarity (*prasāda*) is the purity of consciousness (*cit*) through the subsiding of the turbidity of *māyā*. Its "particle" (*lava*) is its state of being small;

however, when there is fullness, due to the departure of the body, there is only the state of Śiva. The term "Īśvara" [is used] in the locative case to signify non-dual existence; the meaning is that he remains in Īśvara alone. For he is indeed of the nature of consciousness (*cidrūpa*), and thus he himself becomes clear through devotion (*bhaktiprasīdet*).

The state of being to be attained through the realization of the nature of the Lord. The word "iva" (as if) indicates the limited nature of devotion; for when it reaches its ultimate limit, it consists entirely of the savor of liberation. "Upeyuṣī" means having arrived at.
Those two—devotion and grace—are perfectly conjoined with one another, like two youths full of intense love.

They are connected in accordance with their own nature. "In such a body" refers to the full essential nature (*svarūpa*), which consists solely of the density of supreme bliss. "Firmly established" means resting; this refers to that particle of grace directed toward me which resides in the Lord—since even the slightest devotion is impossible without a particle of the Lord's grace—and which is like devotion itself.

Because it is incomplete, the semblance of devotion (bhaktyābhāsa) resides in me; the meaning is that it has reached me in the form of secondary devotion (gauṇabhakti), which is merely a tiny particle of the grace of the Lord (īśvaraprasāda). When these two—grace and devotion—bind one another, at what point will they reach their transformation into the singular body of supreme bliss through the attainment of their full nature?
"He will go"—this is the clear meaning. || 1 ||
May some indescribable essence of satisfaction, born from the constant relishing of your sovereignty, arise within me.
May the greatness of my yoga of knowledge and so forth remain far removed from me at all times in this world. || 2 ||

"From you": from that contemplation (*paricarcā*)—arising by the logic of the previously cited verse "Alas, I roar!"—of your sovereignty and your lordship, there arises an incomparable, extraordinary essence of satisfaction, a flow of bliss. "Here" means in this world; "at all times," even during the occasion of worldly emergence (*vyutthāna*). May it arise solely as the supreme.

May there be joy! Knowledge is the realization of one's own self as consisting of the universe; yoga is the attainment of each respective stage; their "magnificence" is their excellence; and by the word "etcetera," the fruit is understood as the arising of those perfections. || 2 ||
O Blessed One, let there be for me, as in the world, a truly intense thirst for sense-objects;
only because they are your body do I [desire them].
May I, free from the eightfold conceptualization, behold the world. || 3 ||

"Like the world" (lokavat): this is the statement of one who is sealed by the Great Meaning Mudrā (mahārthamudrā). "O Blessed One, just as in my worldly state, let there be an abundant and intense thirst—a longing—for objects such as forms and so forth. However, being free from conceptual construction (avikalpa) and having dissolved the perception of duality, may I [regard] these very objects as the body of Your conscious self (cidātman), with the essence of 'I-ness' (ahaṃtā)."
May I investigate; may I see. || 3 ||
In the same way, you have entered into a state of differentiation within the physical bodies, within the mind, and upon the path of the vital breath.
And on those paths of consciousness, may you become manifest to me as my very own self. 4.

"In the stages of the body" means in the states of old age, death, and so forth. "In the mind" means in that which consists of the essence of conceptual construction (*kalpanā*). "In the paths of the vital breath" means in that which consists of the contact with pleasure, pain, and so on. "In the paths of consciousness" means in the cognitions of blue and other objects.
"In those" refers to these various [states]. "Having attained differentiation" is a neuter residual compound (*napuṃsakaśeṣa*). In all this aforementioned manner—

"Insofar as [the world] consists of differentiation" means: by that [consciousness], which has manifested as wonder within its own self; by the self whose nature is a mass of consciousness (ciddhana); "become clearly manifest"—shining forth through your own primacy—O my [Self]. || 4 ||
O Lord, may these functions of my senses, though they have arisen, fall back into their respective places;
let them not exist even for a moment, nor in the slightest degree.
The rashness of suffering injury to the essence that is non-different from you. || 5 ||

"Mine own," etc. These are my functions of the senses, the goddesses of consciousness such as sight and the rest. "Ullasitāḥ" means they are full of joy through their own extraordinary splendor. Let them flow forth toward their respective objects, such as forms and so on.
The loss of the flavor of non-difference from You—the falling away from immersion—is itself that rashness, that act of acting without reflection.
Let it not be so. Previously, there was thirst—that is, longing—for all objects everywhere; here, however, the distinction is that there is the expansion of consciousness regarding them. || 5 ||
Meditating, through the power of immersion [in the deity], upon a body that is light, smooth, white, transparent, and cool,
one should contemplate the entire range of all objects.
I would not transgress those worldly conventions. || 6 ||
p.
55) "Light" (laghu): by virtue of being possessed by you [the Guru], through the loss of the state of being a guru of Māyā, it is light;
it is pleasant to the touch because it is smooth; it is white because it is a mass of luminosity; and it is clear and cool, as before.

Cultivating and perfecting [this], may I transcend—that is, turn back—all worldly activities and movements pertaining to the entire range of categories, the collection of subjects and objects of cognition. || 6 ||
May my own body blossom as being of the nature of existence;
may all worlds attain the state of being my limbs;
and may all this fluttering of duality come to an end.
Even when it enters the path of memory, it remains indefinable.

"May it blossom": may my own body, which is essentially composed of consciousness (*cinmaya*), blossom as its true nature (*svarūpa*). For this very reason, may the worlds—from the earth up to Sadāśiva—perfectly attain the state of being limbs of me, that is, non-difference (*abhinnatā*), such that they do not arise again. And consequently, may all the play of duality (*dvayavalgita*), the manifestation of differentiation (*bhedavijṛmbhita*), [cease].
Upon entering the path of memory, let it attain the state of being an object of memory, even while remaining indefinable.
O Father,
may that flood of the nectar of beholding your forest-like form arise for me, so that my non-dual state with you may be realized.
The filling of the vast and formidable caverns. || 8 ||

"May it arise": the non-manifestation of the non-duality of existence and the non-manifestation of the unity of consciousness—that is the terrible, insatiable cave that bestows the fear of saṃsāra; its filling is the direct realization of the unity of consciousness.
May that face of yours, which is the cause for the outpouring of the river of supreme bliss, be so disposed toward me that such [realization] may come to pass.
"Śaivī-mukham" and so forth; by its persistence, it is the form of the Supreme Power (para-śakti).
Therefore, "viloka" means looking upon—that is, grace—or the "looking upon" refers to the remembrance of that [grace]. That alone [is the meaning].
He prays for the excellence of immersion into the power of Rudra, such that there may arise a flood of the supreme nectar and a torrent of the essence of supreme touch. || 8 ||
Perhaps at some time, by being sprinkled with even a tiny drop of the nectar of union with you,
may I turn my back upon all worldly pleasures.
Shall I not indeed exist once both have fallen away? 9.

"Even so": union with you (*tāvakasaṅgama*) is indeed immersion in you (*tvatsamāveśa*), which is a sprinkling of drops of nectar (*amṛtakaṇācchuraṇa*), a drenching in showers of ambrosia (*sudhāśīkarāplāva*). By means of that most subtle (*tanīyasā*) and spreading pure nature—even among all worldly pleasures, which, according to the principle that "all is suffering for the discerning," are themselves objects to be abandoned—[it is so].
Because I am sprinkled with the supreme nectar (*parāmṛta*), I shall not turn my back; I shall remain facing it directly.

Of what nature? Having fallen away from duality on both sides—that is, by abandoning both the rejectable and the acceptable—I shall perceive everything as non-dual. [This interpretation does not satisfy the hearts of those who investigate.]

For indeed, even one who is anointed with drops of the nectar of the Goddess’s embrace during a state of possession by Śiva does not desire the manifestation of worldly pleasures; this is because such an inclination is established by nature only for ordinary people. Furthermore, the word *ubhaya* (both) is not conventionally used in the sense of duality (*dvaita*). Its...

Because the word *dvaita* (duality) is well-known for signifying the entire phenomenal world as distinct from Brahman— since it denotes the two things previously specified— and because the qualifying phrase "fallen away from both kinds of duality" (*ubhayasmād dvitāc cyuta*) could not in any way apply to a person who has discarded the perception of duality, [the term *cyuta*] is used.

Thus, because the use of the qualifier "fallen from the highest state" is appropriate [only for one who has fallen], and because its application to one who has ascended to the supreme state where duality has been shaken off is untenable; furthermore, the word *kākimiti*, read at the end of the verse, appears to be disregarded. To the inquiry, "What then is the meaning of this verse?", it is said:

This is the lamentation of a devotee and composer of hymns who desires to attain the uninterrupted bliss of meditation on identity with Paramaśiva; for one who is tormented by even the slightest desire for the pleasure of sense objects that somehow arises during the state of worldly emergence (*vyutthāna*), [he says: "Union with You alone—that is, absorption into You—is the nectar; even by the smallest drop of it..."

The ellipsis to be supplied is: "having become satisfied even by a mere sprinkling or a subtle shower. Furthermore: "Will I ever turn my back on all worldly pleasures? Will I never abandon all sensual joys? By the word "kim" (what?), a sense of world-weariness and detachment (*nairvedya-vairāgya*) is expressed. And so it is said:

In the *Śataślokī* composed by the venerable Śrī Śaṅkarācārya, two kinds of knowledge are stated; therein, the first is dispassion (*vairāgya*). It generally arises from observing suffering, such as [the desire] for home, friends, sons, and wealth, and so forth (verse 14). What am I like now?
He has indeed fallen away from the path of Śiva and from the worldly station; may there be auspiciousness. || 9 ||
For me, the supreme swan, who constantly dwells within the lotus of your feet;
O you who bow down from above, from below the very foundation, and from within, let your lotus-stalk of devotion descend. 10.

"Constantly," it is said. For me, the best of swans, whose nature consists in the relinquishing and grasping of difference and non-difference according to the perspective already explained, your lotus-feet are the mine—the place of origin—and the ground of the Supreme Power (*parā-śakti*). I am one who wanders there; let devotion itself, like a lotus stalk, become a sprout for me. May it come to pass.
"May it be enjoyed. The phrase "above," and so forth, means from all the levels of entry, the center, and rest. *Haṃsa* is the Self. || 10 ||
O Lord, may all things come within the range of my vision, the scope of my thought, and the domain of my perception—
my seeing, my reflecting, and my illuminating.
May those things whose essence has perished shine forth intensely. || 11 ||
"May they come"—meaning, may they reach the state of being objects of thought and conceptualization. "The locus of vision," because it is to be directly realized.

Of "vision and thought"—that is, of the non-conceptual and the conceptual—those whose essence is the nectar of light, the elixir of consciousness itself, which is the most excellent form; those [perceptions] are entirely devoid of the stains of what is to be rejected or accepted.
May all things—nothing else, but solely these—vibrate everywhere, on all sides. || 11 ||
O Supreme Lord, may I be present even when those various hardships should befall me;
not only may I be free from fear through contact with Your limbs, but—
Even one whose excessive joy has been produced, as long as... || 12 ||

"O Supreme Lord!"— in the midst of pure hardships, I alone am free from fear; having abandoned all dread through contact with Your limbs, that which has arisen is even greater due to the immersion (*samāveśa*) in the power of Rudra.

May I be such that even when my prosperity is at its peak, I possess a joy [that is] "excessive"—the intention of the word *adhika* being this: that even when various miseries arise, my state remains undisturbed. (12)
That which is manifested externally by you alone is already projected within your own self;
this is that which is attended by firm conviction.
Let that now appear clearly indeed. || 13 ||

"Being" (*bhavat*): that universe, from the digit of the void (*vyomakalā*) up to the fire of time (*kālānala*), which has been projected within Your own Self and strung upon the thread of Your consciousness—that is manifested by You alone and not by anyone else. The word "externally" (*bahiḥ*) indicates that it is manifested as something external in relation to its perceiver. The word "also" (*api*) implies that even while being manifested externally, it is never devoid of internal manifestation.

Thus, may that reality which is the meaning of the sentence—firmly ascertained, drawn near to the self, cherished with affection, served, and tasted through total immersion—now shine forth clearly even during the state of emergence; may it become directly manifest. May there be auspiciousness! || 13 ||

Thus ends the commentary composed by the venerable Kṣemarāja on the eighth hymn, titled "The Strengthening of the Worldly," within the *Stotrāvalī* (Garland of Hymns) composed by the illustrious teacher Utpaladeva.
Oṃ tatsat! When, having abandoned all else, will [the mind] proceed, eager to savor the enjoyment that is ever-moist with the nine aesthetic flavors (navarasa)?
My mind is set upon touching you. || 1 ||

"Kadā? [When?]—eager for the savoring of that enjoyment (*sambhoga*) which consists of total immersion (*samāveśa*), which is exceedingly moist with the nine aesthetic flavors (*navarasa*) and the fresh expansion of devotion, and which is intensely desirable.
Longing, may my mind abandon all other webs of conceptualization and proceed toward the touch of you, becoming entirely absorbed in you. (1)
Anxious as I am, devoted solely to you and possessing nothing more than the great wealth of worshipping your feet, when shall I behold you face to face? (2)

"O You! [he says]. Attached to You alone and not to Your manifestations (vibhūtis), he possesses great and abundant wealth consisting solely of the worship of Your feet—that is, the service of Your rays. Being eager and unable to endure even a moment's emergence from [meditative] absorption due to the state of his realization being like a completed festival, he asks: "When shall I perceive You directly?"
When shall I become one whose mind has become indifferent through the power of intense passion,
[seeing] all things shattered with a *paṭapaṭiti* sound?
I, Mahārgala, shall come to you. || 3 ||

"Gāḍha" means: he whose mind has become indifferent [to the world], having abandoned all that is inward-turned—such as excretion, physical exertion, meditation, and so forth—is of such a nature. When shall I approach you? That is, when shall I attain you entirely?
Of what kind [are you]? One from whom all the bolts of Māyā have been suddenly shattered—that is, instantly broken—asunder with a "paṭapaṭa" sound.

The nooses of ignorance and so forth belong to him; by the expression "paṭapaṭiti" and so on, the non-recurrence [of rebirth] is stated through the analogy of the severing of the intervening bonds. || 3 ||
O Lord, when shall I bring under my control all the deities, who have their foundation in the heart that is the essence of self-awareness, through the power of devotion to you? (4)

Regarding the term *svasaṃvit* (self-awareness): those [deities] such as Brāhmī and the others, whose essence is self-awareness—that is, whose substratum, locus, and support is the Heart consisting of light (*prakāśa*) and reflective awareness (*vimarśa*)—are by means of which the fettered souls (*paśu*) have been bound, having entered into the state of being objects of enjoyment for the wheel of powers (*śakticakra*). This is the established position.
When shall I bring them under my control through the power of immersion in devotion to you— that is to say, when shall I attain sovereignty over that wheel? || 4 ||
O Lord, when shall I become one whose very name is distinct [as a devotee], overflowing with the joy and vigor of the essence of abundant devotion, and rejoicing in the bliss of beholding You? (5)
He causes [it] to be proclaimed. "Bhūri" means abundant.

By speaking of a festival, he expresses his hope that his own self will be entirely absorbed in that [state], because it is so exceedingly desirable. By the phrase "a distinct name," he indicates supreme state of aesthetic fusion (sāmarasya). || 5 ||
When will one suddenly recognize the Lord— fearless, magnanimous, perfect, causeless, and whose nature is beyond denial?
I shall cause my master to feel ashamed.
"Īśvara" means the Lord, because He is the locus of all manifestations. "Abhaya" means fearless, because He has no rival.

"Udāra" means noble, because He bestows everything. "Pūrṇa" means complete, because He is free from desire. "Akāraṇa" means causeless, because He is eternal; yet, even so, He assumes the form of the world without any external cause or motive.

Because its essence consists in concealing its own nature, it has a hidden self; for while one who is not the Lord (anīśvara) and so forth might conceal himself, the Blessed One does not do so. And yet, he is indeed one whose self is concealed. When, by means of the method of the Śāmbhava-āveśa, does one suddenly recognize such a person as his own master and lord?

Having realized [this], I shall cause [the world] to feel shame; that is to say, by subordinating its form through the predominance of concealment (apahnuti), it should be perceived as being of the very nature of pure, full consciousness alone. || 6 ||
O Lord, when shall I attain that same belovedness toward you, so that it would never be right for you to flee from me? (7)
"Kadā?"—by saying "your belovedness," he says this: "I am indeed extremely dear to you; but for you, I [am so] because of the excellence of your extraordinary devotion (*alaukika-bhakti-prakarṣāt*).

May I attain a state of general favor such that, through my being so beloved, it would never be right for you to turn away from me or to hide yourself; the meaning is that you should remain, constantly entering within me. || 7 ||
O Lord, when shall I be flooded by the savor of joy, witnessed and approved by Your vision, as all living beings truly become one with You through Your worship? 8.

Regarding the phrase "in reality": all living beings, when performing any action whatsoever from the perspective of ultimate truth (*paramārtha*), consist essentially of worship characterized by repose in their own self-deity. By means of the cause that is the recognition of one's own self (*svātmapratyabhijñāna*)—which, through the greatness of Your grace, occurs precisely through the vision of reality pertaining to these beings—[they attain this state].

When shall I be flooded—that is, pervaded—by that very essence which is rejoiced in and praised by them, the outpouring of bliss born of devotion? The word "in reality" (*tattvataḥ*) should be applied by repeating it [with the following clause]. Alternatively, in the phrase "of all beings" (*aśeṣajantūnām*), the genitive case is used in the sense of the object. Thus, the meaning is as follows: when shall I [be able to see] all beings in their true nature as consisting of your worship?

"Having seen [this], may I be flooded by a surge of joy through the savor of sympathetic rejoicing (anumodanā). Here, in the word *anumodita*, the suffix *kta* denotes the abstract state (*bhāva*). In both interpretations, the underlying intention is the aspiration: "May everyone be equal to me. || 8 ||
O All-pervading Lord, I long for that time when my devotion to you— the supreme ground of knowledge and the highest state of yoga— shall become perfect.

Regarding the phrase "of knowledge": since it is stated in all the scriptures that [knowledge] is the cause of liberation, and since liberation is established as having the very essence of *samāveśa* (total immersion), that devotion which takes that [immersion] as its form is the supreme ground of knowledge.
They desire yoga to be the oneness of one thing with another, characterized by the abandonment of [the former] through [the latter].

And when will that longing for your devotion—which consists of the state of yoga characterized by manifold immersion and which takes the form of attaining identity with Bhairava, the Supreme Consciousness—be fulfilled and its purpose accomplished? (9)
When, having suddenly attained [you] and firmly embracing you, shall I— overwhelmed with joy—
reveal everywhere this supreme treasure-trove that is your feet? (10)
"Suddenly" means: having attained [it] instantly through the expansion of intuitive insight (*pratibhā*),

having made it one's own vessel for enjoyment on all sides, and likewise having firmly grasped it— having taken possession of it with effort for the sake of exhausting the state of emergence (*vyutthāna*)— I, overwhelmed by joy and filled with supreme bliss, when?

I shall everywhere manifest Your supreme feet as a treasure-trove consisting of all perfections, a storehouse of Your own power; though hidden within, I shall unveil them through the method of revealed instruction,
preceded by the support of effort and the power of supreme intuition, as well as by the glance of grace and other such means.

The meaning is that the reality (*tattva*) which exists in the instruction on the transmission of immersion (*samāveśa-saṃkrama*) would be capable of bestowing supreme grace upon all. By this, he indicates his own intent to desire to favor the people of the entire universe due to the fullness of his own self. || 10 ||
O Lord, when shall I become one composed of the light of pure consciousness spreading everywhere, such that no stain of the shadow of *māyā* remains for me? (11)

"Paritaḥ" means on all sides. When shall I become one with that consciousness-light (*citprakāśa*) which is pure and non-dual throughout the world? Just as there might be nothing at all in a hole made by a shadow of an illusion—meaning, nothing would remain—so too [may I be one with it]. By the word "shadow" (*chāyā*), he expresses the unreality of the hole of illusion.
Or it may be construed as: "There is nothing turbid or defiled by the shadow of illusion. || 11 ||
O Blessed One, when shall I become the leader of the host of Your devotees—having brought the entire mandala under my own control and being free from all worldly attachment? (12)

"Ātman" means one by whom all the spheres (*maṇḍala*) and worlds (*bhuvana*), from Sadāśiva down to the earth (*kṣiti*), have been made his own and brought into oneness with consciousness (*cidaikadhyam*). "Nirvyapekṣakaḥ" means being without a second (*advitīya*). Who else could be the leader of the host of your devotees? [He alone is] the foremost. 12.
O Lord, you are the unprecedented foundation for those who possess worldly pride;
when shall I become one of great pride, filled with the essence of devotion to you? (13)

"O Lord!"—thus [you address Him]. You alone, whose nature is consciousness (*cidrūpa*), are the basis and the cause of the various forms of ego-inflation (*abhimāna*) belonging to Rudras and individual souls (*kṣetrajña*), such as "I am the creator," "I am the sustainer," "I am the destroyer," as well as "I am wise," "I am a hero," and "I am a performer of sacrifice.
This is to say that you act through your own sovereignty alone, having made yourself unprecedented and without external cause.

In reality, because you alone possess the agency over all things, neither Brahmā nor anyone else possesses the power of creation or even scholarship; it is you alone who, in various places, give rise to such conceits. And just as this is so, at some point by your will alone, the Great Ego—the Soul of the Universe, a mass of consciousness and bliss—[arises].
May I be filled and pervaded by the flavor of devotion, firmly supported by the resolve "I am indeed Śiva.

The intention of one who says "filled with the flavor of devotion" is this: even for one who has attained great self-conceit (*mahābhimāna*), it is only fitting to maintain the state of a servant toward the Lord, consisting of the savoring of total immersion (*samāveśa*). || 13 ||
When shall I lie down, firmly established in the embrace of the glory that is empty of all objective domains, upon the pair of lotuses that are the cool feet of Śiva? 14.

"Without remainder" (aśeṣa): I would lie down, as before, to rest upon the pair of her cool lotus-feet—of what nature? Firmly established by the firm embrace resulting from that [embrace], which is this auspicious fortune (śrī), namely the glory of devotion (bhakti-lakṣmī), which is empty of all other objects and filled with the entire universe. The meaning of the verse is clear. || 14 ||
When shall I reach the further shore of this abundance of the enjoyment of your worship, which is enriched by the wine of devotion? When shall I become a man of fulfilled purpose? (15)

"When shall I reach the further shore—the ultimate limit—of that abundance of the enjoyment of your worship, which is enriched by the wine of devotion (*bhaktyāsava*), that is, the essence of service, and which is the glory of repose in spiritual immersion (*samāveśa*)?
For this very reason, when shall I become one who has fulfilled his purpose? (15)
(64) With a cry faltering, wandering, and stammering due to a flood of tears of joy.
When shall I, with my face brightened by laughter, attain the essence of the taste of touching you? || 16 ||

"Ānanda" means: he longs for that very state of immersion (samāveśa) which has been interrupted by a long period of emergence. "Ākranda" refers to a cry that is faltering, wandering, and long-resonating due to a natural flow of tears from the internal onset of joy during immersion; it is indistinct in its syllables and obstructed at inappropriate moments.
He whose roar is great; he whose path of power is a face radiant with the expansion of laughter; and for that very reason, he whose mouth is wide open, radiant with laughter, and beautiful. 16.
O Śambhu, when shall I cast off this condition, which is shared by the conduct of common cattle, and manifest my own form as is appropriate for Your devotee? 17.
"Behold!

[He says: "Having cast off—meaning having clearly dispelled—this state which consists of the distinction between the emergent and the fallen, and moreover, having overwhelmed it by shaking every limb as it expands through immersion (samāveśa), [one experiences] that which belongs to you, your devotee, consisting of eternally arisen supreme bliss; but not that of anyone else."
When shall I taste my own true nature and experience wonder? || 17 ||
Having attained the supernatural powers such as *aṇimā* and the like, with all the afflictions of suffering and fear dissolved,
[he drinks] the elixir of the rasa of devotion to you.
When shall I become devoted to play? || 18 ||

"Attained" (*labdhā*) refers to the supernatural powers (*siddhi*), such as *aṇimā* and so forth, which, as previously stated, consist of non-duality. For this very reason, his affliction (*upatāpa*) and terror (*santrāsa*) have dissolved and become stilled. [This applies] to those beginning with Brahmā.

Even if I were to attain the powers such as *aṇimā* through the yoga of [attaining] difference, fear of death and the like would inevitably arise; nevertheless, may I remain intent on the joy of drinking the nectar of devotion to You. 18.
O Lord, when will such a cry of mine issue from my speech,
immediately upon which...
Your form flashes forth before me. || 19 ||
"O Lord!"—this is the utterance of one who has long since emerged [from the state]. It is impossible to say that he is "of such-and-such a kind.
A great cry, a loud roar, should issue forth; it should spontaneously surge up. By means of the immersion (*samāveśa*), his form and essential nature (*svarūpa*) quiver and blaze forth. (19)
With a mind intent on the habit of embracing the lotus feet of the Lord most firmly and intensely,
one realizes that this world is unreal without any effort at all.
When shall I behold you? || 20 ||

"Gāḍha" (intense) and so forth: by means of the repetition [of the word] and the two words "vyasana-tatpara" (intent on devotion), he expresses the helplessness resulting from the excellence of devotion.

"I shall behold—meaning I will see—even You, who are Your own form, correctly according to reality, as this universe consisting of existence and non-existence, both real and unreal, effortlessly, that is, without meditation, recitation, and the like. May there be auspiciousness! || 20 ||
Thus ends the commentary composed by Śrī Kṣemarāja on the ninth hymn, titled *Svātantryavijaya*, within the *Stotrāvalī* (Garland of Hymns) composed by the venerable teacher Utpaladeva. 9.
Oṃ! This [suffering] must certainly not be endured by you, the sole lord of the world;
for the devotees of Maheśvara are equal to others among the people. || 1 ||

"No," [you say]. "The Māheśvaras, who are fully absorbed in the nature of Viśveśvara, are equal to others such as Brahmā and the rest, who are characterized by duality"—this you cannot endure; indeed, this is not tolerated by you yourself.

This is indeed established by its very nature, since you alone are the unique, peerless Lord of the universe. The two particles *ca* and *kara* express the reason for contradiction; others [interpret this as] that it is not fitting for you to tolerate the equality of other worlds.
Those who have always followed your feet with devotion...
Wherever they go, they enjoy various pleasures there. || 2 ||

"Those who"—meaning those who, through passion (*anurāga*) or attachment, are connected to Your rays; wherever they may be situated in any state, they enjoy certain supreme bliss-filled delights. || 2 ||
Where you, the Lord who is Time and the Ender, reside, whence could there be any afflictions?
And where your own Fortune (Lakṣmī) dwells, what room is there for the desire for any other enjoyment?

Regarding the word "bhartṛ" (Lord): by the phrase "the ender of time," the meaning is that while the Lord—who devours time—is present, all diseases driven by Mahākāla can no longer arise, for they are destroyed at their very root. Furthermore, there is no desire whatsoever for the fortune of other enjoyments, such as the status of Sadāśiva and so forth, because duality has been swallowed up therein.
Lakṣmī is the perfection of the manifestation of non-duality. || 3 ||
Even by that which is obtained through a moment’s happiness, the Lord is attained;
at that very moment, his entire life is filled with joy in you. (4)
"Merely for a moment": by means of even that devotion which, through the vibration of immersion (*samāveśa*) for just a moment, causes you to be attained;

at that very opportunity, for this devotee, all time—even that consisting of the state of emergence (*vyutthāna*)—is filled with bliss by you. Through entry into the nature of consciousness-bliss, which is not limited by time, it is made identical with that.
And the subsequent time is flooded by its latent impression (saṃskāra). He is all-pervasive, the Lord, and omnipresent. || 4 ||
That drop of the essence of bliss of yours has fallen upon the earth as the moon;
likewise, the sun is your emitted particle of light, the agent of dissolution.
O Lord, we offer this oblation to this third eye of yours,
the sole emblem of some extraordinary greatness. (6)

"Ānanda" [means]: on your earth (bhuvi), that which is the drop of the essence of bliss (*ānandarasabindu*) within the path of the downward power (*adhaḥśakti*), whose nature consists of Agni and Soma—that very thing is the Moon (*candramas*) because it causes delight. It has "flowed down" (*galita*), meaning its nature is liquefied. The drop and the moon have flowed down;
the mind, together with the entire mass of objects of cognition (*prameya-rāśi*), has dissolved right there. Likewise, right there is the "dissolver" (*saṃhārī*), the devourer of duality.

That very spark of fire, a minute particle of the supreme flame, has spread forth as the sun by virtue of its luminosity and its power to dispel darkness; and the sun, in turn, is dissolved into the vital breath (*prāṇa*). For the melted moon and sun are indeed the ground of the Supreme Power (*parā śakti*). To this eye, which is of the nature of that Power, we offer our oblation (*bali*); and furthermore, upon the earth.

That which is the moon is a drop of your bliss that has fallen and flowed forth; and the sun is a spark of your radiance that has spread out and shone. As it is said in scripture: "This power of knowledge of the Lord shines in the form of the sun; that same supreme power of action shines in the form of the moon."
For this purpose—for the sake of causing the sun and moon to shine—we offer an oblation (*bali*) to Your third eye.
Right here, within the great fire, we surrender the state of being a subject (*pramātṛtā*) consisting of the illusory body and so forth. To what kind?
To one who is extraordinary, beyond the reach of Brahmā, Upendra, and others, and transcendent of the world.
"For the sake of a unique token of recognition for one whose sole characteristic is his majesty"—the dative case in *asmai* is used in the sense of purpose (*tādarthye*).
"You have been seen by that very person; from the sight of you, he rejoices. Or rather, whoever experiences some joy has somehow beheld you. (7)

"By him" means: by one who, contemplating the reality devoid of verbal expression through the mind alone—having seen You according to the method of immersion (*samāveśa*) into Śakti and becoming filled with bliss (*ānandamaya*)—exults intensely;
by that very person, intent on the worship of non-duality (*abhedopāsanā*), You have been seen somewhere. "In some way" means: by one who contemplates nothing at all.

Or, by means of the process of immersion into Śambhu, he for whom there is a certain joy—not the joy belonging to one intent on the worship of duality—by him you, as the mass of consciousness, have been seen and recognized as "someone" [the Supreme]. (7)
O Lord, those with whom you are pleased have truly gained your heart;
for having drawn them from your city, they have made the external internal. (8)

"Of those who"—as before, "you are pleased. For this very reason, they have attained and made their own the form of the Heart, which consists of light (*prakāśa*) and reflective awareness (*vimarśa*). Having drawn forth and expanded from your city—that is, from your source, which is the nature of consciousness—this entire external universe, relative to the body and so forth, has been brought back within once more.

"Having encapsulated the creation made of consciousness"—according to the perspective on the meaning of reality stated in the *Śrītriṃśikā*, this means that the universe, which has arisen from consciousness and appears as non-different from consciousness, is indeed composed of consciousness alone for them.
By the power of resonance (*anuraṇana-śakti*), the worldly sense of "Lord" (*īśvara*) is as explained previously. (8)
Behold how the entire universe has become equal in your vision;
yet you alone, O Three-eyed One, remain its sovereign lord who perceives with unequal eyes.

"Except for you": "Possessing equal vision"—that is, he whose perception or consciousness (*saṃvitti*) is equal and uniform, devoid of differentiation; let that pair of eyes be seen as having attained the state of being an object of knowledge (*prameyatā*). He is "the One," meaning without a second.
And he is "three-eyed," possessing the third eye which is the vision or gnosis (*jñāna*) that consumes all differentiation. || 9 ||
Let it be; for without your power, even existence itself would not occur, since for those [beings] whose very discourse of censure toward you cannot be established without you. (10)
