"Let it be so. For those such as the Buddhists, Sāṃkhyas, Mīmāṃsakas, and others,

whose discourse of refutation against you is not possible without your own nature— which consists of the refuter and is of the form of a manifesting consciousness— for them, whose bodies, organs, and intellects are so diverse, even their very existence would not be possible without the power of an intelligent being, and so forth.
Let the multitude of arguments be like a blow struck by one who has already fallen at the heel. || 10 ||
O Lord, if my mind were to abide in You—who are beyond external and internal obstacles and are absolute purity—what else would be required? (11)

Regarding the term *bāhya* (external): external obstacles (*antarāya*) are those such as the conjunction with or separation from various objects in relation to the body as the subject; internal obstacles are those such as mental constructions and the like, which depend upon the intellect (*buddhi*) and other faculties. (p. 69) These are the obstacles.

If my mind were to abide in its object—You—alone, devoid of that *ālī* (lineage) which consists of a succession of thoughts obstructing one's own rest, then what else would be required? For that which is to be attained would already have been attained through this state of exclusive absorption (*samāveśa*). || 11 ||
Others, O Blessed One, wander about, being extremely ill-situated within themselves;
others, O Blessed One, are intoxicated, being extremely well-situated within themselves. || 12 ||

"Others" refers to those who propound a selfless and insentient nature, as well as transmigrating beings; they wander and err within their very own essential nature (*svarūpa*), undergoing an endless succession of birth, death, and so forth.
Being in an extremely wretched state due to the absence of knowledge of reality, they suffer. "Others" refers to certain exceptional individuals who [abide] in the Self alone.
But they are not well-established anywhere else than in the nature of consciousness; being a single mass of supreme bliss, they wander and sport. || 12 ||
O Lord, even without drinking the nectar of devotion to you and without beholding you,
[I am satisfied] merely by your conduct.
Living beings attain success. || 13 ||

"Even having drunk" means: even without having drunk the nectar of devotion to You— the essence of the bliss of the Śākta immersion— and even without being struck by wonder (*acamatkṛtya*), and even without beholding You— that is, without recognizing You, who are the very nature of consciousness, even in the slightest degree— living beings (*jantavaḥ*) who are subject to birth and so forth, attain perfection merely through Your conduct, as described in the various traditions (*āmnāya*) and the *Caryāpāda*.
They partake in the accomplishments of others (*parasiddhi*). By means of the word "also" (*api*) and the word "merely" (*mātra*), astonishment is suggested.

For thus it has been stated by our own teachers in the *Tantrasāra*, following the introduction in the *Āgama* with the words "sometimes through the yoga of devotion and through conduct," up to the conclusion: "the Lord of the entire universe bestows grace upon those in the cycle of existence. Thus says the Supreme Lord.
If you act according to your own will, following many paths and according to your own desires, how can you hope for liberation, which is not attained by one's own whim? || 13 ||
(70) O Lord, we are your servants, just as you support the three worlds;
in that same manner, we too are fully worthy of being supported by you. 14.

"Servants," it says; "of the three worlds," as before. "You sustain" means you maintain and nourish. Regarding the phrase "we too are sufficient," this is the intended meaning: just as by You, who sustain the universe through its internal differentiation, [all things]—though in reality consisting of You alone—are nevertheless grasped through the conceit of the body and so forth.
Since we do not perceive the universe as something distinct—as if we were accustomed to its transcendence—we must be sufficiently supported and nourished by you, for we are your servants. || 14 ||
Even though You, the Self of the universe, who consist of the nectar of supreme bliss, have been seen, I am intensely longing for You, whose essence is the flavor of touch.

Thus he says: "O You, whose essence is supreme bliss, who are the self of the universe appearing in forms such as blue and yellow—even when You are perceived during the state of worldly emergence (*vyutthāna*), and even when You are recognized through that very perception—my longing for You is intense, O You whose nature is the expansion of the touch of deep immersion (*samāveśa*) within the realms of touch and taste. (15)
O Lord, whatever sufferings belong to those in cyclic existence,
when joined with your self called "fortitude" (dhṛti), they become endurable.

"O Lord!"—O God, whose nature is play and the like, all movements beginning from insects up to Brahmā are nothing but suffering because they consist of duality; even these must be endured by subjects (*pramātṛ*) who are intent on transmigratory existence (*saṃsāra*). For, through that which is called "fortitude," [they think]: "This has been obtained by me today; this I shall obtain."
These [elements] are joined with, that is, permeated by, your own self which grasps through the support of conceit such as "desire" (manoratha) and so forth. || 16 ||
O Lord, since You alone are omniscient, omnipotent, and composed of consciousness, the manifestation of this world— which is in every way non-existent— is nonetheless possible.
"Omniscient" means one who [knows] this entire universe in every respect, by way of its essential nature— such as its capacity for causal efficiency across space, time, and form.

Since that which is external to light is not perceived, its manifestation in any way whatsoever is logical only when You exist—You who are composed of consciousness, omnipotent, independent, and the illuminator of all. The term "in every way" (sarvathā) should be applied to both [the external object and its manifestation]. || 17 ||
Animated by you, these qualities, though as worthless as clods of earth, quiver and dance like tufts of cotton blown by the wind. 18.
O Lord, if the self-conceit regarding qualities were not to exist, then by what could the manifestation of the world as having You alone as its essence be diminished? (19)

"Animated by you" means that the qualities (*guṇas*)—the movements of the intellect (*buddhi*) and so forth—which are insentient and comparable to clods of earth, throb only because they are animated by you, sustained by your life-force; otherwise, they would not exist in any way whatsoever. Here is an illustration:
just as the tufts or fragments of cotton, when shaken upward by the wind, appear to dance.

They shine in the sky. And thus, O Lord, if the self-identification bestowed by Śakti—which consists of You—did not exist within the virtues of Your devotees, then for what reason would this manifestation of the world as having a single essence with You, through non-difference from You, ever cease? It cannot be prevented by anything; for the universe of devotees exists in oneness with You.
"Because of its throbbing [with consciousness], for the knower who has reached full maturity, there may be the vibrations and stillnesses of the qualities (guṇas) and so forth"—so it has been said.
(18–19) O Supreme Lord, even those great ones are worthy of worship who, though they have met with dissolution, were purified by the touch of the fire of Your wrath. (20)

Regarding the word "vandyāḥ" (worthy of worship): "te'pi" (even they) refers to Kāla, Kāma, Tripura, Andhaka, and others. The meaning of the word "api" (even) is that not only those who were directly favored [by you], but also those who are devoted [to you]. "Mahīyāṃsaḥ" (most exalted) means endowed with extraordinary majesty; even though they have undergone *pralaya*, which is destruction, they are connected to your incarnate forms such as Śrīkaṇṭha and others.
They have been purified by the touch of the fire of his playful anger, which consists of both the act of punishing and the act of bestowing grace. || 20 ||
(72) O Lord,
since You, whose form is great light, stand clearly manifest everywhere, why then do I spread forth into darkness? 21.

Regarding the term "Great Radiance" (*mahāprakāśa*): this statement is made by one who, due to the helplessness of worldly emergence (*vyutthāna*), has not yet attained the stage of direct realization (*sākṣātkāra*).

For among these [verses], some praise the excellence of immersion (*samāveśa*), others are intent on the desire to abandon emergence, and still others proclaim the manifestation of universal selfhood (*sārvātmya*).

His hymns are devoted to the aspiration for the state of Śiva, which is the complete cessation of all dualities; these have been joined together as appropriate and will be joined further. Thus, one should not consider this true Supreme Lord to be incomplete in such utterances. "Even though it is perfectly clear" means even within the darkness consisting of the manifestation of the universe.
"I shall expand"—thus one becomes helpless in the face of emergence. || 21 ||
You alone are my indivisible, immortal essential nature;
nevertheless, I am the sole abode of mortal attributes.

Regarding the term "indivisible" (*avibhāga*): this expression is also exactly as previously stated. It is you alone, and not some other thing consisting of a mass of blissful immortality; for [you are free] from the exertions of mortals' duties such as rejection and acquisition. In the state of emergence (*vyutthāna*), the notion of "I" consists of the identification with the body and so forth, and is not the nature of consciousness (*cidrūpa*).
"He is indeed one" is as explained previously. || 22 ||
He alone is truly empowered whose name "Maheśvara" serves as an ornament for his speech and whose head bears the mark of prostration. (23)

"Maheśvara"— that which the bards recite as his name-mark, namely "O Maheśvara, O Lord of the Universe, Brahmā, and the rest, O Sovereign"; he whose speech is thus adorned, and who bears upon his head the mark of prostration as well as the token of submission to another's nature— he alone is [the one].

He is without a second in relation to the Lord Maheśvara; or rather, he is known as "marked by prostration" because he is possessed of devotion and, having attained the touch of non-difference from the Blessed One, is empowered and renowned for being marked by that name. || 23 ||

(73) O Blessed One, since you yourself effortlessly establish both existence and non-existence by whatever means, why is it that such accomplishment does not come to me through my own natural disposition? 24.

"Existence and non-existence": since you alone are the universe in the form of both being and non-being, therefore, for me, how is it that the realization of you—your direct manifestation—is not eternally arisen by its own inherent nature, effortlessly and without the web of means? Why does it not exist as ever-arisen? || 24 ||
Śivadāsa, whose very soul is Śiva—what happiness could he not attain?
For by me even the foremost of the gods are gratified with the nectar-liquors of immortality. (25)

Regarding the term "Śivadāsa": precisely because he is a servant of Śiva, and for that very reason, being fully possessed [by Him], he has become one with Śiva; what happiness would he not attain? The meaning is that he indeed becomes composed of supreme bliss (*paramānanda*). For this reason, even among the foremost of gods, such as Brahmā and others who are themselves worthy of being propitiated by others— [The text continues: ...he is the one who is to be propitiated. Therefore, having attained the state of being one with Śiva, he is the one who bestows grace upon all beings. This is the sense. Furthermore, since he is the one who bestows grace upon all beings, he is the one who bestows grace upon himself as well. And since he is the one who bestows grace upon himself, he is the one who bestows grace upon Śiva as well. And since he is the one who bestows grace upon Śiva, he is the one who bestows grace upon the entire universe. Thus, he is the one who bestows grace upon the entire universe. This is the sense. Moreover, since he is the one who bestows grace upon the entire universe, he is the one who bestows grace upon the scriptures. And since he is the one who bestows grace upon the scriptures, he is the one who bestows grace upon the teachers. And since he is the one who bestows grace upon the teachers, he is the one who bestows grace upon the disciples. And since he is the one who bestows grace upon the disciples, he is the one who bestows grace upon the world. Thus, he is the one who bestows grace upon the world. This is the sense. Furthermore, since he is the one who bestows grace upon the world, he is the one who bestows grace upon liberation. And since he is the one who bestows grace upon liberation, he is the one who bestows grace upon bondage. And since he is the one who bestows grace upon bondage, he is the one who bestows grace upon everything. Thus, he is the one who bestows grace upon everything. This is the sense. I am to be satiated—that is, to be completely filled—by the nectars of the sensory deities residing in the heart and other locations, through the outpourings of the bliss of non-dual radiance flashing forth at the moment of the manifestation of the object of knowledge; I am not, however, to be an object of enjoyment like a bound soul (paśu). || 25 ||
Residing in the space between the heart and the navel, you are the embodiment of bile (pitta) for living beings;
as a great fire, you consume all that is moving and stationary.

Regarding the phrase "between the heart and the navel": situated in the region between the heart and the navel, which is the locus of the *ghaṭa* (the vessel), you are the pervader of the bile (*pitta*) of all living beings and are of the nature of bile; because you consume hot food and the like, and because you swallow even external fire, you are a great fire (*mahāvahni*). For this very reason, you devour both the stationary and the moving; by this [statement], [it is shown that] you are everywhere.
The Supreme Lord, who indeed devours the universe by means of locations such as the belly of the knower (*pramātṛ*), is the ultimately real; may there be auspiciousness. 26.

Thus ends the commentary composed by the venerable teacher Kṣemarāja on the tenth hymn, titled "The Breakdown of Non-interruption," within the *Stotrāvalī* composed by the illustrious teacher Utpaladeva. 10.
Oṃ! Whether this world, or friends, or kinsmen— none of these are anything to me.
But since you are all this at all times, who else could there be for me? || 1 ||

Oṃ, this world. Oṃ! Even the triad beginning with the world, though internal according to the order of the universe, is nothing to me, because it is of the single nature of pure consciousness (cinmātra) distinct from that [world]. When, moreover, because it consists of light, all this is you alone, then what else could there be for me—anything separate? Nothing at all; even the world is simply one's own essential nature (svarūpa). Thus ends the first verse.
"O Lord, you are Maheśvara; you alone are the entire world. Even such a prayer that "the reality itself may attain perfection" is merely a form of begging. || 2 ||
"O Master!"—as before, this refers to Maheśvara. "Directly" means by way of the non-dual vision and the act of presiding (*adhiṣṭhāna*).

This very reality is indeed the ultimate truth. Even though it remains exactly so, the request that "this [reality] should attain its own perfection" is merely a request; it is not [a request at all], because by the very fact of saying "you yourself become manifest," one is [already] abashed by such a state of affairs.

The meaning is that it is indeed appropriate. According to the maxim "kamalā-i kamalā-i," the second word for "request" (*yācñā*)—preceded by the suggestion (*dhvanana*) of its lack of beauty and lack of purpose—is [the one intended]. || 2 ||
Even sovereignty over the three worlds appears to you, who dwell in this state, as if it were a blade of grass;
what fruit, then, could there be for such meritorious action?
O Lord, it does not exist apart from the remembrance of you.

"Lordship over the three worlds" means that for those who enjoy worldly existence and are endowed with immersion (*samāveśa*), at this very moment—as indicated by the locative case ending *iha*—there is lordship over the three worlds, which is to say, sovereignty over *bhūr*, *bhuvar*, and *svar*.

To him whose nature is such that he perceives [everything] as if it were a blade of grass, there is no fruit whatsoever—meaning nothing other than you—apart from the remembrance of you; for, since that which was to be attained has already been attained, there remains nothing else. || 3 ||
Since there is nothing whatsoever in the worlds that is distinct from You, and since You are the source of all things,
this wondrous deed is but the manifestation of Your own power.
Even for yourself, a composition of praise does not arise for you. || 4 ||

Regarding the word "yena" (by which): there is nothing whatsoever distinct from you, because everything has the nature of light (*prakāśa*). Even the sources of the worlds, such as Brahmā and others, are merely your own manifestations (*jṛmbhā*), for this reason. Therefore, even regarding wondrous deeds such as the creation and dissolution of the universe, there is no binding of praise to you, because of the absence of distinctions such as hymns and the like.
The essential truth here is this: you alone manifest in the form of the praiser, the praise, and the act of praising. || 4 ||
O Lord, although I am constantly contemplating with natural spontaneity that "I am composed of you" and "I am ever intent upon your worship" without ceasing, [I remain so].
Even when dreaming, I am not like that; how could I possibly be so? || 5 ||

Regarding the phrase "consisting of you" (*tvanmaya*): I am one whose very nature is that which has been described as you; thus, by means of the process of offering the universe into you alone, who are composed of consciousness (*cinmaya*), I am constantly intent on worship.

Even while contemplating this without ceasing, even while maintaining this connection during the state of worldly activity (*vyutthāna*), and even when in the state of dreaming, why should I not [be absorbed] by my own natural impulse, simply through the power of my own will?

In that very same way, why am I not intent upon Your worship even in a dream—that is to say, why do I not enter into [that state], even though it is the essence of the awakening of latent impressions (*saṃskāra*)? || 5 ||
Those who have been touched even slightly by a fragment of the fragrance arising from the lotus of your feet—
Within them, the entire collection of enjoyments sought even by the immortals appears as if dissolved.
Regarding the word "ya" (those who): "The lotus-foot" is as before; "fragrance" refers to the residual impression (*saṃskāra*) of a lingering scent.

A "trace" (*lava*) of that means a mere fraction, not its full form. By that [trace], those who have been touched—even by a slight degree—are made into worthy recipients (*pātrīkṛta*). For them, the entire multitude of enjoyments up to that of Sadāśiva—which is not even to be prayed for by the gods—is [attained] in abundance.

It appears as if there were a foul odor. And thus, for those possessed of full immersion (*samāveśa*), the desire for supernatural powers (*siddhi*) is cast far away by the very logic of the "stick and the cake" (*daṇḍāpūpika*). || 6 ||
O Śambhu, there is nothing else in Your heart, nor anything else in Your speech or Your action;
even for one who exists as the ultimate reality, there is only grace.
Or rather, only one form of punishment should be carried out. || 7 ||

Regarding the word "in the heart" (*hṛdi*): Mahādeva, whose nature is the manifestation of non-dual consciousness, manifests everywhere he begins to manifest; yet, up until the point of the practice of the Heart-mantra, he manifests there. However, where his self is concealed, he remains concealed in the heart, in speech, and in action. For, in the ultimate sense, for the virtuous and sattvic person who truly exists, [he is not otherwise].
Between punishment and favor, only one must be performed and not a mixture of activities;

this constitutes a blend with *arthāntaranyāsa* (corroboration by a general truth). Furthermore, in the present context, "punishment" and "favor" refer respectively to the closing and opening of the eyes, while in the non-contextual sense, they refer to injury and benefit—this also possesses the luster of *śleṣa* (paronomasia). || 7 ||
I am deluded; I am overwhelmed by suffering; I am afraid of the defects of old age and the like; I am devoid of power; I have taken refuge in you.
O Śambhu, act thus so that I may quickly attain the most supreme station, having abandoned the path of suffering.

"I am deluded"—this was said with reference to the state of emergence (*vyutthāna*). Having thus explained the first half of the verse, one should apply the second half by breaking it down as "I have taken refuge in You": "O Lord, bring about (*kalaya*), accomplish (*sampādaya*), that which is most excellent—the state consisting of complete immersion (*samāveśa*). || 8 ||
Having rested upon the region of your ear, my most insignificant lamentations attain great value;
they become like drops of water fallen into the hollow of a bamboo flute.
The fragments bear the nature of pearls and gems. || 9 ||

"tvaditi": Having attained (*adhiśayya*) a state of great value—that is, worthlessness (*anarghatva*)—the phrase "they become even more trivial" suggests a lack of pride (*anauddhatya*). The word "going" (*yānti*), however, implies a firm conviction due to extreme devotion. Thus, the *arthāntaranyāsa* (corroboration by a general truth) regarding "in another lineage" is clear. || 9 ||

O Lord, what indeed cannot be obtained even by those people who are devoted to your name for even a moment, though it be out of hypocrisy? O you who have the moon as your crest-ornament, act in such a way that for me—
Through death by the sword, I attain the powers such as atomization (aṇimā) and the rest, according to my capacity.
What is the point? Even by those people who, out of deceit or pretense—even if not out of devotion to your true nature—take pleasure in your name, is anything not obtained?
From those whose intentions are unknown [to you], one certainly receives desired things such as honor and hospitality.
But those who are devoted to you in reality and constantly, they are by their very nature composed of the ultimate truth (paramārtha). Therefore...

O Lord whose crest is the cool-rayed moon, O remover of all torment, act in such a way that you may attain the sovereign power of *aṇimā* and the other [siddhis] in their previously described forms—free from death, untainted by time.

The intention of this verse is as follows: even though Brahmā and the others possess the sovereign powers (*vibhūtis*) such as *aṇimā* and so forth, they are nonetheless subject to the law of death, as stated by our Guru in the *Kramakeli*: "Even in the state of the venerable Sadāśiva, she who has seized fierce Time will arrive as the ground of destruction with her terrifyingly knitted brows. Therefore, protect me from death.

Make [the self] a vessel for the non-dual mass of consciousness-bliss and the powers such as *aṇimā*. But as for those who meditate upon this [body] because it is desirable for the sake of supernatural powers (*vibhūti*), O Lord, do you ever remember their desire?
Thus, by this truth, O Blessed One, the entire collection of enjoyments appears like a dream; and so forth—[all such claims] are indeed contradictory. 10.

O Śambhu, O Śarva, O moon-crested Śiva, O three-eyed one, wearer of the garland of skulls, you who take delight in the fierce mark of the skull, whose weapon is the gleaming and terrible trident; O ocean of compassion, whose fierce power is the architect of the three worlds, whose essence is Śakti!
O Śrīkaṇṭha, quickly destroy the burden of my inauspiciousness and grant me supreme perfection. 11.

"O Śambhu! [He is] he whose insignia are the formidable and terrifying skull-bowls belonging to all [beings], beginning with Brahmā; [he who bestows] the supreme [state], which consists of the bliss of ultimate non-duality, by shattering the burdens of impurity and the manifestations of duality. 11.
Therefore, O Lord, what state could there not be wherein the Blessed One exercises his creative power? What being, even one possessed of consciousness, could exist that Śaṅkara does not destroy?
Thus, you are ever supported by the unassailable great power of the Supreme Lord.
In this saṃsāra, I suffer alone, constantly beset by miseries from beginningless time. || 12 ||

What does this mean? The state of being the reality of those elements—the state of existence of the worlds and so forth—is the "being" (*sattā*) that belongs to the conscious [subject], from Sakala up to the Mantramaheśvaras. Thus, the activity known as "becoming" is indeed the sovereignty of the Lord.
By virtue of this state of abiding, the quality of being a ruler—consisting in the capacity to govern all subjects—belongs to the Blessed One alone, and not merely at some time. It is always so.

The state of being distressed by uninterrupted suffering arises from the failure to attain immersion during the period of emergence; this is the intended meaning here in the passage "I am alone" (p. 79), which pertains to the realm of Māyā.

If the state of being a subject centered on the body and so forth has dissolved, then all this is said to be identical with You alone; thus, it remains that the very sense of "I" regarding the body and so forth must be uprooted. 12.

Even if these— pain, old age, and death, which are most arrogant in granting boons— were to last but a moment, or even if the unstable objects of sense such as sound were highly esteemed, I, longing for perpetual happiness, would still desire that which endures for a long time.
To the supreme life-force of those devoted to the tasting of enjoyments, through meditation upon Your lotus feet. 13.

"Even though it is so"—here, in this world of *saṃsāra*, "let the most arrogant and unbearable [sorrows] remain for a moment" means let them stay for now; this is worldly speech. "One who is highly esteemed" means one who is desired by the whole world; "one whose nature is such" (*tacchīla*) means one who constantly longs for happiness in the form of non-dual bliss. "For the life-force that persists for a long time" (*cirasthāsnave*) means for that which has the habit of remaining for a long duration.
I long for life of such a kind:
one endowed with the supreme bliss and wonder of meditating upon the lotus of Your feet, which is the highest form of contemplation;
and primarily characterized by reflecting upon the lotus-like rays of Your splendor, which are united with the supreme joy of aesthetic rapture (camatkāra). For this very reason...
The state of being desirable. || 13 ||
O Lord, O Dhūrjaṭi, you who are skilled at destroying the suffering of those who bow before you, O treasure-house of welfare;
for me, who am terrified by birth and death and for whom [this world] is the sole abode of misery,
act now so that there may be supreme [attainments] that grant the taste of delightful sense-objects.

Those which grant the taste of the formative activity of form and so forth are the supreme, immovable accomplishments (*siddhi*); [this occurs] while still living, not upon the fall of the body, but indeed in the state of being alive. (p. 80)
Homage to him whose sole activity is the destruction of the great darkness of delusion, who possesses the mark of the moon, and who is the light that excels all other forms of illumination. 15.

*Namo moheti*: Salutation to Him whose activity is the dispelling of darkness; who, with no other task, is ever-striving to destroy the gloom of great delusion (*mahāmoha*) and the obscurity of illusion (*māyā*); and who possesses such a radiance that it surpasses all the lights of Agni, Soma, and the Sun—[salutation] to Him in His function of illuminating the destruction of darkness.
And the designation "Indulakṣmaṇa" is likewise appropriate; may all be auspicious. || 15 ||

Thus ends the commentary on the eleventh hymn, titled "The Assurance of Longing," within the *Stotrāvalī* composed by the venerable teacher Utpaladeva, as written by Śrī Kṣemarāja, the best among the wise. 11.
Oṃ! Nothing is accepted by you as a cooperative cause, nor is anything seen to be an obstacle to cognition.
For you yourself have indeed immersed yourself in everything; how is it that even now you still do not perceive it as such? || 1 ||

"Oṃ, sahakārī (the auxiliary cause). In Your vision—that is, in Your self-manifestation—there is no such thing as the ripening of impurities (*mala-paripāka*) or anything else that acts as an auxiliary cause (*sahakārin*), nor is there any obstacle whatsoever; for even that which is considered an auxiliary cause and so forth is pervaded by You alone. Nevertheless, why do You not see [me] even now? Why do You not look upon me despite such an extensive manifestation?
The meaning is "you reveal yourself to us"; the genitive case (*bhavataḥ*) is used in the sense of the object (*karman*). || 1 ||
Even from the collection of entities, even from the first of the sense faculties, and even from the midst of awakening,
it always arises of its own accord.
May I behold [the Lord] from whom all worldly activity has been removed.
"Even so"— how might I constantly perceive You alone as the Lord, everywhere and on all sides, from all existing things, from the senses, from cognitions, and from the Self,
having set aside all duality, that is, having cast off every distinction? || 2 ||
How could they possibly be born, and how could they ever come within the range of your vision?
Yet, rising again and again from every source— whether from land, water, or grass— you scatter all such objects with floods of nectar flowing from your gaze.

How so? By means of the repetition (*vīpsā*) "rising up, rising up from every single object," it means that in an extraordinary manner, at each successive stage of the objects of knowledge, one rises up, [thereby] [transcending] duality.

Having submerged [them] and manifested as the nature of consciousness (*cidrūpa*), those whom You sprinkle with the surging masses of nectar consisting of gnosis (*jñāna*)— they are revealed by the sign of manifestation, such as the state of being perpetually bristling with horripilation due to their great natural majesty; they are neither subject to birth nor are they perceived by worldly marks.
"How? [is used] in the sense of impossibility. || 3 ||
Satiated by the nectar flowing forth from having directly realized your true nature, their thirst is uprooted; intoxicated with joy, they wander according to their pleasure.

"Directly" means: nectar is bliss; those by whom thirst has been uprooted—meaning thirst for worldly power and the like has been extinguished so as not to arise again—are intoxicated and rejoice, sporting with independence, whereas others are entirely dependent upon their desires. || 4 ||
That in which there is no cognition of time— neither "always," nor "then," nor even "at one time"—
this indeed is your philosophical system.
And it is neither eternal, nor is it described otherwise.
"No," [he replies]. Because "always" (*sadā*) and "at one time" (*ekadā*) are used in mutual relation, the form of "at one time" is also "then" (*tadā*);
likewise, forms such as "when" (*yadā*) and "now" (*idānīm*) do not constitute any notion of time at all, because [Your] nature is not delimited by time.
Therefore, that which is non-general (*asāmānya*)—the "that" (*tat*)—and this manifest form, the "this" (*idam*), Your knowledge is not said to be eternal.
Nor is it impermanent, because permanence and impermanence are mutually contradictory; thus, linguistic usage is untenable regarding a form that realizes the nature of all things. || 5 ||
May this much alone be my constant perfection in yoga: that my mind, longing for the sight of you, may know [you] through mere intention.
[We have come] to your abode of nectar for the purpose of worshipping you.

83) *tvaditi* | To this extent—meaning not merely directed toward limited fruits—but by the mere intention (*abhisandhi*), that is, by the mere will (*icchāmātra*), [one prays]: 'May I always enter Your nectar-abode, the seat of supreme bliss; may I be completely absorbed therein. This is worship."
As before. || 6 ||
For those great-souled ones whose minds have blossomed through attaining your non-conceptual vision, stainless [qualities] manifest with ease.
And their actions and words were clearly manifest. || 7 ||

Regarding the term "non-conceptual" (*nirvikalpa*): for those devoted to devotion whose minds have blossomed through the attainment of direct realization that swallows up all conceptualization, their stainless deeds and words—which are capable of uplifting the world—shine forth clearly, having been rendered manifest with effortless ease. As the scripture says: "Whether by seeing or even by touching..."
"Established in the Kula conduct, these lords of heroes shall cause [beings] to cross over the vast ocean of existence. || 7 ||
O Blessed One,
dwelling within the very interval between your feet, I am fearless amidst those various stages of worldly existence.
He worshipped the Lord with unrestrained action. || 8 ||

"O Blessed One! [Thus he says: "Dwelling right in the middle of the two feet—that is, the powers of knowledge and action—I shall therefore remain fearless amidst those various and exceedingly vast planes of worldly existence; with my activities unconfined, may I be devoted to worship in all conditions, just as before. (8)
Completely absorbed within the interior of the lotus-bud of your feet,
he has shed all other desires.
"O Lord, at Your feet...

[means: I would wander from step to step by my own will, having become soiled while clinging all around and on every side to the interior of Your lotus-feet as before; that is, I would become a partaker in treading upon them.
Of what sort? One for whom other desires—that is, longings distinct from the yearning for the embrace of Your rays—have melted away and been stilled.
For he was completely satiated by the excessive and intense enjoyment—that is, the tasting—of the honey-like essence of bliss. || 9 ||
Even for one in whom the resolve to worship you has arisen as if out of hypocrisy, your presence necessarily arises in a manner appropriate to them. (10)
Regarding the phrase "of whom": for one such as the afflicted and so forth, this resolve arises not from hypocrisy or the like, but through the yoga of exclusive devotion devoid of wretchedness;
here, it is merely a mental construct, evidenced by the sign of being endowed with the pride of a single repetition, which protects the people of the three worlds from falling into all the hells.
The example is "proper" (ucita), meaning that which is capable of fulfilling the requirement of merely that much [of the object]. || 10 ||
O Blessed One, by means of a mind that is entirely independent of others and entirely of a single flavor,
it is easy to attain [the state] that rests in total tranquility.
"Shall I drink from my Lord until I am satiated? (11)

"O Blessed One! [he asked]. "How may I experience identity with You—You who are the Lord, the resting place of all, and omnipresent—and therefore easily accessible? With what kind of mind, characterized by an absolute and supreme intensity, should I experience this oneness with You, solely through the devotion of absorption in You, and not for the sake of any fruit whatsoever?"
By this qualification—"one who has a longing for the nectar"—unfeigned devotion is expressed as the opposite of the meaning of the previously cited verse. || 11 ||
"All that has been rejected by you is indeed to be abandoned; however, that which consists of you alone is to be accepted—this is the summary of the essential point. (12)

"By you": whatever is to be abandoned without the recognition of identity with You, that very thing, when recognized as being composed of You, is to be accepted; this is the "Collection of Essences," the true nature of all traditions. 12.
The multitude of entities that move within you is worshipped primarily as being identical with your own self;
even those existing outside of you are [worshipped] merely as non-existence [relative to you].
How can he become the Lord, or how is he to be worshipped? || 13 ||

"O Bhavanta! [The meaning is: that multitude of entities which exists as non-different from you, moving within you, is primarily—that is, by virtue of its very preeminence—worshipped as the Lord by the knower of reality. But for you, whose nature is Light, let alone external entities, even mere non-existence does not exist externally; why is this so?
Furthermore, [the Lord] is worshipped again because everything exists solely as the nature of conscious light; otherwise, it would lack consciousness.

The word "only" (mātra) is intended to express an emphatic exaggeration. For it has already been established in the *Pratyabhijñā* that even non-existence, when being cognized, is nothing but the nature of consciousness, and so forth. By this, the impossibility of worship for those who maintain the doctrine of duality is indicated. 13
May I behold it constantly— soundless, free from conceptual construction, and undistracted—
even amidst agitation, as a direct perception.
O Three-eyed One, [I seek] you alone from every side.

"Silent" means: O Three-eyed One, even amidst agitation and the expansion of the perceived and the perceiver, having rendered [yourself] directly present and free from conceptual construction, you alone—whose sole nature is the light of consciousness—are eternally and constantly without expectation.

Having removed all obstacles everywhere, I shall behold and realize it for myself—of what nature? It is "soundless," distinct from the *śabdabrahman* (the Word-Brahman) described by the Grammarians and others. According to the principle that "my source is the Great Brahman," because the Blessed One, the Supreme Brahman, is the most excellent, [it is free] precisely from conceptual constructions (*vikalpa*) consisting of mental cultivation and the like.
It has emerged in the form of infinite pure consciousness alone. || 14 ||
O Lord, reveal Your own abode,
wherein You are ever united with the Supreme Goddess;
[therein dwell] those who are of equal rank to the dust of the Master’s feet.
How much less can servants be objects of trust? || 15 ||
"Reveal [Your] own abode, the nature of consciousness! Thus the Supreme Goddess, the Sovereign Parā, speaks;

and the servant's appropriate address—"O feet of the Lord," and so forth—indicates that we are to be held and nourished as servants, expressing our constant attachment through our status as being on the same level as the quality of *rajas*. || 15 ||
Even when you have come within the range of my sight, why do you withdraw? O Lord, how can you not remain here for even a single moment with me, your servant?
To what living being is he not an object of sight? || 16 ||

"Into the path of vision": even though you have reached the path of vision—the range of direct perception—even so, why do you withdraw from my trusted servant, my slave? You do not withdraw at all; rather, the sense is that I remain standing having seized hold of you. Now, one might ask: "Having perceived me directly, why are you not satisfied? To this he says: "Of what living being's sight... [the rest of the verse follows].

O Knower, even when unknown, you indeed become the object for everyone in states such as being momentarily enraged or delighted; for you manifest at some time or other for all. Yet I am your unmetaphorical servant, never abandoning you for even a moment.
Or rather, even if you are directly perceived, why do you [withdraw] during my emergence from meditative absorption?
It should be understood that even for a servant who has been comforted, [the master] moves away. || 16 ||
O All-pervading Lord, by means of the continuous and ever-flowing stream of the nectar of the consciousness of oneness, which is pure and transparent—
Bringing about the supreme non-duality through immersion, may I attain You and my own true nature, and experience joy. || 17 ||

"Unity": that very non-dual vision of the consciousness of unity is the stream belonging to immortality—that is, to supreme bliss—which is clear and capable of reflecting the universe. By means of that stream, which flows forth continuously and without interruption, there is a flooding, a complete filling from all sides; because of that, [I behold] You and my own body.
When shall I attain joy and contentment, bringing my own contracted nature—which I hold dear—to a state of supreme non-difference and oneness? || 17 ||
From this world of yours, which is the very essence of my realization, I have obtained [the sense of] "I" from that [source]; yet,
even an atom's worth of it is established in the universe.
May it be accomplished so that I may be honored by you. || 18 ||
"I" — that which resides in all things, whatever appears to me anywhere, in which the entire world is contained and the fullness of everything is embraced;
this "I" of yours is the essence and the most excellent nature of all perceptions everywhere. Therefore, grant me even a particle as small as a drop of musk.
"May I become worshipped by You through whatever [means] presents itself for union—that is, through the process of swallowing each respective object of knowledge—be it even as much as an atom.
This statement is made out of an extreme longing; however, there are no parts to the fullness of one's own I-consciousness (ahantā). || 18 ||
Perceiving that very form of yours in its infinite manifestations at every moment, may I clearly behold you alone, the Lord of all, whose nature is the universe. (19)
"Immeasurable" (*aparimita*) means that whatever it may be, it is you alone; because it manifests as such, it is of your nature.
"The universal form" (*viśvarūpa*) refers to the fact that even a single location is Brahman.
It is excellent because it is full through its stability, effortless, and by virtue of having the nature of truth. || 19 ||
Why does your mind not wander toward that very same desired object which has come within the range of your senses?
For there is no such impairment of its nature.
And for the fulfillment of my desire, she alone is the supreme [means]. || 20 ||

"May it be so! [He says: "Tameva—" whatever desired object the mind wanders toward, that very thing may exist within Your limbs through its nature as pure consciousness; therefore, why does it not wander toward the desired object?
Act in such a way that it indeed wanders thus. This being so, there is no injury to its essential nature (*prakṛti*).
Because there is no obstruction to this desire, my own essential longing—to obtain the nature of the pure mass of consciousness—is fulfilled.
By this, he says in his mind: "I shall wander within the mind according to my pleasure, so that I may become the very essence of full manifestation. (20)
O Blessed One, by your power, it is said that hundreds of people—
even those who act like common plowmen— have indeed perceived [the truth] with this very eye.
They always behold your form before them. || 21 ||

"By the hundreds" means: even while acting with the behavior of a plowman, by Your power— that is, through the activity of experience instigated by You— they always see and enter Your own body, Your beautiful form of consciousness, right before them in every direction, even at the very moment the senses are opened.
The meaning is that among hundreds and thousands, some are rare and extraordinary (alaukika). || 21 ||
That thought does not arise which is not composed of your will; O Blessed One, you always ordain that everything other than the auspicious is otherwise.
Therefore, being identical with you, as I wander or remain constantly upon this earth, I am established in the festival of worshipping your stainless feet, which are never subject to contradiction.
"No," [he says]. By the first quarter, it was stated that all cognitions are, from the perspective of ultimate reality (*paramārthataḥ*), composed of devotion to Śiva;

by the second, that all activities are performed by the Lord. "Just so" means that his joy in worshipping the rays of that [Lord] is free from contraction and remains uncontradicted—unremoved by anything whatsoever. || 22 ||
May eloquence arise clearly before me regarding your profound utterances;
for even though my power is exercised therein, [it remains dependent upon them].
And his devotion to the worship of the Lord was incessant. || 23 ||

Regarding the phrase *bhavadīyaiḥ* ("by yours"): regarding the phrase *gabhīrabhāṣiteṣu* ("in the profound utterances"): may my *pratibhā*—a discerning intelligence (*prajñā*) characterized by ever-new flashes of insight—arise before me first, with respect to your sentences which, although appearing on the surface to have a meaning consisting of distinctions, actually contain within them secret meanings; and immediately after that, may that [insight] arise, which is supramundane.
Having made your worship uninterrupted, let devotion arise as your very addiction.
Even in the context of worldly discourse, this entire collection of objects always appears to me as a part of you,
and not otherwise.
He has attained a state of being worthy of reverence by his very nature. || 24 ||

Regarding the word "vyavahāra" (worldly transaction): may this entire collection of objects appear to me as being non-different from the Lord who consists of consciousness, such that it stands as if it were a limb or a constituent part of Him even in the sphere of worldly transaction;
let it not, however, become something to be valued in itself as a cause of pleasure and so forth, while remaining unknown as being identical with You. 24.
(90) Wherever the mind wanders day after day within its objects by its own natural impulse, [it becomes] his sphere of activity.
Even though I am active, may I always remain undisturbed and skillful in serving you. || 25 ||

Regarding the word "manasi" (in the mind): even though one has extended or is engaged in grasping toward objects such as those to be abandoned (*heyādi*), may I remain unagitated—that is, free from craving—and indeed skillful (*catura*) in that service to You, Your worship. The particle "eva" (indeed) is placed out of its usual order. || 25 ||
O Blessed One, it is solely by Your will that I have become Your servant; I possess no power of my own in this matter.
How then can I [describe] Your radiant countenance?
I do not see this as anything wonderful at all in you. || 26 ||
"O Blessed One! [He says: "By the will of the Blessed One alone"—by the word "alone" (eva), he expresses the absolute sovereignty of the descent of power (*śaktipāta*).

"Even so" (*tathāpi*) means: even though such service has been obtained, I do not at any time (*jātu*)—that is, during the state of emergence (*vyutthāna*)—behold the beautiful reflection of the Face, which is the path of the Supreme Power. This [reflection] is the nature of the subject consisting of the body and so forth, appropriate to the state of emergence. I do not see it.
I do not find it. || 26 ||
Alas, what might have befallen those who, full of longing for you, gaze upon you with eyes fixed on your form?
Or what means of accomplishment would have borne fruit? || 27 ||

"Samutsukāḥ" means those who are intensely eager, longing with a weight of devotion. Regarding the phrase "from every form," having encountered object after object, what that [experience] is can only be personally realized by him; it cannot be described, nor can we conceive of what the means for it might be. || 27 ||
(91) May existence be for me through the state of being both existent and non-existent;
likewise, may nothing whatsoever exist, nor anything other than you. 28.

Regarding the phrase "existence and non-existence": may those things which are designated as "existent" exist for me as existent by virtue of being composed of you; and whatever is spoken of, let that be nothing at all without being composed of you. || 28 ||
That which is nothing at all, let that remain as nothing; yet let there be something for me. In every way, may you be that very thing for me.
He becomes honored everywhere by all. || 29 ||

Regarding the phrase "that which is 'not something'": that which is spoken of by the world as "nothing at all" because it is not to be accepted—that for me is indeed "not something," yet let it be "not something" consisting of all differentiation. However, that which is intended as "something" because it is to be accepted—for me that is indeed "something," and as "something," it is unique (asāmānya).

Let that reality which has only one witness—namely, one’s own direct experience—be as it may; or rather, whatever in the world exists as a mass of consciousness, because it is not recognized for what it is, it does not appear as anything at all. But that which consists of duality and is non-existent, appearing as something due to the delusion of *māyā*, let that "something" be nothing for me, and let nothing be anything.
The meaning is that there should be no perversion as occurs in the worldly state; by this much, you, whose nature is consciousness, have been found everywhere and honored—may it be auspicious! (29)

Thus ends the commentary composed by the illustrious Kṣemarāja on the twelfth hymn, titled "The Revelation of the Secret," within the *Stotrāvalī* (Garland of Hymns) composed by the venerable teacher Utpaladeva.
p. 92) Oṃ tat sat.
In brief, [this is] the definition of pleasure and pain.
O Lord, hear this which stands before me:
union with you, my master, is happiness; separation from you, O Lord, is indeed suffering. (1)

Regarding the phrase "in summary": now we shall explain the *Saṃgrahastotra*, distinguished by the beautiful composition crafted by the author of this hymn. As for the designation "Prayogarūḍhi" (Established Practice) seen in the manuscripts, that is merely an intermediate term;
[the true state is] having entered into the Bhairava of Consciousness through direct realization, even during the state of emergence (*vyutthāna*).
Having brought that [object] into manifestation through its powerful latent impression (*saṃskāra*), he speaks in order to discern the object as it appears:
"O Lord, hear in brief—that is, in summary—the nature of pleasure and pain manifesting for me alone, and not for anyone else. The address "O Lord" is used here.

By means of the process of absorption into one's own self alone, for the sake of bringing the Supreme Lord face-to-face, [the author], like a secret mantra containing extraordinary words such as "feet," states His definition: "This," namely, the union manifesting through direct perception, [has been taught] by you, the Lord, the Master of Consciousness (Cinnātha).

The bliss that arises from attaining oneness through immersion (*samāveśa*) is "sukha"; here the suffix *ṣyañ* is used in the sense of the word itself (*svārthe*). That very state is "sukhya," and it is indeed "sukhya" alone—the particle "eva" (indeed) present in the subsequent clause should be applied here in both ways as well. For separation from the Lord—that is, the failure to recognize the true nature of the Lord—is itself suffering. || 1 ||
O Lord, having completely polished away even that state of mine which was exceedingly beautiful during the time when You were not manifest, [reveal Yourself].
Reveal your own stainless true nature.

"Antar" means: since this is so, therefore the word "api" (even) is displaced in its order [to be read after "atitarām"]; thus, "antar" refers to that internal impurity of your non-manifestation (*akhyāti*) belonging to me, which occurred at the time when you were not manifest—even though it was exceedingly beautiful (*atitarāmaṇīya*).
In this immersion (*samāveśa*), there exists that form consisting of the impressions (*saṃskāra*) of the vital breath (*prāṇa*) and so forth;
indeed, since the descent of power (*śaktipāta*), you have cast that away for me many times.

Having wiped it away and completely rubbed it out—even that which is most subtle—both internally and externally, [you have revealed] your own consciousness-nature (*cinmaya*), which belongs to all as their very self.
Reveal your stainless true nature; expand it! || 2 ||
And he says that this alone is my supreme desire: "In your body, which is filled with the universe, consists of the essence of the nectar of consciousness, and is free from decay..."
Whether I live or whether my life be otherwise, let it be so for me as I constantly remain worshipping the Lord. || 3 ||

Regarding the word "tāvaka" (your own): that which shines must shine only while being of the very nature of light. And since space, time, and so forth are themselves shining, it is established without effort that their own nature cannot be the differentiator [of that light]. Thus, the state of being the form of the universe belongs to the essence of consciousness—which is of the nature of bliss—within its unchanging and indestructible self-nature.

The suffix *śatṛ* (in *tiṣṭhan* and *arcann*) indicates the cause—that one is unable to stand while worshipping, and unable to worship while standing—and it expresses their state of being perpetually engaged (*nityapravṛttatā*). "Standing" (*sthiti*) refers to the attainment of various states of being; "worship" (*arcā*) is the preoccupation with focused contemplation of that [object]. Thus, in what follows, by the word "other" (*anyat*), there is a high regard for the state of the nature of consciousness (*cidrūpatā*).
This expresses disregard for the state and its object. || 3 ||
Now, one might object: "Since the stages beginning with 'living' (jīvat) consist of ego-inflation (abhimāna), why are they accepted?

Anticipating this doubt, he says the following in order to state that even the ego-inflations of one established in Your true nature are indeed endowed with extraordinary wonder; otherwise, even the absence of ego-inflation would amount to nothing at all.
"I am the Lord,
I alone am handsome, I am learned, I am fortunate; who else is there like me in this world?"— thus he considers himself to be magnificent.
But those who are devoted to you are held in the highest honor.

"I am the Lord" (p. 94). For one who is devoted to You—who has attained identity with You through immersion in You—there is no "Supreme" other than You; rather, he alone is the Lord, entirely independent, and I myself am possessed of form as the conscious Self.

Endowed with a praiseworthy nature, I am one in whom has arisen *paṇḍā*—wisdom that correctly perceives reality—and thus I am fortunate (*subhaga*), being desirable to all because of the intensity of the essence of supreme bliss. What more need be said? Who else is equal to me? None at all; for I alone am the self consisting of consciousness and bliss.
"Because of the direct realization of the Self of the universe"—such is this "honored state" (*mānitā*); this state of self-identification shines and blazes.
Otherwise, however, even if it is free from conceptual construction (*avikalpitā*), that which is considered [merely] awakening and so forth is contracted and indeed impure;
like one who has ascended the steps of his own staircase, his standing would be near the Lord. But as for the other, [the state] of conceptual constructions...
Because he belongs to the external level due to his aversion, even though he is thus honored by one who is devoted to you, it is fitting;
O God of gods, [he is so] because his birth was obtained through the withdrawal of the proclamation of the non-dual nectar of your being.
Therefore, by means of the consciousness of things as they truly exist, make me worthy of worshipping your feet.

"O Lord! [He says: "O God of gods, O Sovereign of the Ashoka tree! By means of that consciousness—which has obtained its birth through the withdrawal of the manifestation of the bliss of oneness with You, which is proclaimed as the nectar of non-duality—make me, who am worshipped by Your own rays, one with all existing objects whose nature is pure Consciousness. The word *tat* (that) refers to this.
In relation to the preceding verse, it refers to the reason. || 5 ||
Anticipating the Lord’s statement, “Of what nature is this prayer? I shall do what is appropriate for you,” he says:
“The Supreme Lord himself is meditated upon, then beheld, and thereafter touched.”
By your grace, may that place where the great festival of Pūrṇima is celebrated always belong to me. || 6 ||

Therefore, being identical with you, as I wander or remain constantly upon this earth, I am one for whom there is an uninterrupted festival of worshiping your stainless feet, which are themselves unassailable. (22)
"No," [he says]. By the first quarter, it was stated that all forms of knowledge consist essentially of devotion to Śiva from the perspective of ultimate reality (*paramārtha*);

by the second, it was stated that all activities are performed by the Lord. "Just so" means that the joy of worshipping His rays—which has lost all contraction and is unimpeded—cannot be removed by anyone. 22.
Therefore, may eloquence properly arise before me regarding your profound utterances;
for even though my power is exercised therein, [it remains insufficient].
And an unceasing devotion to the worship of the Blessed One. || 23 ||

Regarding the phrase *bhavadīyaiḥ* ("by yours"): regarding the phrase *gabhīrabhāṣiteṣu* ("in the profound utterances"): may my intuition (*pratibhā*)—a wisdom that manifests ever-newly—arise before me first, correctly and without error, with respect to those sentences of yours which, although appearing to have the primary meaning of differentiation, contain within them secret meanings; and immediately after that, "that" (*tat*), which is supramundane.
Having made this uninterrupted, may a passionate devotion for the worship of Bhava arise. || 23 ||
Even in the context of worldly discourse, this entire collection of objects always appears to me as a part of You,
and not otherwise.
He has attained a state of being worthy of respect by his very nature. || 24 ||

Regarding the word "vyavahāra" (conventional usage): may this collection of objects appear to me as being non-different from the Lord who consists of consciousness—just as these very parts exist as constituent limbs within conventional usage—and not as something that, while unknown to be identical with You, has attained a state of being worthy of regard merely on its own account as a cause of pleasure and the like. || 24 ||
(90) Wherever the mind wanders daily through its own natural impulse within its objects of perception, [it is there that one should apply the antidote].
Even though I am active, may I always remain unagitated and skillful in serving you. || 25 ||

Regarding the word "manasi" (in the mind): although I may be extended toward objects such as those to be abandoned (*heya*) and so forth, or engaged in grasping them, may I remain unagitated—that is, free from craving—and indeed skillful (*catura*), that is, proficient, in your service, which is your worship (*yuṣmatparicaryā*); the particle *eva* is used here with a shifted position [emphasizing "skillful"]. || 25 ||
O Blessed One, it is solely by Your will that I have become Your servant; I possess no power of my own in this matter.
Nevertheless, how is it that this [servant] beholds Your orb-like face?
I do not see this as anything wonderful at all in you. || 26 ||

"O Blessed One! [He replies: "By the will of the Blessed One alone"—by the word "alone" (eva), he expresses the absolute sovereignty of the descent of power (*śaktipāta*). "Even so" (*tathāpi*) means: even though such service has been obtained, I do not at any time (*jātu*)—that is, during the state of emergence (*vyutthāna*)—behold the beautiful reflection of the Face, which is the path of the Supreme Power (*paraśaktimārga*). This [reflection] is the nature of the subject consisting of the body and so forth, which is appropriate for the state of emergence. I do not see it at any point while in that emergent state.
I do not find it. || 26 ||
Alas, what might have befallen those who, full of longing for you, gaze upon you with eyes wide with wonder?
What means of accomplishment would have borne fruit thereby? || 27 ||

"Samutsukāḥ" means those who are intensely eager, longing with a weight of devotion. Regarding the phrase "from every form," having encountered object after object, that [experience] must be realized by oneself alone; it cannot be described, nor can it be said what its means are, for such a thing is inconceivable to us. || 27 ||
p.
95) Regarding "one meditates": by means of the state of abiding, one meditates while contemplating the reality with the mind alone, devoid of vocal utterance;
that [reality] is observed, it shines forth through immersion (*samāveśa*), and from that, it is touched.

In this great festival of worship, indicated by the term "mahotsava" (great festival) which signifies its supreme desirability, one is made one with [the deity] through a most intense embrace, spontaneously and not through a succession of rituals such as recitation or performance; and this occurs by means of one's own unconditioned, conscious body, which is devoid of any distinct form other than that [of the deity].

By saying "through my own experience" (*mamānubhāvataḥ*), he proclaims his state of being filled with joy due to attachment to that [experience], meaning "through the operation of your experience. || 6 ||
Praising this very point, he said: "The vision of things as they truly are,
and that great festival of worshipping you— "
This pair, mutually dependent upon one another, ever flourishes among those possessed of devotion. || 7 ||

Regarding the word "yat" (which): the perception (*vijñāna*) of things as they truly exist is not the great festival of your non-dual worship; yet, without that [worship], there is no knowledge of things as they truly exist. Thus, these two are mutually dependent, and both of them always flourish through you alone for those possessed of devotion.
Because of simultaneous manifestation. || 7 ||
The elixir of the nectar of worshipping you, continuously poured through the various doors of the senses,
fills the goblets of all states of being.
Even while drinking [the nectar], may I become intoxicated. || 8 ||

Regarding the word "tat" (that): one intent on this aspiration, preceded by the throbbing means (*upāya*), says that all existents (*sarvabhāva*) are indeed cups (*caṣaka*), vessels for drinking; when these are filled—that is, saturated—with the nectar of the identity of consciousness through the vision of the Great Reality (*mahārtha-dṛṣṭi*) via the gateway of the eyes and other senses, then, by the process of taking [that] up, there arises the form of the ascent to the Fourth (*turya*).
(96) May I drink this elixir of the rasa of worshiping you on all sides until my intoxication arises; this is what I pray for—I entreat the Lord himself. 8.
O Lord, not even an atom of anything else exists;
everything unfolds as self-luminous within Your city.
In that regard, grant [your favor] always to me, your worshiper. || 9 ||

Regarding the phrase "knowable by another" (*anyavedya*): in that city of yours, within the form of the self which is consciousness (*cidātman*) during inhalation (*pūraka*), because there is no other distinct entity whatsoever, there is not even an atom of a knowable object (*vedya*) that is different;
rather, everything consisting of the grasped and the grasper unfolds as nothing but self-luminous. In that state, for me who am intent upon your worship—
Always maintain a state of firm immersion.
O Supreme Lord, although I have been appointed to the station of a servant by Your own will,
have I not been made a worthy recipient through Your very glance?
Or even by the act of massaging the feet. || 10 ||
Regarding the phrase "in the state of a servant" (*dāsadhāmnīti*): although he has thus petitioned, not obtaining what the world desires, he speaks as if dejected, saying "servant" (*dāsa*).
For it has already been stated that the descent of power (*śaktipāta*) is indeed independent, occurring neither through the prompting of another nor by other means;

one who has been made a fit vessel (*pātrita*), that is, rendered a worthy recipient, by means of the Śāmbhava immersion (*samāveśa*), which consists in entering into the direct realization of the Supreme (*parasākṣātkāra*).

Through the act of massaging the feet, which brings the joy of immersion into the power (*śakti*) of Rudra, the meaning of the worldly Lord is expressed by way of resonance (*anuraṇana*), as previously described. || 10 ||
O Lord, at the time of the descent of power (*śaktipāta*), you never engage in deliberation.
What has come upon me today, that you delay in the act of revealing yourself? (11)
Regarding the term *śaktipāta*: as if reproaching the Lord, he addresses Him by saying "the descent of power" (*śaktipāta*).

The address "O Lord" (*īśa*) is appropriate because it accords with the sequence of the independent descent of power (*svatantra-śaktipāta*). [The questioner asks: "What has arrived?"—meaning, what is this manner [of yours] when the descent of power, which consists of grace, has already occurred at some time, on some occasion, or today? What has come about? What is this way of acting?
If you delay even now, making a waste of time, regarding that necessary duty which consists of the manifestation of your own Self as pure consciousness—do not do so! (11)
In each and every object,
whether external or internal, you are always present together with the Supreme Goddess, filling the three worlds.
I would behold that which was worshipped by my own hands. || 12 ||

Regarding the word "therein" (*tatra*): once again, one intent on aspiring for immersion into the Blessed One says, "therein. "Externally" means in external objects such as blue and so forth, and "internally" in [states] such as pleasure and so forth; I would behold—that is, I would directly realize—you who shine forth, joined with the supreme power of the Supreme Lord (*pārameśvarī parā śakti*), eternally connected, and—as before—filled with the universe consisting of the three worlds.

It is worshipped here by one’s own hand through the process of awakening the central vital power (*prāṇa-śakti*) within the midst of the five whirlpools, by means of the fuel consisting of the offering of the entire universe; for the hand is *śakti*, as it is stated in the *Āmnāya*: "The hand is proclaimed to be *śakti*."
This is worthy of worship. || 12 ||
By merely directing my intention toward the palace of the Lord, may I always ascend it without obstruction and become one who drinks the supreme nectar-wine of his grace.
Having attained tranquility through the medicinal drink. || 13 ||

"Master" (svāmī): Desiring as his fruit precisely that state of form which consists of the eternal immersion in the Light, he says "Master. [He refers to] the Master's own mansion, most desirable, a collection of his own abodes, exceedingly lofty, and pertaining to Śakti.

The phrase "merely by intention" means that, independent of vocalization, instruments, and so forth, having established a firm resolve through mere will alone, one ascends and takes possession of the ground of the body and other elements by placing them beneath oneself;
thus, one attains bliss through the play of drinking the supreme nectar-liquor of grace, as previously explained.

May I always be filled with bliss through the power of resonance; by means of the suggestion (*dhvani*) of the poetic figure of illustration (*dṛṣṭāntālaṅkāra*), the meaning of the Lord of the World is [conveyed] as before. || 13 ||
Because it bestows that aesthetic wonder through the mere act of contact upon all objects of auspicious meaning, your body [is so].
Those possessed of unwavering devotion worship [them]. || 14 ||

Regarding the word "yad" (that which): he states the means of worship already established with the word "yad. Although, by the power of *māyā*, all things possess the nature of being either to be rejected or accepted, nevertheless, because they are in reality composed of consciousness (*cinmaya*), all objects have only auspicious purposes (*subhaga-prayojana*). Among those [objects]...

Whatever among the objects of the senses has come within the range of the senses—such as their form, touch, and so forth—is perfectly offered and bestowed as an extraordinary wonder (*camatkṛti*) by means of the activity of consciousness (*saṃvid-vyāpāra*), which consists of perception, conceptualization, and mental construction (*saṃvit-saṅkalpa-vikalpa*), according to the rule of mere contact (*sparśamātra-vidhinā*). This is that which is referred to by the word "that" (*tām iti*). By means of that [activity] which is indicated by the pronoun "yat," [the object is offered].

Worshipping Your body—which is of the nature of consciousness—in its true essence with unwavering devotion and ever-fresh immersion, they honor You through the process of satiation and thus find rest in You alone. 14.
Throbbing with your own self, you expand the entire universe;
perceiving your own form, you perceive the world;
for you yourself reel with your own inner essence.
From that, the mandala of phenomena shines forth. || 15 ||

99) You expand [the universe]. Now, having raised the objection as to how there can be worship of the Lord, whose nature is pure, by means of impure objects, he says the following in order to state that objects are pure because they possess the nature of the Lord in all states.
"You expand" means: throbbing and shining by means of your own consciousness-nature (*cinmaya*), you expand the entire universe;

through the vibration of the manifestation of your own blossoming self, you cause it to bloom. Likewise, while intuiting your own nature—that is, while marveling at your own essential being—you intuit the entire universe.

Through relishing, you bring about a mass of bliss; and you who yourself whirl with your own essence of consciousness, because of your fullness, you throb with an upward surging—within that sphere of being, the entire multitude of objects shines forth and blossoms upon the ground of consciousness. Thus, by this, the essence of non-duality belongs to the universe.

The maintenance, withdrawal, and emanation, which are appropriate to their respective states, have been described in sequence as having the nature of the vibration of the powers of knowledge, will, and action;

for even in the state of pure consciousness (*saṃvit-tattva*), where there is no sequence, the inseparability of the powers of emanation, maintenance, and withdrawal is described as eternal through the distinction of their functional exclusions (*vyāvṛtti-bheda*). It is with reference to this that [the following] is said:

This is the conventional usage regarding the sequence. And so it is stated in the *Śrīpūrvaśāstra*: "Because of being the sovereign of activity, because of being the impeller dependent upon that [activity], because of the cessation of desire, and because of abiding in one's own nature, [the Lord], though non-different, is fivefold.
This is the presentation of the processes of emanation (*sṛṣṭi*), maintenance (*sthiti*), and withdrawal (*saṃhāra*) by way of their inversion.
For the sake of revealing the ultimate reality, which is non-sequential due to its nature as pure consciousness. || 15 ||
O Lord, he who perceives this entire circle of objects as conceptual construction sees it all as Your own body,
for the world is completely filled by the side of Your own Self.
For him who is eternally happy, whence can there be fear? || 16 ||

Regarding the word "ya" (who): One might object, "Granted that objects distinct from the state of being the Supreme Lord may possess purity; but how can this be so in the realm of Māyā, which is agitated by the obstacle of duality? Anticipating this doubt, [the author] speaks of the destruction of the expansion of the obstacle of duality with the word "ya. O Lord, the circle of objects...
Having rendered the entire range of objects of cognition free from conceptual construction, and by abandoning the intellect that engages in rejection,

acquisition, and so forth, the excellent yogi— abiding in the potency of the Śrī-Bhairavī-mudrā— makes his own body consist of pure consciousness and perceives it, directly realizing it like a reflection appearing upon the opening of the surface of a mirror.
When the universe has been filled on all sides by his own side— that is, by identity with consciousness— and has been brought to a state of non-difference from himself,
how could there be any fear for one who is eternally blissful and a mass of supreme bliss, since the obstacle of duality has been uprooted?
It was rightly said by you previously: "For some reason or other, they worship your form, being endowed with unwavering devotion. (16)
O Lord, even the Kālakūṭa poison resting in the hollow of Your throat is a great nectar to me;
whereas even the nectar consumed by Your body—
If this mode of functioning through differentiation does not please me. || 17 ||

Regarding the word "kaṇṭhe" (in the throat): praising this very non-dual vision (*advayadṛṣṭi*), he says "kaṇṭhe. Even the great poison Kālakūṭa, though situated within the corner of your throat, remains in contact with your body; appearing as non-different from you, it is for me a great nectar (*mahāmṛta*) because it bestows supreme pervasion (*paramavyāpti*). For it has been said: [The original Sanskrit verse follows: *kaṇṭhe kālakūṭam api te saṃsthitaṃ mṛtyudāyakam | tvadaṅgasparśanād eva jāyate sudhāmayam ||* (Note: The provided text fragment ends mid-sentence regarding the citation.)
"Even poison acts as nectar"—this means that if the dualistic state of your body appears without touching the vision of non-dual consciousness, then because it is unreal, it does not please me;
that is to say, it is not an object of my desire. || 17 ||
Even though I am adorned by a face constantly occupied with the songs of your own delirious, blood-stained speech,
may I nevertheless be engaged in the act of worshipping you.
His heart is always encompassed by his beloved.

"From you" (tvat). Desiring thus to always maintain this non-dual immersion within oneself, he says "from you. Being constantly joined with songs that consist of your own outpourings—which, due to the power of immersion, are uttered without deliberate intent, yet are red with the manifestation of devotion and passion, and are sweet and beautiful—[he remains ever united].
"May I be adorned with a face of exceedingly beautiful luster; moreover, by the very act of worshipping you—the beloved who explains the eternal reality—may I [attain this]. (p.

May I always be one whose disposition—that is, whose mind—is encompassed by fearlessness, and who has likewise encompassed—meaning thoroughly understood—the disposition, that is, the true nature, of her as well. (18)
Alas, the will of the Supreme Lord cannot be measured, even by me;
for thus has my body been granted, overflowing with nectar.
In the same way, he does not permit himself to drink his own [blood]. || 19 ||

Regarding the word *īhitam*: one might indeed wonder, "Even though you have attained the wonder of immersion (*samāveśa*), why are you still intent on desiring immersion again and again? Anticipating this doubt, he says *īhitam*. Alas, the *īhita*—the playful manifestation (*vilasita*)—belonging to the Supreme Lord cannot be counted or measured; and thus it is with me.

The meaning is this: although my own essential nature—a body consisting of a mass of bliss overflowing with nectar—has been granted and bestowed as a favor so that it might be drunk and tasted, [the mind] does not permit nor consent to drinking it "thus" (tathā) according to its desire without cessation;
rather, it impels one back toward the very plane of worldly emergence (vyutthāna). Therefore, this [state] is called "longing" (ākāṅkṣā). For...
Thus, from that [it follows]. || 19 ||
O Lord of Umā, may I always enter into you— your own essential nature, which is unfathomable, free from conceptual construction, non-dual, and the devourer of all objects.
I would worship him and offer praise. || 20 ||

"Thou"— [entering] Thee, who art unfathomable, indefinable, free from conceptual construction, the non-dual nature of consciousness, whose essence is non-duality, one's own self, the very nature belonging to all things composed of the six paths (*ṣaḍadhvan*), and whose habit is to devour [all things], O Lord of Umā, Sovereign of the Supreme Bhaṭṭārikā, I am always [thus].

"I shall worship; for that worship is indeed absorption through reverence"—with this conviction, one should worship on all sides and in every way, and one should praise with the essence of the perfect contemplation of non-duality. May there be auspiciousness! 20.
Thus ends the commentary composed by Śrī Kṣemarāja on the thirteenth hymn, titled *Saṅgrahastotra*, within the *Stotrāvalī* composed by the venerable teacher Utpaladeva. 13.
Oṃ! Before my own Lord, the treasury of victory and Lakṣmī, may I for a moment savor the nectar-like essence of the proclamation of his triumph. (1)

"Victory to Lakṣmī! This *Jayastotra* (Hymn of Victory) is also indeed the intention of the author himself. Immediately upon the direct realization that the city is the "repository"—the fitting abode—of Jayalakṣmī, the supreme glory of excellence, the very proclamation of victory provides such bliss that I savor it like the essence of nectar and experience a moment of wonder.
The repeated mention of the word "moment" (kṣaṇa) suggests the ease with which this savor may be attained. || 1 ||
Victory to you, O sole Rudra, sole Śiva, Mahādeva, Maheśvara!
O Śarva, beloved of Pārvatī, first-born of all the gods.
"Victory to the One" (jayaika): first, the two vocatives are for the purpose of manifesting non-duality (*advayatā*). There is a Vedic scripture stating "Rudra is one";

there is one Śiva, but not many according to the standpoint of dualism (*bhedavāda*). Pārvatī is the supreme power (*parā śakti*), and he is the progenitor—the first—of all the gods (*gīrvāṇa*). || 2 ||
Victory to you, O Lord of the three worlds, whose eye is marked by the unique sign of the lotus!
Victory to you, whose neck bears the Kālakūṭa poison that removes the distress of the afflicted world! 3.

"Victory to Him of the Three Worlds! Regarding His status as the Lord of the three worlds: He possesses a single, non-dual, indicative, and peerless supramundane mark—the eye on His forehead with its bee-like lashes—because, apart from the Blessed One, no other being has opened a downward-facing or downward-looking eye for the sake of those distressed people who have been swallowed by the world of suffering.
