Because it was the cause of distress for all the gods and demons, that great poison Kālakūṭa is metaphorically imagined as having the form of suffering; he whose neck (kaṇṭha) is marked by that [poison] is "Kālakūṭakaṇṭha. Furthermore, by virtue of the Kālakūṭa being on his neck, the Lord's capacity to remove the suffering of the entire cycle of existence (saṃsāra) is indicated. || 3 ||
Victory to you, whose form consists of the three powers and whose hands shine with a sharp trident!
Victory to you, whose lotus-feet are worthy of worship, for all objects are accomplished by your mere will! 4.

Regarding "Victory to the Embodiment" (*jaya mūrti*): His hand is uplifted by means of a sharp trident (*śūla*)— which severs the cycle of transmigratory existence (*saṃsāra*)— belonging to one whose self (*ātman*) consists of the three embodied powers (*mūrtāḥ śaktayaḥ*) in the form of will, knowledge, and action.

The hand of whom—by this, it is stated that the three powers are solely dependent upon the Blessed One; from whom the purpose is accomplished by mere will; and whose lotus-feet, being such, are therefore worthy of worship as before. || 4 ||
Victory to you who possess a transcendent body overflowing with hundreds of splendors!
Victory to you who have taken up ashes as a substitute for the Gaṅgā through your single matted lock! 5.
"Victory to the One of Splendor! Splendors are those qualities that produce light and joy; his body is his true nature. "Ekajaṭā" means one with a single matted lock;

that which is diminished there in the form of the Gaṅgā is the very ash assumed by him. Thus, the Lord is one whose head (ka) possesses such ash; that he has ash upon his head is indeed beyond dispute. || 5 ||
Victory to you, who are anointed with the pale luster of moonlight spread across the Ocean of Milk!
Victory to you, whose cold jewel-ornaments arise from the radiance of gems produced by contact with the body of the Lord!

Victory to Him who is like the Milky Ocean! His body is anointed with a brilliant unguiment that possesses the luster of the moonlight—the radiance of the moon—spread and diffused across the Milky Ocean.

His ornaments are the beautiful serpents, such as Śeṣa and Vāsuki, who have become lovely through the jewels arising from contact with His limbs; for by contact with the body of the Lord, the snakes [attain beauty].
For the scripture states: "It is the attainment of the jewels. || 6 ||
Victory to you, whose refuge is like a single digit of the imperishable moon;
victory to you, who have always performed the consecration for universal sovereignty with the Gaṅgā!

Regarding the phrase "the one imperishable": the Lord alone is the fitting refuge for that single digit of the moon named Amā (the New Moon), because He too is of an exclusively imperishable nature. Indeed, by this digit of the moon, the supreme reality of the Lord is indicated; for it has been eternally commenced by the Gaṅgā.
He whose consecration is for universal sovereignty.
Victory to you, who have purified Gokula by the touch of your lower limbs!
Victory to you, who remain ever-present in the assemblies initiated by those possessed of devotion! (8)

Regarding the phrase *jayādharāṅga*: the "lower limb" (*adharāṅga*) refers to the foot; by the touch of that foot, the cowherd settlement (*gokula*) was purified by the Blessed One who has the bull as his vehicle.
Since the bull was touched by his feet, the purity of the entire bovine species is universally acclaimed by the devoted throughout the assembly (*goṣṭhī*) where they have gathered.
One whose presence is certain and inevitable.
Victory to you, who have deceived the foolish by assuming the guise of an ascetic at your own will!
Victory to you, the vessel of good fortune worthy of Gaurī’s embrace! 9.

"Victory to You!"— those fools were deceived and terrified by the mere sport of the Blessed One, who acted according to His own will through a simulated possession; for they believed that He wore matted hair and other such things solely as a rite to purify Himself from the sin arising from the decapitation of Brahmā's head.

Some say this is for the sake of spiritual attainment (*siddhi*); others say this is the true form of the Blessed One. That is not correct, because it is impossible for the Blessed One—who is the ultimate reality of independent consciousness—to possess such a form. Gaurī is the supreme power (*parā śakti*), the vessel of that auspiciousness worthy of her embrace and of being desired by all. (9)
Victory to You, who are greedy for the offering of states of being ever-moist with the essence of devotional rasa!
Victory to You, who are delighted by the dancing words of devotees exulting in their devotion! 10.

"Victory to You, O Lord who are greedy for the offering of the moistened heart!"—meaning, You who instantly take as Your own that very disposition or intention which has become exceedingly moist with the sentiment of devotion (*bhaktirasa*) and has overflowed from the heart.

"Gladdened by the dance of their speech"—meaning, You who are pleased by the garlands of hymns flashing forth from the words of those devotees who are unrestrained in their roaring due to the intoxication of devotion. || 10 ||
Victory to you, O Lord of the gods beginning with Brahmā, whose arising and passing away are caused by your own power!
Victory to you, whose command is borne upon the heads of the rows of world-protectors! 11.

"Victory to Brahman! [This refers to] that from which arise the origin and dissolution—the production and destruction—of the power and creative capacity of the lords of the gods, beginning with Brahmā, as well as that of the entire series of world-protectors.
His command—his authoritative decree—is borne upon the head, which is the abode of Indra and the other world-protectors;
for there are hundreds of scriptural declarations stating that Indra and the others, following the command of the Supreme Lord, abide [in their offices] during initiations and other rites. 11.
Victory to you, whose majesty is manifested through the self-seal (svamudrā) bestowed upon the entire world!
Victory to you, the Great Lord (Maheśvara), the Sovereign of the Universe, who extends even to the gift of your own self! 12.

"Victory to Him whose sovereignty, pervasiveness, and lordship are manifest through His own seal (mudrā) placed everywhere in the universe—a seal consisting of the pervasion of the powers of bliss, essence, knowledge, and action, and taking the form of firm support. As the scripture says: "Neither marked by wheels..."

"Somewhere living beings are seen marked with the vajra; the universe is marked with the yoni and the liṅga; therefore, the world belongs to Maheśvara. Let alone the granting of prosperity and such to Brahmā and the others from You—You grant even the very existence of everything, for without Your own nature, which consists of self-luminosity, there would be nothing at all.

O Viśveśvara, because it would entail the consequence of being formless—extending this argument up to the self—it is for this very reason that, since nothing else possesses the nature of form, you are the Great Lord. || 12 ||
Victory to you, who have no second when desiring the creation of the three worlds!
Victory to you, whose sole companion was the Goddess when bearing the weight of sovereign power! 13.

"Victory to Her who [creates] the three worlds! At the time of the creation of the three worlds, there was no second [principle] consisting of material cause and auxiliary conditions that He required;
for if there were no second, how could it be proclaimed that there is "Power" and "the Possessor of Power"? To this He says:
"To Her whose very self is the course of all worlds manifested by Her own will during the marriage ceremony of the mass of sovereignty"—by this principle, She is the Goddess alone.
He whose companion is supreme power itself, which is the essence of His own capacity, possesses sovereignty, which consists in the performance of the fivefold cosmic acts. || 13 ||
Victory to you, who have completely traversed the three worlds with your stride! Victory to you, whose sound as the Lord is sung without exception by everyone from children upwards! 14.

Regarding the term *jayākrama*: it refers to that Viṣṇu by whom, through his two strides (*kramābhyām*), the entire three worlds— *bhūr*, *bhuvar*, and *svar*— as previously described, have been simultaneously, eternally, and perfectly traversed in their entirety, leaving nothing remaining, because they are directly manifest.

The Lord, presiding over and pervading the three states of existence, non-existence, and that which transcends both—namely, the *akrama* (the timeless)—is thus expressed through the resonance of distinction (*vyatireka-dhvani*). Having established this as a matter of common consensus and without dispute, the resonance of "Lord" (*īśvara*) is sung even among children; it is he whose nature is the reflective awareness of the primordial sound (*nādāmarśa*). || 14 ||
Victory to you, who are naturally exalted, indifferent to compassion and its conditions;
victory to you, O Bhairava, who preceded the manifestation of the great death of Bhīṣma! 15.

Regarding "victory through compassion": Bhīṣma’s majesty is an innate, natural, and uninterrupted loftiness that does not depend on qualities such as compassion; however, according to the established tradition—that whoever is superior in quality over another is said to be above him—his loftiness is indeed unprecedented.

Even Bhairava, who is unprecedentedly terrifying even to that which is to be feared— the Great Death (Mahāmṛtyu) who causes the entire world to tremble, whose very nature is the devouring that consists in the movement of one's own form— shines forth in the hearts of those afraid of death as the bestower of fearlessness, for he is the "frightener" (*bhīṣaṇīya*) of even the "frightener" (*bhīṣaṇīya*), according to the secondary derivative (*taddhita*) meaning "the fear of the timid. || 15 ||
Victory to you, whose fierce activity in destroying the universe leaves no adversary; victory to you, whose very name, when proclaimed, follows upon hundreds of virtues leading to supreme welfare.

"Victory to Him!"—he whose name is thus celebrated: he from whom obstacles have departed during the fierce activity of universal dissolution (the *saṃhāra*), and whose followers, numbering a hundredfold, are most excellent as they run behind him. 16.
Victory to you, O ocean whose essence is the nectar bestowed through sport! Victory to you, O fire of wrath that consumes the entire universe in an instant! 17.

Victory to Him! By whom the ocean of nectar, the source of immortality, was bestowed with ease upon Upamanyu—this very gift which follows a hundredfold blessings; by whom, even for a moment, the fire of His wrath, capable of destroying the universe, was suppressed through His anger. 17.
Victory to you, the sole lamp for the world of living beings blinded by the darkness of delusion! Victory to you, the Supreme Person who remains awake while the world sleeps! (18)

Victory to the Delusion-Dispeller! He is the sole, peerless lamp for the world of living beings—who are blinded by the darkness of delusion, that is, by the gloom of non-recognition (akhyāti)—and who thus have their vision of non-duality obscured;
he is the illuminator of the ultimate reality, shining forth pre-eminently while Māyā remains in deep sleep, rendered inert by its own slumber.
In this world, he is ever-vigilant toward all beings; therefore, being eternally awakened, he is the Supreme Person whose very nature is that of the presiding Lord.
Victory to you, O Jīvajīvaka bird warbling within the grove of the body and its members!
Victory to you, O noble Sārasa crane sporting in the sky of the pure mind! 19.

"Victory to the one who [gives life] to the body and so forth. The very body, due to its insentience (*jaḍatva*), is like a mountain bower—a cave or mountain-grotto. He is the one who gives life to, that is, causes the living of life for, the *jīvas*—living beings—who are crying out (*nikūjataḥ*) therein. Furthermore, by the power of resonance (*anuraṇana-śakti*), even though the literal meaning is cast aside, there is the sense that in a mountain cave there are birds called *jīvajīvaka* that are crying out; this is the meaning for the wise.

Because it possesses qualities such as purity, the minds of devotees are indeed like the sky; therein, the Supreme Soul—the royal swan—shines, possessing the conduct of that [mind] and moving through the sky as a magnificent swan. || 19 ||
Victory, O Lord of Mountains, arisen from the supreme Jāmbūnada gold!
Victory, O moon of portents, who causes the falling of meteors and censures among the most wicked! 20.
"Victory to her who is like Jāmbūnada gold! Jāmbūnada is gold; by that [gold], she is exalted (*udagra*), empowered (*ūrjita*), and born of the elements (*dhātūdbhava*).

Furthermore, she is the Mistress of the Mountain (*girīśvarī*), produced from the essence-element (*rasadhātusambhūta*) of Mount Meru. And likewise, she is the *Avadhūtā*. Regarding the phrase "by whom [the face] is stainlessly radiant," and so forth:

among the most wicked (*pāpiṣu*), who are within the scope of her power to utterly dissolve them, even censure (*nindā*)—because it is a cause for a calamitous state—is like a meteor (*ulkā*), a flash of lightning.
Indeed, by the descent of power (*śaktipāta*) that causes absorption into the Blessed One, even sinners revile the Blessed One;
like a portentous moon during an eclipse, he is like the moon—a sign of inauspiciousness—yet his nature as a constant cause of delight is indicated by his lunar form. || 20 ||
Victory to you, who are difficult for even gods and sages to approach due to your arduous austerities;
victory to you, who are beheld by the worlds as the wrestler who has ascended all ten stages of devotion! 21.
"Victory to the one who is difficult to attain" (p. 108). Because her asceticism is arduous and she is thus afflicted, she is attained with difficulty even by Agastya, Brahmā, and others.
For it was said previously: "Neither yoga nor austerity [is the means]; devotion alone is the means there. Thus he says, "in all... [referring to the verse beginning with *sarvāsu*].
Victory to You, who are beheld—that is, directly perceived—by the world of devotees who have ascended to the states beginning with waking and have been previously described;

victory to You, who have made Your own dependents vessels for the expansion of Your own perfections! Victory to You, whose sole purpose is the cherishing of the multitude of those who have sought refuge in You! 22.

Victory to Him whose own abundance flows forth! He by whom His own devotees—who have taken refuge in Him—are made into vessels for the expansion of His own abundance, that is, brought to the state of being recipients of its taste; and who, according to the principle "I carry the yoga and kṣema [acquisition and preservation] of those who are eternally devoted," is the bearer of their yoga and kṣema.
Victory to you, whose sole heroic deed is the cause of creation, preservation, and destruction!
Victory to you, the great festival of the playfully swaying lotus held by those full of devotion! 23.

"Victory to the one [who performs] creation and maintenance. According to the principle that the cause of creation and so forth always delights in the sport of creation, he whose single, supreme, and noble deed is such that his playful movement—tremulous, desirable, and pervasive—is characterized by an intense immersion born of the intoxication of devotion; [this refers to] the one named Utpala.
This is a great festival for our supreme ancestor.
Victory, victory to you, O vessel of victory! Victory to you who have conquered birth, old age, and death! Victory to you, the eldest in the world!
Victory, victory, victory, victory, victory, victory, victory!
Victory, victory, victory, victory, victory, victory to the Three-Eyed One! || 24 ||

"Victory! Victory! [is the exclamation]. The state of being a recipient of victory belongs to one's own self, the Lord whose nature is consciousness (*cidrūpa*), because, by virtue of being of the nature of consciousness, it is supreme over all. Although, in reality, its activity consists of universal excellence, it is [called victorious] through its sovereignty.

In the non-dual system (*advayanaya*), because the Self is concealed during the state of distraction toward sense objects, the meaning of the imperative suffix in "be victorious" (*jaya*)—which consists of a prayer that brings [the Self] face-to-face as if it were turned away—is appropriate here;
with this intention, it is said that [the Lord] is "the recipient of victory. However, in the dual system (*dvayanaya*), because it is characterized by duality, the Lord is not [the recipient].

Since he exists in a state of supreme excellence, the benediction "Be victorious" (jaya) is indeed redundant; even if he were to exist [in a state of non-excellence], what would be the use of a prayer made by another?

Furthermore, the imperative sense (*loṭ*) found in injunctions and the like is entirely inappropriate with respect to the Lord. Thus, the utterance "Be victorious" (yaj-jaya) based on a distinction [between the Lord and the worshipper] is simply untenable. The meaning is that birth, old age, and death have already been conquered by relying upon [the Lord's] victory.

The "seniority in the world" [of Śiva] results from his being beginningless; the repeated proclamation of "Victory! Victory! indicates the utter helplessness born of the devotee's intense immersion in devotion; and the address "O Three-eyed One" (tryakṣa) is intended to manifest His possession of extraordinary excellence—may there be auspiciousness. || 24 ||
Thus ends the commentary on the *Jayastotra* within the *Stotrāvalī* composed by the venerable teacher Utpaladeva, written by the venerable Kṣemarāja.
Thus, with these fourteen sections, there is a hymn to the Sahaja-unmudraṇās. 14.
Oṃ tatsat!
There exist treatises that wash away the three stains, as well as those who have reached their further shore.
The wise yogis who are established in their own true nature are, in reality, your devotees alone.

"Trimala" means those who wash away the three impurities—the *āṇava*, *māyīya*, and *kārmika*—namely the scriptures of the Supreme Lord consisting of the stages of knowledge (*jñāna*), action (*kriyā*), yoga (*yoga*), and conduct (*caryā*). Furthermore, there exist those who have reached the further shore of these, such as commentators who perceive their beginning and end; yet, in truth, they are your devotees.

Therefore, those who have reached the further shore of that [knowledge] are truly yogis and wise, and they are established in their own self; "those who have reached the further shore of that" should be construed with the word "truly" (*tattvataḥ*) by repeating it. In this context, they desire yoga as oneness, as in the passage beginning, "Those who, having fixed their minds on Me... These yogis are characterized by constant absorption (*nityasamāveśayuktāḥ*). The suffix *ini* is used here in the sense of praise (*praśaṃsā*) and constant connection (*nityayoga*). By this [verse], [the Lord] states: "But those who worship Me with devotion, being endowed with single-mindedness, they are in Me and I am also in them. This is because they are devoted to Me alone, without any other object of meditation. Therefore, they are in Me, and I am also in them. Because they are in Me, they attain My nature. And because I am in them, I grant them liberation from the bondage of karma. Thus, there is no distinction between them and Me. For this reason, they are equal to Me. "Equal" means non-different. They are equal to Me in the same way that the various jewels in the ocean are equal to the ocean. Just as the various jewels in the ocean are not different from the ocean, so too these devotees are not different from Me. Therefore, they are equal to Me. "Just as the air is equal to all beings"—just as the air, which is one, is equal to all beings, so too these devotees are equal to Me. "Just as the sun is equal to all eyes"—just as the sun, which is one, is equal to all eyes, so too these devotees are equal to Me. "Just as the earth is equal to all bodies"—just as the earth, which is one, is equal to all bodies, so too these devotees are equal to Me. "Just as water is equal to all tastes"—just as water, which is one, is equal to all tastes, so too these devotees are equal to Me. "Just as fire is equal to all odors"—just as fire, which is one, is equal to all odors, so too these devotees are equal to Me. "Just as ether is equal to all space"—just as ether, which is one, is equal to all space, so too these devotees are equal to Me. "Just as I am equal to all beings"—just as I, who am one, am equal to all beings, so too these devotees are equal to Me. "I am not in them"—I am not present in them in the manner that I am in others. "They are not in Me"—they are not present in Me in the manner that others are. "Because they have attained My nature"—because they have attained My nature, they are equal to Me. It has been stated that these [masters] are established in the secret essence of the *yogapāda*. Their "scholarship" (*paṇḍitatva*) consists in their constant ascension to the reality of the *vidyāpāda* and the *kriyāpāda*. In this context, by the etymological derivation "that by which one knows," the *vidyāpāda* is the singular knowledge consisting of the means (*upāya*), which is the nature of Paraśakti and Śiva; and by the etymological derivation "knowledge as the act of knowing" (*jñapti-jñāna*), it is that which consists of the goal (*upeya*).

The second [reality] is designated as the essence of repose, whose nature is a mass of consciousness and bliss; it is also described by the *kriyāpāda* (the section on action) as consisting of the essence of potency (*vīrya*), mantras, tantras, and the various ritual procedures (*itikartavyatā*).
Furthermore, action is defined as that which has the essential core of self-reflection (*svātmavimarśa*) attained through the sequence of those very means, pertaining to the tantras and mantras.

I am the essence of the supreme vitality (*para-vīrya*), whose core is the reflective awareness (*vimarśa*) of the entire multitude of words and meanings, which is a mass of supreme bliss and the true reality of the totality of speech; and I am the power of reflective awareness (*vimarśa-śakti*), whose nature is intuition (*pratibhā*), consisting of non-dual radiance, and having the form of the great universal vibration (*mahāsāmānya-spanda*).

The lower [power], however, consists of the realization of non-difference with the forms of the respective deities to be meditated upon, which manifest through the force of reasoning such as differentiation; this is the sealing (*mudraṇā*), which is the very essence of those various consciousnesses—the heart, as well as the sacrificial pit, the mandala, and the ritual procedures. This is the supreme potency primarily characterized by emission and withdrawal.

Reality (*tattva*) is precisely the pervasion of the powers of knowledge and action belonging to the Supreme Lord; likewise, proficiency in resting within the ultimate reality of *vidyā* is "self-abidance" (*svasthatva*), which is described in the section on Conduct (*caryāpāda*) as being, like the Supreme Lord, eternally present through the process of the opening and closing of the instruments of perception.
(111) The performance of creation, dissolution, and so forth, as well as abiding in one’s own true nature—all this exists in reality only for your devotees; enough [of further elaboration]. || 1 ||
O Lord, those on the shore of the world who possess devotion and are nourished by the sustenance of illusion, time, destiny, passion, and so forth, become happy. (2)

Regarding the phrase "by the illusory one" (māyīya): by devouring the five [principles] beginning with Time (kāla), they are satiated; through that counteraction, they attain their own essential nature—which is unconditioned by time, all-pervasive, free from desire, the agent of all, and omniscient—and thus they become blissful, consisting of pure bliss, satisfied, and moving in happiness. || 2 ||
Whether weeping or laughing, these devotees call out to you loudly; their offerings consist solely of the utterance of words of praise. (3)

Regarding the phrase "they weep": these devotees who possess immersion (*samāveśa*), whether weeping or laughing, being present in every state, loudly proclaim You as supreme; they clearly contemplate You.
These alone are the true devotees; the mere utterance of words of praise is a formal ritual (*upacāra*), a mode of service, and a mode of coloring [the mind].
The meaning is that those who are their devotees are indeed distinct from [other] people; they are outsiders. || 3 ||
May I not be dispassionate, nor even a lord seeking liberation;
rather, may I be one who worships you, intoxicated by the flavor of wine through overflowing devotion.

Whether he be dispassionate and devoted to the path of renunciation, or a lord endowed with sovereign power, your worshiper—seeking liberation according to his own respective fitness—[approaches you]. || 5 ||

"No," [he replies]. "One who is dispassionate, whose duty is renunciation, a lord endowed with sovereign power, who worships You according to his own respective fitness and desires liberation—such a one does not say, 'May I not be liberated while living' (jīvanmukta), nor 'May I not exist';
rather, he is intoxicated by the overflowing, intense nectar of devotion and the excellence of the wonder of spiritual immersion (samāveśa)."
May I experience arisen bliss. || 4-5 ||
O Lord, I bow to that person who, having withdrawn the external [form] into the very heart, worships you with floods of the nectar-essence of devotion. (6)

Regarding the word "external" (*bāhya*): within the very heart— which is one's own essential nature consisting of the reflective awareness of light— one draws in the universe from within as if it were external, and having fully appropriated it on all sides without leaving anything remaining, O Lord, O Master, whoever worships You with floods of nectar that are devotion itself— the cause of the expansion of supreme bliss— [him [You protect]].
"I bow to the one possessed of devotion," as before. || 6 ||
Alas, the devotees experience some indescribable taste within the duality of merit and demerit, as well as within action and knowledge, and likewise within pleasure and pain! (7)

Regarding the word *dharma*: it is known in the world as having the nature of both auspicious (*śubha*) and inauspicious (*aśubha*), and thus its status as *dharma* or *adharma* is established by worldly convention, not because it is practiced in such a way by the devoted. The word *antar* means "situated within" or "in the midst.
Furthermore, the phrase *kimapi* refers to that which is of an extraordinary nature, bestowing supreme bliss. (7)

O Lord, even those who are blind and even those afflicted with leprosy, when adorned with the ornament of supreme and unrestrained devotion to You, shine brilliantly, whether they be mobile or immobile beings.
"Moving and unmoving," etc.; the meaning is that even those who are blind or afflicted with leprosy, and even those who are despised by the world—up to this point [is the meaning]. || 8 ||
O Lord, even those whose limbs are withered by the heat of the sun, subsisting on gleaned grains and wearing garments of bark,
command even the king of kings through the great warmth of their devotion to you.
"Living by gleaning" (śiloñcha): "gleaning" (śila) means that which is gathered by gleaning; "piccha" means a wing; "kaśipu" refers to food and clothing.

Those whose limbs are emaciated by this very "gleaning and wing" (śiloñcha-piccha)—that is, by *kaśipu*—and who thus lead lives of extreme emaciation, yet possess great inner heat (*mahoṣman*) due to devotion to you.
Then, possessing exceedingly radiant and powerful forms, they lord it over Vaiśravaṇa, the king of kings; the meaning is that they surpass him in sovereign power. || 9 ||
O Lord, some who stand all around you worship you with their very minds alone— minds that, though they roll in devotion moistened by nectar, still long to ascend. (10)
Regarding the phrase "sudhārdrāyām": *sudhā* is the essence of supreme bliss (*paramānanda-rasa*); *ārdrā* means moistened, which refers to the immersion in devotion (*bhakti-samāveśa*).
One who rolls about there—even while abandoning their own state through the thorough treading upon His feet—desires to ascend;

such a person seeks to grasp [the Lord] with the mind alone, through an unartificial support, and not with external offerings such as flowers and the like. "Some" (refers to those who possess this realization).
The supreme yogis stand all around you; both internally and externally, everywhere, they find rest in you alone. || 10 ||
O Lord, this great wealth of devotion to you—which removes the miseries of cyclic existence—must be protected, increased, and held in high esteem. (11)

"Should be protected" means: protection is non-removal through rising [from meditation]; increase is the production of expansion by gradually entering into the intervals; and high esteem is respect due to its being the most excellent of all. || 11 ||
O Lord, although Your devotees are full of passion for You,
nevertheless, O Master, may their mistress always be satisfied with them, having cast aside her jealousy.
"Nātha" means: the devoted folk are full of passion; like a mistress, there is the abandonment of jealousy. "Avadāna" means pure; "tuṣṭā" means blossomed.
The Mistress is the Supreme Power (*paraśakti*)—this is the primary sense; in the secondary sense, however, the Mistress is the Great Goddess (*mahādevī*). 12.
When devotion to you arises, the state of worldly existence that was previously imminent is destroyed;
it is like the greed for curds vanishing once a great jar of milk has been obtained.
Regarding the phrase "the state of being You" (*bhavadbhāva*): when devotion arises and there is immersion into You, the state of being You will manifest before one;

Your own form is already imminent and need not be sought after. For the greed—that is, the longing—for curd when a large jar of milk has been obtained is destroyed and rendered useless, since the curd is already contained within the milk itself. || 13 ||
Is this not an incomparable accomplishment?
Or does it not flow with the primary happiness?
This devotion to Śambhu, which is ever-present, becomes ever-increasing. || 14 ||
What is it? Is this devotion to Śambhu—which, as it increases and reaches its highest pitch, becomes eternal and attains the nature of supreme devotion—not itself an incomparable accomplishment?
And is it not that very incomparable, supreme devotion which flows forth on all sides as the primary bliss or the ultimate joy?
The meaning is that it indeed flows away. || 14 ||
Alas, the jewel-creeper of devotion to you has sunk into my defiled mind;
it does not even extend toward those who are its own.
[They are] non-human [in origin], shining forth from their own perfection. || 15 ||

Regarding the word *manasi*: "In the mind"—that is, in that which is defiled and stained by the impurity of emergence (*vyutthāna*). Immersed and obscured by such emergence is your very devotion, the jewel-creeper that gives birth to all spiritual accomplishments (*siddhi*). Its "jewel-branches" are those innate and natural [powers] which, through intense absorption (*samāveśa*), flash forth as supramundane; they consist of the supreme bliss that fulfills all longing, and take the form of the subdued powers such as *aṇimā* and the rest.
Why indeed would incomparable success not be attained now, since it has just been stated? || 15 ||
Devotion toward the Blessed One indeed arises through the Lord of the Three Worlds; however,
it is not because of the attainment of powers such as *aṇimā* and the rest.
The thought that "this very [state] is not complete" does not exist for me. (16) [In the manuscript used as a mirror, no commentary on this verse is found.
Exquisite and auspicious, with the intense fragrance of clusters of *tryambaka* flowers blooming both externally and internally,
they perfume even those whose mental impressions (*vāsanā*) are contrary.
All the yogins who dwell nearby. || 17 ||

Regarding the word *bhakti*: those auspicious yogis whose fragrance— the sweet scent belonging to the blossoming, intensely radiant, and unfolding cluster (*stavaka*) of the Three-Eyed One (*tryambaka*), that is, the bouquet of Śiva’s flowers— pervades both their exterior and interior through worship, [overcome] even those hostile latent impressions (*vāsanā*) that were previously untrustworthy.

They cause all the people living nearby to dwell [in peace] and make them intent upon your worship; externally, there is a cluster for the sake of Tryambaka, but internally, Tryambaka himself is the cluster.
Thus, there is fragrance, delight, and wonder; and furthermore, by means of the intense cluster of Tryambaka—

The suggested meaning (*vyaṅgyārtha*) based on resonance (*anuraṇana*) is that the *dhattūra* flowers, perfumed by their own fragrance, honor even those standing nearby who possess a different scent. (16–17)
Not even by description is there any light whatsoever; the entire universe is in a state of profound deep sleep.
O Lord, while I am at this station of Śivarātri—
The devotee constantly worships you.

Regarding the word "light" (*jyotiḥ*): light is the knowledge arising from both the external and internal; where there is no name whatsoever because of the withdrawal of the entire manifestation of *māyā*, even the whole universe is profoundly asleep—here, in this state of Śivarātri, which is the ground of immersion into Śiva, [there is the cessation] of the manifestation of all ignorance.
Like night due to its withdrawal, it is "night" (rātri) in her place or station. || 18 ||
May there be truth in the virtuous and auspicious worship of the Blessed One; may the masses of dust falling from the feet of Śambhu shine upon my crest.

O Śambhu, let the darkness that obscures even the latent impressions of mindfulness regarding passion and the like be dispelled; or rather, let the entire triad of worlds be dissolved into Your own self within me.

Regarding the word *sattvam*: may *sattva*—that is, luminosity (*prakāśa*)—expand within that Lord Śiva, who possesses real, ultimate qualities such as omniscience and the like; for worship of Him consists in the essential nature of resting in consciousness.
Furthermore, may *rajas* arise from the power of Śiva at the crest, that is, in the central tuft of hair.

The expansions of *sattva*, *rajas*, and *tamas*—whose purposes are illumination, activity, and restraint—are like clusters of rays that reveal one's true nature; may they blossom forth. And may the subtle body, known as the self-delusion (*moha*), exert itself toward the total eradication of even those latent impressions (*vāsanā*) which cause attachment and the like, and which serve as the cause for memory [of worldly existence], so that there may be no further rebirth. Or alternatively:
May that dissolution of one possessed of the three qualities (guṇas) within You—which is their complete cessation—occur; the meaning is that [the soul] should become dissolved in You alone. || 19 ||
The path of saṃsāra is exceedingly long, its body-staff scorched by various most harsh diseases;
though there may have been some happiness, no enjoyments were ever truly experienced.
May that [state] be ours for a long time!
Thus have I become one whose head is rendered useless by being trampled upon by the feet of the Moon-bearer (Śiva), which are beautiful with their excellent form.
And may he be your devotee; therefore, grant me immediately these very long-lasting, great riches. || 20 ||

Regarding "saṃsāra": it is extremely distant, its limit being difficult to reach; "enjoyments" (bhoga) here refers to the highest [objects of experience]. "Never" (jātu)—meaning at no time—is used in the sense of negation regarding the notion "I am," which consists of the subject-form such as the body and so forth.

However, because of the treading upon the feet of the Moon-bearer—that is, through the descent of the Lord's power (īśvara-śakti-pāta)—it becomes lovely, radiant, and dominated by consciousness (saṃvit). Therefore...
Thus, he whose very nature is the supreme head (the highest state), being such a devotee of Yours,
even while serving You alone, [attains] from me [blessings] that are exceedingly long-lasting.
May he bestow eternal and great prosperities, non-dual in nature as before; may there be auspiciousness! 19.

Thus ends the commentary on the fifteenth hymn, titled *Bhaktistotra*, within the *Stotrāvalī* composed by the venerable teacher Utpaladeva, as written by the venerable teacher Rājānaka Kṣemarāja. 15.
Oṃ. For the worlds, there is nothing at all that constitutes an obscuration regarding Bhava;
for the devotees, there is nothing at all that constitutes an obscuration regarding Bhava. (1)

"Nothing at all"—with respect to the obscuration of Your own conscious nature, for transmigrating worldly beings, it is indeed "nothing at all" (na kiñcit) only by way of irony (*kāku*), but rather everything;

the entire universe is [an obscuration] because it is veiled by the wheel of all powers (*śakticakra*) in their ultimate state. But for devotees, however, there is indeed nothing at all—that is, none whatsoever.
The meaning of "something" (kiñcit) is that everything up to the level of the Śiva-tattva has been made an object of knowledge by being conceived as one's own limbs. || 1 ||
Even though You are attained through the sequence of skillful means and are complex with manifold attributes,
You, as the Self, appear once and for all in Your pure state to those who possess devotion.

Regarding the phrase "also by means" (*apyupāya*): the sequence of means (*upāyakrama*) consists of the knowledge, ritual action, yoga, conduct, and so forth, as taught in various scriptures; it is characterized by innumerable attributes such as omniscience, omnipotence, and the nature of possessing all powers. As it has been said:
"Even the words for creation and accomplishment would be exhausted," and so on; thus, for those who possess such powers, [the manifestation occurs] simultaneously and continuously.

The single ultimate reality of pure consciousness shines forth through total immersion (*samāveśa*), yet that which is attained through gradual stages appears as a chaotic mass; how then can it appear both simultaneously and purely? This is an apparent contradiction (*virodhābhāsa*). || 2 ||
Even the victorious laugh, and even the defeated laugh;
O Lord, those who are intoxicated by drinking the nectar of devotion to you are truly something extraordinary.
"Jayanto'pi" (even Jayanta). Entering [the state] by not making distinctions the basis for division, they laugh—that is, they blossom—even when defeated;
that is, even when being drawn back into the state of emergence (*vyutthāna*), they blossom outwardly due to the latent impression (*saṃskāra*) of immersion.
They laugh indeed at both worldly victory and defeat. "Matta" means exhilarated or joyful; furthermore, those who are *matta* are intoxicated.
Some extraordinary people laugh at both victory and defeat. || 3 ||
May I never attain perfection, nor may I ever be liberated;
rather, may I be completely filled with the nectar of devotion for You, which has reached the sweetest and highest pinnacle.

(119) "Dry" (*śuṣkaka*) means precisely "dry"; it is an adverbial modifier meaning that one has made [the practice] dry, devoid of immersion in devotion (*bhakti*). Such are the enjoyment (*bhoga*) and liberation (*mokṣa*) for those who maintain the doctrine of duality.

Having made [the self] completely full with that essence of immersion in You—which is most delicious, characterized by unsurpassed aesthetic wonder, and rooted in the continuous stream [of practice]—thereby, indeed, the state of dryness is removed. || 4 ||
O Lord, just as this essence of devotion to you has been fashioned by me, though previously unknown to me,
may that very same essence flourish.

"Yathaiva" (just as): "Ajñātapūrva" means that this [state] has never been known before, even amidst millions of births; it is the manifest form of the aesthetic flavor of devotion (*bhaktirasa*), the expansion of immersion (*samāveśa*). "O Īśāna, O Sovereign One," "tadvat" (in that same way) means that it is suddenly unknown, just as you alone know the manner (*yathā*) in which it occurs. This is the meaning. || 5 ||
O Blessed One, by virtue of this truth, there is no other scope for my prayer;
may I simply possess that same kind of immersion in devotion toward You forever.

"By truth"—this expression arises from extreme intimacy and familiarity. "Another" means distinct from mere petition; he is "such" that he transcends all mental constructs (*vāgvikalpa*). This immersion in devotion is the absolute state of *samāveśa*. 6.
Even if intoxicated by devotion, I might become angry and harbor latent enmity toward worldly existence;
likewise, I might laugh, weep, or cry out "Śiva! excessively.

Regarding the word *bhakti*: "I might be angry with existence" means that I might view worldly existence (*saṃsāra*) as something vulgar; "I might harbor regret" means that I might experience remorse, thinking, "How was I so deluded for such a long time?"; "I might laugh" means that I might blossom with joy; "I might weep."
May I be bathed in tears of joy; may I be vocal with "Śiva, Śiva"; and may there arise for me a manifold recurrence of [this state], like that of one intoxicated. || 7 ||
O Lord, through devotion may I be well-established even when in adversity, joyful even when weeping, and composed even when agitated. May I be so, O Lord. (8)

(120) "In an adverse state" means that even when situated in adversity and afflicted by misfortune, one who rests in his own bliss through devotion perceives worldly pleasure as being of the nature of suffering, like a person sitting upon a cluster of needles; and thus...
Even while weeping in such states as the death of a kinsman, he rejoices inwardly through the attainment of the expansion of consciousness;

likewise, even while laughing amidst worldly pleasures, he weeps and considers them pitiable; and though he is profound in worldly conduct and unperceived by others, he is disoriented, regarding that state as a calamity.
Even when my mind is distracted by various thoughts, or even when my memory is lost during occasions such as a physical collapse, may I remain profound;
and even when scrutinized by others, may I be filled with the joy of contemplating the pervasiveness of the inner state (antardaśā). || 8 ||
For your devotees, there is nothing to be perceived, whether within or without you;
for where you, whose nature is consciousness, abide yourself in a state beyond conceptualization, there is nothing else.

Regarding the phrase "of the devotees": that which is to be experienced—the play of saṃsāra and so forth—is Consciousness itself, possessing the attributes of consciousness; it shines forth directly, not by means of another substrate. || 9 ||
Even when imitating your censure, your devotees rejoice within as if pierced by the nectar-drops of your words, which are like sharp needles of horripilation.

Regarding the word "devotees" (bhaktāḥ): even when imitating your censure, those devotees who imitate the praise offered by afflicted beings rejoice indeed; possessing their throbbing, true nature, they attain the pervasion of supreme bliss.
For this very reason, they are pierced on all sides by sharp needles of horripilation that pierce through the fetters. || 10 ||
Even painful sensation serves as a source of enjoyment for those devoted [to You], for whom every consciousness is moistened by nectar and consists of the moonlight of Your presence. (11)

"Even painful [feeling]" means that feeling (*vedanā*), even when it is painful—that is, even when it causes suffering—is for the sake of experience (*bhoga*). This is because suffering is something to be marveled at; thus, for the sake of attaining the state of the subject who is a mass of bliss whose essence is the power of wonder, [it serves as a means]. For this very reason, he says: "I am everything; I am the power of consciousness (*citiśakti*), which is moist with nectar due to its being a mass of supreme bliss, and which consists of moonlight."
She is the form of the supreme power (parā-śakti).
(121) For devotees who are confined here and there, whether outside or within,
the bliss of tasting the flavor of the touch of Your body is equally genuine.

Regarding the phrase *yatra*: for devotees who have been restrained—that is, established—in the forms of pleasure, pain, and their causes, Your body is free from the impurity of various internal latent impressions (*vāsanā*) due to its sincerity; because it consists of consciousness (*cinmaya*), the bliss of the touch, taste, and savoring that pertains to Your essential nature is equal, being the same in all respects. And it has been said:
"One of equal intelligence excels. || 12 ||
O Lord, some, having eliminated the element of wretchedness that relies on both [the self and the deity] within the worship of Your devotion, taste Your pure form which consists of nectar. 13.

"Thine": having utterly destroyed—that is, having severed even the slightest trace of wretchedness, which is the portion of misery connected with duality—belonging to that devotion and service toward Thy worship previously explained;
only some rare ones, through the dissolution of duality, [attain] that very same state, which is transparent and stainless.
They relish the body, which consists of nectar and is the essence of the flavor of bliss, and they marvel at it as a portion of wretchedness.

Herein lies the intention: non-dual devotion (advaita-bhakti) consists of immediate immersion (*samāveśa*), whereas dualistic devotion (*dvaita-bhakti*) does not; therefore, it consists of the longing for the state of Śiva. || 13 ||
The views of the non-Buddhist outsiders are deluded and divided, for their very divisions arise from delusion itself; yet you alone shine forth as the one, peerless reality for your devotees. (14)
"Deluded" means that the views of the non-Buddhist outsiders (*tīrthika*) and the perspectives of their scriptures are deluded; therefore, they are distinct.
Since this so-called "distinctness" is the cause for the non-recognition of unity—that is, the delusion—it does not exist in reality.
You shine forth (*rājase*), blazing with the singular, non-dual reality of the devotees—a fundamental truth that is without rival and eternally certain. 14
How could that person who possesses a mind purified by the ripening of pride, contempt, passion, and the like, ever become equal in character to the world? || 15 ||

Regarding "honor and dishonor": for that devoted one, the "ripening" (*niṣpāka*) of honor and dishonor as well as of passion and the like— that is, their complete cooking (*niḥśeṣeṇa pacanam*) or being reduced to a state like burnt seeds— is the cause by which the mind [is transformed].
His own mind is stainless and without blemish. || 15 ||
Among those great souls who have conquered even the darkness of passion and hatred with the light of devotion—who among them could be considered truly possessed of knowledge? (16)

Regarding the word "rāge" (in passion): the intention of the suffix *īyasun* in the phrase "mahīyasām" (of the greater) is that there is an equal pervasiveness among both the possessors of knowledge (*jñānin*) and the devotees (*bhakta*).
However, the distinction for the devotees lies in their victory over the darkness of passion and hatred. || 16 ||
For one whose means for performing the rites of bathing and drinking consist of the nectar of devotion,
there is a state of supreme ease throughout the stages of the beginning, middle, and end of their *prārabdha* karma.

Regarding the phrase "of whom": devotion itself is the nectar (*sudhā*); it is the means for that collection of activities—such as bathing, drinking, and so forth—which result in purity, satisfaction, and the like, throughout their beginning, middle, and end; that is, in the initial, intermediate, and final stages of all activities, it is preeminent.
Sukhāsikā is the state of resting in supreme bliss. || 17 ||
Since you alone are the object of fame’s pursuit, the locus of thought, and the one to be worshipped, the worldly course of those devoted to you is praiseworthy, for it is permeated by you. (18)
Regarding the word "kīrtya": the word "yena" (by which) indicates the cause; "uditi" means that for this reason, worldly conduct consists of praising and so forth. || 18 ||
O Lord, it is through devotion alone toward You that the notion of liberation has ripened;
having ascended to its first stage, we are therefore as if already liberated.

Regarding the term "liberation" (mukti): those who have ascended to the first stage—having reached the state where [the realization] is fully matured and completely perfected—and who, though striving to achieve ever-increasing excellence, have attained stability in that initial ground, are called "almost liberated" (muktakalpa). This means they are slightly incomplete in their liberation, but not yet fully liberated. || 19 ||
(123) Even though the arrival of suffering may be great for me, whose soul is filled with devotion to you,
O All-pervading Lord, let there not be even a succession of pleasures that turns away from You. 20.
"Regarding 'the arrival of suffering': she is turned away from you, with her face averted from you. (20)
O Lord, you are pleased by devotion, and when you are pleased, there is devotion;
that this is a mutual dependence is logical, as only you know it to be so. (21)

Regarding the word "you" (*tvam*): as long as the Supreme Lord is not pleased, there is no devotion; and as long as there is no devotion consisting of total immersion (*samāveśa*), the Supreme Lord is not pleased. [Rather,] He reveals to the devotee a body composed of consciousness and bliss (*cidānandamaya*).
This is a case of mutual dependence (*anyonyāśraya*); in what manner, by what means, and how this becomes logically consistent is as follows.

In the same way, by your very sovereignty, you alone bring about both [the impossible and the possible], for you perform what is exceedingly difficult to accomplish; human reasoning has no power here. || 21 ||
O Lord, whether with form or without form, whether within or indeed without, you are entirely composed of nectar to those whose souls possess devotion. (22)

Regarding the phrase "sākāra" (with form): for those whose souls are intensely delighted with me through devotion, you are composed of nectar everywhere; for they perceive you as the self of all. || 22 ||
For one who possesses devotion toward Him who is immanent within this very world, joy is the fruit of manifestation; the rest of the world remains as it is. (23)

Regarding the phrase "in this": although, in that which is most terrible to all people, the world appears to those possessed of devotion merely upon its first encounter just like [the world] to ordinary folk, nevertheless, when sought after, this [world] for them consists solely of dense light and bliss. || 23 ||
Devotion to the secret, devotion to the supreme, and devotion to the Great Lord of the universe—O Śambhu, O auspicious God, what indeed is this thing called "devotion" within you? Ah! 24.

Regarding the word "guhye" (in the secret): in the secret, which is of the nature of a mystery, the supreme, the full, and the uncommon, there is the utterance of the Name for the purpose of proclaiming its unsurpassed nature; what indeed is this extraordinary reality? || 24 ||
Devotion, devotion to the Supreme; devotion is indeed that which is most intense.
I cry out loudly: "May there be supreme devotion for you, my Lord! (25)
Regarding the word "bhakti": it is precisely through its repetition that it manifests a state of helplessness; it is supreme, intense, established in a continuous flow, and exceedingly fierce.
Blazing forth like the flame of a kindled fire, it flashes instantly without depending on practice or other means—and this is indeed appropriate. || 25 ||
Since you, O Lord, are the source of all beauties,
whatever is attached to you becomes priceless— whether it be a jewel or even a blade of grass.

"Since you are... means: since you are the source of all beauties and splendors, therefore, from the perspective of the world, whatever is considered a jewel—meaning something of superior quality—or even a blade of grass, which is worthless and not to be taken up, if it is attached to you, that is, connected through union with you, it becomes truly priceless. || 26 ||
Those for whom there is no separation from the path of consciousness—whether from the subject or from the object—triumph; they are the ones who truly enjoy worldly existence.

He makes known: those for whom there is no separation from You even amidst the disturbances of the object and subject within the path of consciousness—which consists of pure awareness—triumph as they serve You with devotion. (27)
O Lord, you are embraced by some outside the assembly hall of saṃsāra,
while by others there itself, who are distressed yet free from restraint.

Regarding the word *saṃsāra*: outside the assembly hall of *saṃsāra*, having transcended the hall of worldly existence, you are surely embraced—that is, closely embraced—by certain yogis who abide in such states as the "twelfth limit" (*dvādaśānta*) and who are intent upon the meditative absorption of closing the eyes (*nimīlana-samādhi*); and by others who, through direct experience and their mastery of the reality of reasoning, are skilled in the meditative absorption of opening the eyes (*unmīlana-samādhāna*).

Furthermore, right there in the midst of that assembly hall of saṃsāra, those who have cast off all constraints and abandoned the exertions of meditation, recitation, and ritual performance, languish, rendered helpless by intense passion;
for such indeed is the condition of those possessed by deep passion. (28)
By Śivā, who has enjoyed the entire universe as her food, drink, and ornament.
I bow to Śiva, who is firmly embraced by her with the impetuous joy of the festival of cosmic dissolution. || 29 ||

Regarding the phrase "pānāśanā": I bow to, praise, and—as far as possible—enter into Śiva, who is the Bhairava of Consciousness (cid-bhairava), firmly embraced and closely clung to by Śivā. How is she?

She is one by whom the entire universe has been enjoyed through drinking, protection, maintenance, eating, and adornment. Through "drinking" (pāna) is meant preservation or sustenance; through "eating" (aśana)...

By that Śivā, whose nature is supreme bliss, who is of the form of the Fourth (turyā), and who is for this reason the festival of dissolution— by whom the entire universe has been perfectly enjoyed, protected, consumed, and likewise properly cast away through the process of withdrawal in the form of morsels, through its manifestation, and through the excellence of the attainment of supernatural powers (siddhi) and so forth.

By means of her exalted state, which consists of the dissolution even of the processes of creation, maintenance, and destruction, she intensely expands [the universe] through such drinking, the extraction of the essence, eating,
the consumption of the remaining refuse-like matter, and adornment— all of this that remains.

For this very reason, even the entire universe, leaving behind only its residual impressions (*saṃskāra*), is consumed and made into an object of one's own enjoyment during the festival of cosmic dissolution; that is, by means of the external ritual sequence— through the impetuous and rapid drinking of wine and the like, the eating of meat and the like, and the adorning with ornaments such as bones and the like.

And by that [Power] which, impetuous and intensely engaged in the sport of causing the dissolution of the imagined state of the Destroyer during the festival of cosmic reabsorption, has cast the entire universe consisting of the thirty-six principles back into itself, properly setting it at rest—
by that very Power of Resonance (anuraṇana-śakti), the universe has been fully enjoyed through drinking, chewing, and adorning.

She, the beautiful one, by whom the entire universe in its form of manifold manifestation has been brought to a state of enjoyment, becomes impetuous during the festival of dissolution; embracing the Possessor of Power (Śaktimān) within the self-nature of the attainment of dual bliss, she remains closely united with him. || 29 ||
O Lord of the Universe, your unprecedented supreme lordship triumphs, in that it is devoid of anything to be ruled.
There is yet another [power] of yours which is likewise; by it this world shines forth, yet it does not shine in the way that it appears.

"O Supreme Lord!"— O Viśveśa, Your unprecedented, supreme, and most excellent sovereignty in the form of Paramaśiva is victorious; for this [sovereignty], being devoid of any separate object to be ruled over (*īśitavya*), because You have assimilated the entire universe into Your own Self, is "other" (*aparā*) even while being "supreme" (*paramā*) in relation to Paramaśiva, and though "gross" (*sthūlā*) from that perspective.

The meaning is that your sovereignty, which is of the nature of Sadāśiva and Īśvara, likewise triumphs as something unprecedented; for by this [sovereignty], this world— which appears in such a manner through the distinctions of blue, pleasure, the body, and so forth— being manifest in that very way, remains free from conceptual constructs within the Self, precisely because it has attained a state of essential identity with the light of "I-ness" (ahantā).

These inert things exist only as manifestations; indeed, manifestation alone exists. The meaning is that it shines by means of its own self and the selves of others, according to this established state.
Thus all is auspicious.
Thus ends the commentary composed by Śrī Kṣemarāja on the sixteenth hymn, titled "The Piercing of the Bonds" (Pāśānubheda), within the *Stotrāvalī* composed by the venerable teacher Utpaladeva.

127) Oṃ tatsat! Aha! Victorious is this wondrous and great festival of sweet worship, for it abundantly bestows even tears that taste like the flavor of nectar. (1)

Oṃ! Aho! Victorious is this festival of worship, which consists of the essence of immersion (*samāveśa*), characterized by some indescribable, delicious bliss that is witnessed by direct experience; for from this great festival of worship, even tears and weeping provide a full taste of nectar and nourish nothing but the wonder born of bliss. || 1 ||
All activities preceded by Your worship grant success; for devotees who are absorbed in You, all those very activities are themselves the perfections.

Regarding the "activities": those activities which constitute the commencement of your worship grant success; however, for devotees, successes are indeed immediate, because they manifest as being identical with you. || 2 ||
Those who incessantly worship you— who at all times and in all things manifest in every form simultaneously— they are my presiding deities.

"Always" means: those who, at all times and in all places, worship You—who possess every form simultaneously, who encompass the entirety [of reality] without succession, and who are never at rest—they are, for me, the very forms of the presiding deities. (3)
May that festival of touching you, which is accomplished by disregarding the exertion of meditation and is renowned as the ritual of worship, always be mine, O Devotee. (4)
Regarding the phrase "through the exertion of meditation" (*dhyānāyāsena*): the term "meditation" (*dhyāna*) also implies the utterances, ritual acts, and so forth.

Thus, by means of the setting aside—that is, the casting off—of the exertion involved in those respective utterances, ritual acts, meditations, and so on, that very festival of touching You, which is accomplished through effort (*prayatnasiddha*), is itself the rite of worship for devotees.

As it is said: "That worship is indeed the dissolution [of the mind] with reverence in the great void that is free from conceptual construction"—may this very method of worship be mine forever. || 4 ||
For devotees, the equinox of the essence of equanimity is ever-present;
their worship consists of the nectar-like juice of the flavor of your being. (5)

Regarding the phrase "of the devotees": that very worship which is prescribed as a duty during the equinox (viṣuvat) is, for those devotees whose essence consists of the expansion of identity with Śiva and equanimity, always present at the time of the equinox. Likewise, the nectar-like flavor of meditating upon You is itself the essence of ambrosia; by means of that, their worship is perpetually performed. || 5 ||
O Lord, that ritual action which has neither beginning nor end and no succession of time is essentially worship; its performers are those who take refuge in You, the Supreme.
Regarding the phrase "whose [action] is without commencement": there is no sequence of time, nor is there any sequential nature even in the interim;
this action consists of the repose of immersion (*samāveśa*). And of that action, only those who enjoy You—those who know the reality of immersion in You—are supreme agents, and no others. || 6 ||
They are the lords even of Brahmā and the other gods, and they are partakers of good fortune—
those for whom the festival of your worship remains present even in dreams or in moments of delusion.
Regarding the phrase "of Brahmā and the others":

because they possess immersion (*samāveśa*) into the Great Lord who is beyond all commonality, even Brahmā and the others are indeed *īśvaras* (lords); this is a statement of fact and not a mere figurative eulogy (*arthavāda*). They are "possessors of good fortune," for being filled with the essence of bliss (*ānanda-rasa*), they are desirable to all.
"Even in a dream, even in delusion"—meaning not only while awake, but even during dreaming and deep sleep—there arises the spontaneous festival of touching You, the dawning of immersion in You. (7)
Not only for those who recite prayers, offer oblations, bathe, or meditate, but for devotees at all times, whenever they perform worship unto you—oh, how wonderful! (8)

"Let them recite!"—thus [he says]. Indeed, while devotees may be intent on the worship of Īśvara during the stages of recitation, meditation, and so forth, they are nevertheless always permeated by the festival of your own worship. || 8 ||
Who indeed is equal to Indra and the other gods, headed by Brahmā, who are always made happy by the enjoyment of tasting the nectar of your worship? (9)

(129) "Worship of Your Honor" (bhavatpūjā): Worship of Your Honor alone is the enjoyment of the taste of nectar; by that, for the devoted one who is happy, who among Brahmā and the others is his equal? None at all. The reasoning for this has already been stated. || 9 ||
In this great festival of your worship, which alone causes the agitation of the world,
whatever may be attained is known only by those who possess devotion.

"Jagaditi": That great festival of your worship produces a state of agitation—meaning a loss of self-control through the dissolution of one's own nature—in the universe, by means of the body (whether gross, subtle, etc. which consists of the thirty-six principles; and therein, whatever is full and of the nature of supreme bliss is one's own.
Those who are His devotees alone know that true nature, which is worthy of being attained, is actually attained.
Abiding in Your consciousness-natured abode, O All-pervading Lord, I shall always worship You through the activities of the thirty-six principles, including the movements of body, speech, and mind.

"In Your abode" (*tvaddhāmni*): *dhāma* means splendor (*tejas*). The "actions" (*karmāṇi*) of the thirty-six principles (*tattvas*) are known as the movements of body, speech, and mind; by these, which thus manifest Your pervasive presence, O Lord, I worship You, who consist of the thirty-six principles beginning with the body.

That [the body] consists of solidity, fluidity, and luminosity has been taught in many scriptures; likewise, in the *Triśiraḥśāstra*, beginning with the statement "the body consists of all the gods," it says, "Earth is proclaimed by its solidity,
and water by its fluidity," and so forth, until it concludes that Bhairava, as the *Triśiras*, directly pervades the universe.
Thus, everything up to the word "established" has been taught. || 11 ||
May all time, even if it be infinite, pass for me—who am made happy by the bliss of enjoyment arising from unattached devotion to Your worship—only for this purpose; this is what I pray for. (12)

"May it be so. [This means: "May my entire, exhaustive, infinite, and boundless state of being—belonging to one who is blissful and at peace through that enjoyment which arises from being intent upon the attachment consisting of worship of You—proceed; this much I request, and nothing else. (12)
O Lord, may my greed for enjoyment, which is nourished by the nectar-like essence of worshiping you,
increase day by day and always bear fruit for me. (13)

"Your worship": as long as I obtain the enjoyment of the nectar-essence of your worship, so long and ever more so shall my longing for it continue to increase; and may it always bear fruit through the attainment of its supreme excellence. || 13 ||
May I always remain worshipping you, the Great Soul, in your ocean which is filled with the singular flavor of nectar born from the dissolution of the world. 14.

Regarding the word *jagat*: may I remain, forever worshipping You alone—the Great-Souled One who pervades the universe—in Your ocean which is overflowing (*nirbhare*), filled with that very essence consisting of nectar (*sudhāmaya*) produced by the dissolution (*vilayena*) or withdrawal of the entire world (*jagataḥ*). || 14 ||
In the performance of your sweet worship, your devotees always offer their minds, made straight by the severing of the knots of all latent impressions (vāsanās). 15.

Regarding the word "aśeṣa" (without remainder): in the ritual of Your worship, the devotees always offer their own mind—which is sweet and whose essence is wonder—to You alone; how so? It is "straight" (sarala), meaning clear and free from the crookedness of devious ways, due to the severing—that is, the crushing—of all knots consisting of latent impressions (*vāsanā*). || 15 ||
Presiding over these very objects, the functions of the senses send forth the nectar-liquor for the worship of You on behalf of Your devotees. (16)

"Having presided over," etc. These functions of the instruments—the deities of the eyes and so forth—having presided over, that is, having taken possession of, their respective objects such as form and the rest, send forth the nectar-essence within for the sake of Your worship by Your devotees, according to the sequence of the arising of the deities responsible for creation, preservation, and so on. || 16 ||
For devotees whose souls are rendered helpless by the great heat of the intensity of their devotion, what other cause for liberation could there be than immersion in the nectar of your worship? (17)

(131) "Of the devotees" means: for those whose souls are overwhelmed by the great heat of the intensity of devotion—that is, by the splendor intensified by devotion—and whose very selves are aflame, there is no other cause for liberation than immersion in the nectar of your worship. 17.
O Lord, please ordain for me the great festival of drinking the nectar of constant worship at Your feet, which is attained solely through Your grace. 18.

Regarding the word "constantly" (*satatam*): the worship of Your feet is, as before, always a great festival of drinking nectar because it bestows the pervasion of bliss. Of what nature is it? It is that which is the sole cause for the attainment of the purity of one's own essential nature, since Your grace consists of the bliss of consciousness (*cidānanda*). May that [worship] be mine constantly.
May it be accomplished; may it be brought about. || 18 ||
O Lord Īśāna, having experienced at every moment the great joy of the sublime savor of drinking the nectar of your worship, may I remain ever devoted to each ritual act.

"Having experienced... [means: In every action and every activity, moment after moment, again and again, having experienced the great joy—that is, the supreme bliss—arising from that savoring which is characterized by intoxication and intensified by delight, pertaining to the drinking of the nectar of your worship; [the word] *āmudam* means "from joy."
And at the end, there is a great joy from the savoring of the worship. || 19 ||
For devotees, the great effort of worshipping you has its purpose realized right here and now, because they experience even that very moment a happiness which was previously inconceivable. (20)

"Having the visible goal" (dṛṣṭārtha) means that because what was to be attained has already been attained, they have no longing for anything else; therefore, their great exertion is directed solely toward your worship. For it is at that very time, at the moment of worship itself, that those devotees taste an inconceivable happiness, which is supreme bliss. || 20 ||
As long as one has not obtained the great festival of tasting the nectar of your worship, I consider that not even a fraction of the wealth of happiness has been tasted.

Regarding the word "yāvat" (as far as): the intention behind the phrase "even a moment" (*lavo 'pi*) is this: worldly pleasures are indeed not true pleasures because they are artificial; however, that which is non-artificial—the bliss of total immersion (*samāveśānanda*)—is the ultimate perfection of happiness. || 21 ||
For devotees, that state of abiding in Your abode arises effortlessly during acts of worship, even without the exertion of searching for sense objects. || 22 ||

Regarding the phrase "of the devotees": at the time of immersion during acts of worship, that state which is spontaneously accomplished and radiant within Your abode arises for the devotees as something transcendent, even without effort such as meditation; how then could there be even the appearance of seeking, that is, the perception of searching for external objects such as flowers, incense, and unguents? It is that [state].
The meaning is: "just so, even without that [effort], by being separated from it. || 22 ||
There is nothing unattainable for devotees, nor is there anything difficult for them to obtain;
they wander about solely intoxicated by the pride of worshipping you.
No, it is not so. Because they have attained their own true nature, which is identical with the perfect Śiva, there is nothing whatsoever for devotees to acquire that is difficult to obtain;
intoxicated by the wine of devotion, they wander about solely for the sake of no further purpose. || 23 ||

Oh, how praiseworthy is this extraordinary mode of worship toward you, the Giver of Boons, performed by those whose hearts are noble with the weight of devotion—a rite that is untainted by the blemish of begging! (24)
"Aha! How noble-minded you are! It is for this very reason that they are extraordinary—unworldly in that not even one among them asks anything of you, even though you are the granter of boons. (24)
What beauty is there, what joy, what prosperity, or what other excellence? What liberation is there, or what else at all, when this Great God (Mahādeva) is worshipped? (25)

"What is it?"—it refers to that splendorous radiance which is worshipped as the Great Lord (Maheśvara), the conscious Self (cidātman) who is "some unknown one" (ko'pi); the meaning is that it is not merely "everything.

Likewise for the other [questions]: "What is liberation?"—it is the essence of supreme bliss (paramānanda-sāra), which transcends the liberations taught by the Sāṃkhya, Vaiṣṇava, Śākta, Nākulapa, Pāśupata, and other traditions.
Because of the attainment of liberation, which consists of the fullness of the universe. || 25 ||
May this body of mine, nourished by the nectar of pure and transparent devotion shining from within, be for the purpose of worshiping you. (26)

Within— this body of mine, nourished by the nectar of immersion, which is like mercury purified by the elixir of time (kālikākṣapaṇa), shining with auspiciousness and made entirely composed of well-being through the exceedingly clear nectar of devotion capable of reflecting the entire universe, which flashes forth within the state of pure consciousness.

May this [offering], prepared for the purpose of your worship, having entered into you alone—who are a dense mass of consciousness and bliss—dissolve away, even though it is already established as the essence of immersion (samāveśa). || 26 ||
O All-pervading Lord, Sovereign of the World, may I always be dependent upon the enjoyment of worshipping Your feet, acting solely according to my own will. (27)

"From you": I, who am the Lord, the Master, and the independent sovereign of the worlds—from Kālāgni up to Sadāśiva—may I become dependent solely on the joy of worshipping your feet. For this alone is that extraordinary sovereignty over the universe and independence [of yours], which consists in being overwhelmed by absorption into your feet, whereas other feet exist even in a state of dependence.
"Sovereignty that is without equal and absolute independence" is the suggestion of the marvelous sentiment (adbhuta-rasa-dhvani). || 27 ||
O Lord, for those who thirst for meditation upon you, the sight of you, or the touch of you,
there arises the great lake of your worship— cool and sweet.

Regarding the phrase "tvaddhyāna" (meditation on You): when there exists that thirst for seeing and touching You within meditation on You—thinking, "May I see even the Supreme Lord, who is a mass of consciousness and bliss; may I touch Him"—then for certain individuals who have been directly graced by You, the great lake of Your worship becomes cool and sweet.
The meaning is that the ocean, filled with your worship which possesses the marvelous power of removing all torment, is as if produced anew.
Just as you alone are the vessel for the world's offerings and enjoyments, so too is the one possessed of devotion the vessel for offerings and enjoyments. (29)

(134) "Just as" (*yathā*): O Lord, O Master, just as you alone are the vessel— that is, the support— of the enjoyment of worship in its explained form from within the midst of the entire universe, so too is only the one possessed of devotion, that is, the one characterized by immersion (*samāveśa*).
The meaning is that such a person is a vessel for the enjoyment of worship and is one who brings about cessation [of suffering]. || 29 ||
O Lord, may this great festival of Your worship be victorious;
for therein the agitation of even the thirty-six principles exults intensely.

"Someone" (ko'pi): for he is one who possesses the penetration of *nīti* (the way of conduct), and thus is addressed as "Lord" (*svāmin*). "Even of the thirty-six"—this refers to the agitation (*kṣobha*) of the principles (*tattvas*), both those residing in the body and those external to it by means of that [body], which is a state of imbalance caused by the burning of the fire of consciousness (*saṃvid-agni*). || 30 ||
Salutations to them, O All-pervading Lord, by whom even the implements for Your worship become worthy of worship through the nectar-water of their devotion.

"Salutations to them": salutations to those for whom the implements of worship—flowers and so forth—become worthy of offering through the nectar-water of devotion, that is, through the essence of immersion [in You]; they become fit for worship because Your bathing manifests their state as Śiva. || 31 ||
O Lord, at the commencement of worship, having meditated upon the identity with You that is to be infused by the mantra,
the devotees abide within their own supreme self and do not find room anywhere else for their joy.

He worships. Having meditated upon—that is, having contemplated at the commencement of the worship—the state of identity with You (*tvadātmatā*), which is to be accomplished through the mantra characterized by the protection of contemplation (*manana-trāṇa*) and which excels in the majesty of pure consciousness (*cinmāhātmya-prakarṣaka*), according to the principle that "one must become Śiva" and thus establish that very [state] as its arising (*udaya*) precisely at the moment of the desire to enter into the worship consisting of the utterance of the mantra; so it is said.

Through the excellence of their devotion, having become one with Śiva, the devotees do not find room—that is, they do not remain—within their own selves, which are now the supreme, perfect form. || 32 ||
As if blooming at the attainment of a kingdom, some, during the great festival of worship,
share the entire world with the nectar of their exhilaration.

Regarding the word "rājya" (sovereignty): by means of the "fully blossomed" [lotuses]— that is, through the method of great expansion— and having entered the mudrā of Śrī Bhairavī, the entire world, which is the ground of both the object of knowledge and the knower, is shared out by means of the nectar-liquor, the drinking of immortality.
It is clear that the entire earth is filled and made full of one's own bliss by those blossoming with the festival of attaining sovereignty, and it is shared with them like wine. || 33 ||

For those whose enjoyment at every moment consists of worship and the drinking of the nectar [of truth], are they gods, or are they liberated souls, or are they some other kind of people altogether? (34)
One worships them; for enjoyment is a wonder that, like the uninterrupted presence of a friend at every moment, cannot be fully described even by hundreds of hymns. || 34 ||
Through the universal penetration that serves as the means for worship, there is reverence; oh, how indescribable is the devotion of the faithful, and how indescribable indeed is their humility! (35)
He worships that which has become the instrument and the equipment for worship—the body consisting of the thirty-six principles (*tattvas*) as well as the external [world].
Through that immersion (*āveśa*), which is the entry into the expanse of consciousness (*cidbhūmi*), oh, what a wonder! What an extraordinary thing indeed!
There is a shadow of contradiction in how devotion simultaneously brings about weightiness and lightness:

through effort, it involves the total acceptance of all things (weightiness), yet it also effects the cessation of the burden of the duality created by *māyā* (lightness); for how can there be lightness within weightiness? || 35 ||
From the agitation caused by the distraction of the senses during worship, there arises nectar for the devotees,
just as for the gods it arises from the churning of the ocean of milk.

Regarding the term *pūjāmayī*: the sense-faculties (*akṣāṇi*), which consist of the emergence of the circle of deities (*devatācakra*) and bestow rest upon the ground of universal consciousness (*cidbhūmi*), are the instruments of worship.
