Their distraction—their preoccupation with grasping their own respective objects—is itself agitation (*kṣobha*), that is, turbulence. From that...

Thus, even in relation to a limited awakening, there occurs for devotees the emergence—meaning the manifestation—of the nectar of great bliss from that which is desired; even when the confusion of subject and object persists, it is simply the manifestation of the bliss of consciousness for the devotees.

That is the meaning; as it has been said: "Even when directed toward an object of perception, its nature remains [unchanged]. Just as for the gods, the churning of the milk-ocean results in the emergence of *amṛta*, the nectar of immortality, so too here, the agitation (*kṣobha*)—which is the process of drawing in and pulling back—the distraction of the eye (*akṣa*), that is, the gaze of the one to be worshipped who is the Nāga King himself, is itself the agitation.
Thus [ends the section]. || 36 ||
Some consider worship to be like a wish-fulfilling cow;
others, with their faces turned inward, drink it as having a flavor exceeding a stream of nectar.

Regarding the word "pūjām" (worship): just as the wish-fulfilling cow (*kāmadhenu*) fulfills one's desires, so too do some who long for fruits consider and resolve that worship alone is the essence; others, however, regard it as a flow of nectar—a stream of bliss exceeding even a torrent of ambrosia.
The meaning is that those who are inward-turned drink from the wish-fulfilling cow; they suckle it and immediately experience wonder.
Even this distraction of the senses for devotees is regarded as conducive to worldly life;
for it brings forth something within and nourishes the great festival of worship. (38)
Regarding the phrase "of the devotees": the scattering of the senses—the outward movement of the faculties toward the world—is generally regarded as worldly transmigration (*saṃsāra*).

However, by bringing about—that is, by causing one to attain—something extraordinary in the form of bliss, it nourishes for the devotees, who are immersed in the expansion of the Śrīcakra, the great festival of worship, which is the repose in their own full nature.

And so, those who, disregarding the glories produced by the churning of the great ocean of my own wisdom— the Mandara mountain— through the revolutions of the casting of the dice, drink only the nectar, they alone are the gods worthy of praise in this world. || 38 ||
O Lord, because of the agitation of devotion, worship directed toward You, who are one's own self, is not strange;
rather, it is not for the sake of wretchedness, for wretchedness is the ultimate fruit of such [worldly] humility.

Regarding "devotion": that worship which arises from the helplessness caused by the intense immersion (*samāveśa*) and agitation of devotion toward You, who are one's own self (*svātmabhūta*), is wonderful and marvelous; it does not lead to wretchedness, nor does it result in any state of misery.

For others, this [desire for liberation] is primarily characterized by longing; it is not merely such, but rather, through a sense of wretchedness regarding worldly craving, it is the supreme, ultimate form of bliss—the fruit of even fruits such as prosperity, and indeed the highest and most perfect fruit. (39)
For some devotees, ritual service is the means for attaining Your state;
for them, however, it is the expansion of bliss through identity with You. (40)
Regarding the term "upacāra" (metaphorical designation): for some who are intent on duality, the attainment of your state is merely a metaphorical designation for your state;

it is simply a means of propitiation consisting of ritual action. But for devotees, that "prasara"—meaning its expansion or unfolding—is of the bliss whose nature is identity with you; this [refers to] that which is to be predicated.
The masculine gender. || 40 ||
Even an image whose form is unconnected [to ritual rules], when displayed by those unrestrained by the intoxication of devotion, attains an indescribable stability within you. (41)

Regarding the word *api*: it is used in the sense of "even" (*manāk*). Thus, there would be a transgression (*pratyavāya*) if the prescribed procedure were otherwise, as is established in the technical treatises (*prakriyā-śāstra*). However, this is truly marvelous: through the intoxication of devotion and the helplessness of being possessed by immersion (*samāveśa*), even that which is disconnected in form—due to the unrestrained forgetting of the rules of prescribed procedure—is [accepted].

Even when performed improperly—being expanded and extended by those intent on mere ritual action—it attains a firm and complete establishment in You, a singular station that cannot even be conceived; this is a suggestion of wonder (adbhutadhvani). || 41 ||
O Śambhu, you alone are the graceful recipient of all offerings—those which have descended from minds rendered motionless by the savoring of the taste of delicious food. 42.

"O Śambhu, you alone are the delightful and heart-fitting conscious self (cidātman) of those offerings and acts of universal surrender, which have flowed forth from that mind whose flickering instability has been stilled by the tasting of that devotional rasa whose essence is aesthetic wonder (camatkāra)."
"O treasure of excellence, [you alone are] the vessel and the refuge"—
this is the meaning of the statement "it is indeed fitting," implying that this alone is logical for anyone else.

Since Brahmā and the others, being composed of duality, lack the fitness to be recipients of such worship, the plural form "of the worships" (*pūjānām*) is used to manifest that their essence consists in various forms of repose. 42.
O Lord, may my means of accomplishment (sādhana) for the ritual of your worship be complete, pure, full of devotion, and steadfast. (43)

"Complete" means: in the ritual of worship of you, O Lord of Consciousness (*cin-nātha*), which must necessarily be performed, my eyes and other senses are my instruments of practice; therefore, because they consist of rays of consciousness, they are pure, devoted, intent on serving you through the offering of the universe, and—because they have never been touched by animalistic (*pāśava*) latent impressions—they are steadfast.
May they always remain exactly like this. || 43 ||
O Lord, in this rite of worshiping you—which is a treasury of every kind of offering—oh, some indescribable splendor unfolds within the entire collection of my senses! (44)
Regarding the word "aśeṣā" (without remainder): reflecting upon this very state, he says:

"O Lord, whose nature is the source of the emergence, expansion, and so forth of the powers; in your act of worship, which is a beautiful treasury (*satkośa*)—that is, a magnificent storehouse—for all the various kinds of worship."

In this repose within the nature of the glorious Nāthabhairava, who is a mass of full consciousness and bliss, a certain splendor—beauty witnessed by one’s own self-awareness—unfolds and flashes forth as the radiance of the wheel of rays belonging to the multitude of instruments.
Thus, these well-spoken verses, which rain down the essential instructions for this [system] filled with the Great Meaning (Mahārtha), shine forth. || 44 ||
O Lord, this very gentleness of yours alone is indeed perceived,
since even you, the Sovereign of the Universe, are worshipped by your servants and are attained by them.

"This one" refers to those very qualities: "gracefulness and straightforwardness belong to you alone. Although all selves are the lords of the universe by virtue of being the mass of consciousness (*cidghana*), you—being the master even of Sadāśiva and others—are worshipped, entered, attained, and freely made one's own. || 45 ||
Whether from a manifest form or an unmanifest one, or even from existence or non-existence, may the great festival of your worship arise for me, who am ever praiseworthy. (46)
"Existing" (sadā): A formal entity (*mūrta-bhāva*) is such things as a jar; an informal entity (*amūrta*) is such things as pleasure; a formal entity consists of the shards of a jar;

and non-existence (*abhāva*) is of the nature of a non-presuppositional negation (*prasajya-pratiṣedha*) constructed by conceptual thought (*vikalpaka*). [The phrase] "arising from that" completes the compound.
The meaning is that one should emerge, having cast aside the state of existence and non-existence.
"The great festival of your worship is the arising of your own repose"—in this phrase, "from existence" (*bhāvāt*) and so forth, the ablative case is used with the elision of the suffix *lyap*.
46. [I offer] you always with desire, anger, and pride, which have been made into offerings.
To those who offer worship and salutation, you are truly pleased with them in reality.

Regarding the phrase "kāma-krodha" (desire and anger): since all mental fluctuations (*citta-vṛtti*) are subsumed under desire and the rest, their specific mention is for the purpose of offering them up; for you are truly satisfied by those [fluctuations] when they have been examined and surrendered unto You. Furthermore, because it is stated: "He who is liberated from joy, envy, fear, and anger is dear to Me," is it not so?
In this hymn composed by himself, which consists of the words of the *Śrīmanmahārthasāra*, this verse serves as the "place of the eye" (the central point).

Furthermore, it should be remembered that even such verses as "all knots of latent tendencies (*vāsanā*)... and "O You who are like the world, yet distinct from it; O You who are the manifestation of the destruction of the thirst for knowledge within this very world; O You who have not gone anywhere else... are all consistent with this [central theme].
Furthermore, there are no verses here concerning Udayana, who spread his bed upon the uneven ground; this is simply the grace of Viśvāvarta.
In the same way, much has been composed in other hymns of a similar nature, yet we have not disclosed it; so, enough—let us follow only the well-spoken verses. || 47 ||
Victorious is this supreme rite of worship for those who partake in devotion to you;
for even when performed with blades of grass, it becomes equivalent to being performed with jewels.

"Victory!"—the word "even" (*api*) is displaced in its position; thus, even that which is performed with mere blades of grass, yet which is fashioned as if with jewels and provides complete rest, that supreme and perfect pinnacle of worship (*pūjādhiḥ*) of those devoted to the Lord, who are graced by immersion into You, is victorious. May there be auspiciousness! 48.

Thus ends the commentary on the seventeenth hymn, titled "The High Regard for Divine Play," within the *Parameśvarastotrāvalī* composed by the venerable teacher Utpaladeva, the author of the *Śrīmadīśvarapratyabhijñā*, as expounded by the venerable Kṣemarāja. 17.
Oṃ tat sat. Having attained you from within the world, they again obtain this [world] from within you.
O Lord of the Universe, for those who possess devotion unto you alone, nothing whatsoever remains far away in this world. || 1 ||

Oṃ *jagataḥ*. O Lord of the World (*jagadīśa*), those who possess devotion to You alone— their own self whose nature is consciousness (*cidrūpa*)— having reached You from within the midst of this world, the universe, and having obtained You, who are the very form of light, from the very state of manifest worldly activity, [they find] once again from within that world of Yours, whose nature is consciousness...

Because those devoted ones—having correctly realized that your essential nature is the Self of the universe—obtain [everything] from the midst [of all things], for them nothing here in this world is distant;
since everything manifests as being like their own limbs, it has been said: "He who sees me everywhere, and sees everything in me..."
"He beholds," and so forth, in the Gītās. || 1 ||
In some places you alone exist, and in others Bhavānī exists, who is the primary one pregnant with the sequence of all objects;
yet in the state of ultimate reality, there is no distinction between you and the Goddess.
Nor is there any distinction between you and the three worlds. || 2 ||

Regarding the word "kvacid" (in some cases): in liberation (*mukti*), in its means (*tadupāyatā*), and in worldly enjoyment (*bhoga*), Bhavānī is the supreme power (*parā śakti*). Within her—within the state of ultimate reality where conceptual construction has dissolved—the entire objective order, the aggregate of objects of knowledge beginning with *kāla* and ending with *kṣiti*, is contained within her womb like the seed inside a pod (*śimbikābījavat*), being in intimate contact with her.
Furthermore, from the perspective of ultimate reality, there is no difference between you and even the three worlds— which consist of existence, transcendence, and fearlessness—
let alone from your own power.
People do not recognize even that which is naturally beautiful when they treat it with contempt;
for all things become beautiful through effort.
But this mind, alas, does not even recognize its own true nature despite being so intent; oh, what a pity! I am ruined.

Regarding the phrase "no jānata" (they do not know): people, being full of arrogance, do not recognize that the nature of all things is the beautiful, conscious Self (*cidātman*), because they fail to realize through effort and with absolute certainty that all things whatsoever are indeed beautiful and supreme, since they are composed of consciousness by virtue of their manifest nature; let this suffice for now.

This is the utterance of one who, failing to attain the excellence of immersion (*samāveśa*) in the world and thus languishing, thinks: "I am ruined!"—for even when the knowledge of the true nature of existence arises, and even when the form of the Self itself emerges, the mind perceives only that [worldly state] which, though seized by the friction of the desire to ascend the stream of immersion, does not attain identity with Consciousness (*cidaikātmya*). 3.
Having worshipped Your feet with an abundance of wealth acquired by dwelling within my own self, which consists of pure existence,
I do not even desire food or clothing constantly.
I bow to him who has no such dependence. || 4 ||

"O Bhagavan!"— he by whom your feet have been incessantly worshipped, being firmly embraced through non-duality, by means of an abundance of prosperity consisting of the expansion of supreme bliss obtained through resting in his own self, which is of the nature of consciousness (*cidrūpa*) as is your own essential form. He who is such...
I bow to him who does not even require food or clothing, who remains indifferent to worldly affairs whether he eats this or that, and who is solely intent on worship.
Although this world always dwells securely within your body, it burns intensely within; therefore,
by your will, act so that it may find peace here.
May I become filled with the bliss of worshipping you. || 5 ||

"Always" (sadā): by dwelling in Your body—which is eternally augmented and Your very nature—this world, though in reality established in its own state and consisting of bliss, [appears] through Your will in the form of a continuous flow of duality.

Therefore, it is excessively consumed by Your power within me; since I shall be afflicted by those sufferings, act accordingly—by Your will and out of a desire to favor me—in this realm fashioned for this purpose, so that I, Your devotee, may become filled with the bliss of worshipping You. || 5 ||
May my mind, liberated by drinking the nectar of worshiping the two lotus feet of Your Majesty— which arise spontaneously—
be such that I may become [a master] over the entire collection of all goals.
His worldly journey consists merely of pleasant contact. || 6 ||
Regarding the phrase "by one's own impulse" (*svarasena*): that worship of your feet which arises spontaneously and effortlessly is itself the attainment of immersion into you;

it is the drinking of nectar. One whose mind is attached to that, whose consciousness finds rest therein, and who—regarding all objects of worldly experience, whether deemed acceptable or rejectable—is [established as] the "I,"...
May my worldly journey consist merely of pleasant touch; may the activities of the world have the essence of the radiance of my own bliss.
O Lord, when You clearly flash within me, You who are the object of all worldly activity!
My objects come and go incessantly; may they shine forth for me at all times.

"Always" means at all times, perpetually, without cessation; while You, whose nature is consciousness, clearly manifest within me—the sphere of worldly experience—all things come into being and pass away, being created and withdrawn. May I always remain permeated by You.
The meaning is "I shall be the agent of the creation and destruction of all things. Regarding the reading "they approach and they depart," it should be explained as follows:

even while arriving, they appear only as if dissolving like reflections in a mirror, and do not possess even the slightest degree of stability; the word *ca* (and) is used here in the sense of *eva* (only). Just as they appear in the world, so too do they arise and perish.
Or it should be construed as "bhāntu" (let them shine). || 7 ||
Or rather, may I always wander even in your own city, never separated from you.
May not even a single moment or a fraction of a second pass for me without victory, wherein You, who are composed of all things, are not present.

"Constantly" means: I would wander in the tranquil state of the *pura* (the city) belonging to you alone—that is, I would be possessed by the immersion (*samāveśa*) of Śakti; or, being separated from you, I would consist of the immersion of Śambhu;
or, being "consisting of you," I would be of your very nature, liberated in essence, wherein I do not "prevail"—that is, I do not exist with supreme excellence.

"May even that moment, that fraction of a second, not pass for me"—this [utterance] is indeed a deliberation (*vitarka*) focused on the longing for ever-increasing, increasingly superior states. || 8 ||
O Lord, when this place is filled on all sides by the floods of cool nectar flowing from Your limbs,
may the devotees here [attain] the perfection of worshipping You.
They move within the lake of saṃsāra. || 9 ||

"O Bhava! Your devotees, distinguished by the perfection of worshipping you and the perfection of resting in you, move about—that is, they conduct their worldly affairs—within the midst of this ocean of existence, the lake of saṃsāra. In what kind of place?
In one that is thoroughly cooled by [the waters] flowing from all sides from your limb, which is the form of your supreme power (paraśakti).
"Filled," that is to say, completely brimming and saturated on all sides with floods of nectar—the outbursts of bliss—which bring about the subsiding of the heat of the fire of suffering. || 9 ||
O Lord, may I always dwell within my own self in your great forest, which is cooled by the shade of the great tree of mantras, as your worshipper.
"Mahāmantra" means: the Great Mantra is the nature of the supreme speech (*paravāk*), which is pure self-reflection (*ahaṃvimarśa*) itself;
because it has spread forth through hundreds of branches of power (*śakti*), it is a tree, and [the state] is cooled by its shade—that is, its splendor.
O Great Forest that removes the torment of duality! You alone are the Great Forest, the vast expanse whose nature is consciousness-bliss (cidānanda), the place of ultimate rest.
O Lord, may I always dwell there within my own self, in my true nature, as your worshipper, intent on your adoration, and maintain that state. || 10 ||
O Lord, just as you appear before me as the embodiment of creative intuition (*pratibhā*), manifesting from every object as the totality of all living beings, so may you extend your presence.
O Vraja, you are adorned with the splendor of three eyes that pierce like a trident.
Regarding the phrase "prativastu" (in every object): in every object, in every being, you are the one who exists for all living beings;

just as you appear as the nature of manifestation (*pratibhāmaya*) and the form of consciousness (*saṃvidrūpa*), appearing through the impossibility of otherwise accounting for the perception of blue and other objects—even though you are not recognized—you nonetheless shine forth in reality, so too, O Lord, you are present before me, your servant, everywhere.

Adorned with three eyes and a trident, being correctly recognized by this unsurpassed and unique identifying mark, "attain renown" means become manifest; that is to say, shine forth through immersion (*samāveśa*).
The reference to the three eyes and the trident is intended to characterize the unique identifying marks, and there is no emphasis here on their literal form.
In the case of the yoga [of the suffix] *ta* from the root *samasta-jīv*, there is *śam*. 11.
When will you be satisfied by the offering of my own conceit, fashioned with a weight of devotion toward equanimity?
May my vision be such that it perceives the state [of reality] everywhere. || 12 ||

Regarding the term *abhimāna*: *Abhimāna* is indeed the ego (*ahaṅkāra*), which is itself the sacrificial porridge (*caru*)—the cooked offering in the vessel. Its *upahāra* (offering) is its dedication to the Blessed One, that is, the grasping of the supreme state of "I-ness. From that, by means of the essence of devotion (*bhaktirasa*), which is the expansion of service characterized primarily by equanimity, [one realizes]: "The Great Lord is my Master. Thus it is said.
Having attained satisfaction from what was fashioned and accomplished, being thus pleased,
when [all conceptual constructs] have dissolved, may you at some time become the resting place— the ground of repose— for my vision everywhere.
However, when there is identification with the body and so forth, the meaning is that one should directly realize the entire universe as consisting of you alone. || 12 ||
Dwelling in the midst of the supreme ocean of immortality, with my mind immersed solely in the ritual of worshiping you,
may I conduct myself in all the affairs of worldly life.
Even a mere portion of elixirs from any source whatsoever [is beneficial]. || 13 ||
"Living thus": with my mind immersed and attached solely to the method of worshipping you,

dwelling within the ocean of consciousness-bliss in the midst of the supreme ocean of nectar, may I perform every worldly activity— the movements of the people— while remaining as if nothing at all were happening from anywhere or in the midst of anything.
Tasting his desired nature, which is supramundane bliss.
Let the true nature of your reality remain here;
for who indeed is worthy of being the vessel for this matter?
For it is precisely this—name, form, and activity—[that constitutes it].
Because you take away [all things] at the end of the day, you are Hara. || 14 ||

"Belonging to you": whatever exists here in this world, all that is yours, being of the nature of your own manifestation; let this be so, simply as "Om. Who indeed, being devoted, is not a fit vessel to explain the true meaning of this? For as soon as we begin to investigate it—

To this, the analysis of the objection is as follows: This very [reality] of yours is extraordinary, established by experience, and consists of name, form, activity, and so forth—such as "Maheśvara" and the like;
its form is a mass of consciousness, and its activity, by the inclusion of terms such as "performing the creation and dissolution of all," implies omniscience.

Manifesting at the very outset in the form of autonomy and so forth, He seizes that [state] by inducing a deficiency in immersion (*samāveśa*), thereby rendering us forgetful of our own activity; and this is fitting, since you bear the etymological name "Hara" (the Seizer) because you seize [everything]. 14.
O Lord, they have no desire for happiness even for the sake of peace, nor do they harbor even the slightest pride born of devotion toward You.
Even a request for the fruit of seeking liberation is not remembered before one who captivates the heart. 15.

Regarding the word "for peace": in those servants of Yours, there is not even the slightest desire for pleasure—that longing for enjoyment arising from the wish for happiness—for the sake of peace, that is, the cessation of suffering, because they possess intoxication brought about by devotion; and [this occurs] "in the presence of the Lord," meaning before Him who has been directly perceived.

Even the seeking of the fruit of the path to liberation is not remembered for such a Lord who captivates the heart; for He pacifies the illusory perceivers, and thus, since their very hearts have been stolen away, how could they remember anything else? Therefore, it is said that these [devotees] are solely intent upon immersion (*samāveśa*). || 15 ||
Whether it be the state of waking, the other [sleeping] state, or any other subtle condition whatsoever, for a person who is a vessel of devotion, all of that is [the Lord].
For those whose minds have you as their protector, there is a great festival.
Regarding the word *jāgara*: whatever state of waking, dreaming, or deep sleep belongs to the worldly condition (*jagadvyavasthā*)— even if it is slightly contracted—
it is all a great festival, a supreme exaltation, for one who possesses devotion, whose mind is protected by You, and whose consciousness is presided over by You.
Precisely because you are our protector. || 16 ||
The functions of my own senses,
though their movements were slack on all sides,
have become firm and far-reaching upon reaching you.
O Lord, how [can there be such a thing] for those whose wealth is devotion and whose essence is heat? || 17 ||

Regarding the phrase "of the self" (*ātmanaḥ*): O Lord, from the *āmanas* up to the *manas*, the functions or activities of the circle of senses— that is, the collection of the faculties— which are everywhere slack in their operation and even fickle, [are all] by means of the wealth of devotion...
"How is it that we— who were once hot, vigorous, firm, unyielding, and long— having attained You, whose form is consciousness,
have become of the nature of pure awareness through our identity with You and have come to abide just like You?"— this is his wonder within his own self. (17)
And nothing distinct was created; furthermore, nothing here was fashioned that was other than happiness. And yet, it is entirely characterized by suffering and differentiation.
Salutations to you, the abode of both the incomprehensible and the marvelous. || 18 ||

"Nor" (na ca): At the beginning of the primary creation (*ādisarga*), nothing distinct was created by you, nor does anything exist that is inherently separate. The word "atha" has the sense of "also" (*apy-arthe*); because everything is of the nature of consciousness (*cinmaya*) due to being cognized, difference is impossible. Furthermore, nothing in the form of pleasure or its opposite, pain, was fashioned.

For the very reason already stated, the word "kiṃcit" (something/somewhat) is to be joined three times; and thus, [Thou art] both entirely suffering and yet distinct—this is indeed the meaning of the particle "api.
Furthermore, because there is no recognition of identity with You, [Thou art] thus the abode of incomparable wonder and the ground of extraordinary marvel; salutations be to Thee! || 18 ||
For me, whose stains of conceptual construction have been washed away by the overflowing nectar-filled sword that negates harshness,
and who has crushed the enemy of invincible doubt—
May there be your uninterrupted vision. || 19 ||

"Khara" means harsh or uneven; that which is the cave of non-recognition (*tvadakhyāti*) is a pit of negation. Its filling with the nectar of You—the ambrosia of non-duality—causes it to overflow and surge upward. Consequently, for one whose impurity of conceptual construction (*vikalpa-mala*) has been thus washed away, the enemy that is doubt—difficult to conquer—has been shattered and pulverized.
For me, who am such as I am, may the vision of You—the continuous and dense manifestation of the Self as the mass of consciousness—be ever-present. (19)
Enter me clearly, O Lord, so that I may enter you constantly, since I am yours.
With impetuous zeal, having attained the state of supreme proximity, I would worship Your very form in person. || 20 ||
"Clearly," [it means]: O Lord, you should first enter me clearly and manifestly, not by way of being hidden;

then, immediately thereafter, when you are in such a state, having acquired the necessary capacity, I shall enter you constantly—I shall indeed accept you with firm support. The optative (*liṅ*) is used here in the sense of a command (*niyoga*). Thus it is said.

"Being present, having reached the state of supreme proximity and being very near to you, I would, through your own impetuosity—that is, with haste—properly worship, meaning enter into, your very own true form, your essential nature. || 20 ||
No one possesses the power to praise you, or rather, they do indeed possess it because you are so exceedingly beautiful; yet,
this is what I have constantly requested of you.
May I behold the Lord who rests within the dyad. || 21 ||

"In you"—meaning even for anyone, including Brahmā, Upendra, Rudra, and others—because they are composed of duality, there is a failure to recognize the nature of the Supreme Lord as a mass of consciousness (*cidghana*). "Exceedingly beautiful" means that because your own nature is a mass of consciousness and bliss, you are most desirable and captivating to the heart; therefore, he who [recognizes] you as the Self...

One recognizes that there exists in you the power to praise some extraordinary being—this phrase "of some one" (*kasyāpi*) should be understood as being repeated [to apply to both]. For me, however, the constant prayer and desire is this:
that I might behold, that is, directly realize, you, the Lord, without ceasing and without interruption. May there be auspiciousness! (*śivam*)
Thus ends the commentary on the eighteenth hymn, titled "The Manifestation," from the *Stotrāvalī* composed by the venerable teacher Utpaladeva, as written by the illustrious Rājānaka Kṣemarāja. 18.
Oṃ! Victorious is Śiva, the wish-fulfilling tree, whose history is unprecedented, who transcends the stages of prayer, and who bestows manifold fruits. (1)
"Oṃ, [this is] the prayer. The wish-fulfilling tree grants only that which is desired; Śiva, however, grants even that which is impossible to pray for—such is an unprecedented account. (1)
Since everything is indeed obtainable from yourself, who are the sole treasury containing the collection of all things;
yet for me, this [body] is my own self.
But you alone do not strive; let others be supreme. || 2 ||

Regarding the phrase "all things": from you—that is, from your own self (*svātman*), which is indeed the sole substratum of all objects—the universe is to be obtained. For me, however, who am constantly intent upon contemplating my true nature, let there be nothing further to be attained than you yourself;
yet you, my own self, my very essence, do not manifest, meaning that at the time of emergence from meditative absorption (*vyutthāna*), you do not shine forth. || 2 ||
The Self, whose body consists of consciousness and action,
is in every respect the Supreme Lord himself;
yet his body [is manifested] within all things.
In these [beings], even the name [of "self"] does not exist; how much less anything else? || 3 ||

Regarding the phrase "knowledge and action": in all things, it is conceived that the Supreme Lord Himself—whose body is consciousness and whose nature is knowledge and action—is the very Self (*ātman*) in every respect; His body is His own essential nature (*svarūpa*), and He exists as this very one who shines forth in a manifest form. Indeed, [He is the cause] of diverse effects and instruments which possess various locations and forms.

How can the state of being the self of the one Lord be conceived? To this he says: "Otherwise, in regard to entities, there would be nothing but names—that is, mere designations—and what else [could there be], such as the nature of cause and effect? This is because nothing whatsoever is established without being composed of light (*prakāśa*); the word "otherwise" (*anyathā*) is to be supplied here. || 3 ||

O Lord, by means of this fruit— which is your very self in the form of my vision and which removes the pain of adversity— may I, having merged with it, attain a state of being identical with you through that path. (4)

Regarding the word *viṣamā*: that path which consists of your vision—your direct realization—which steals away the painful affliction of the heat of saṃsāra; by means of that path, may there be for me, through its fruit, a goal (*gati*) consisting of you alone, being of your very nature. [The phrase] "by means of that" is like the expression "the journey of Devadatta has been completed. Regarding the term *abhilīya* (having merged): [it refers to merging with the fruit].

Having applied the *ktā* suffix, it should be joined with "let it be" (*astu*) following it; if the reading is *abhilīlā*, it should be explained as "the play of the bliss of consciousness shimmering as delight. || 4 ||
When will there be success, adorned by the creeper of the wish-fulfilling gem that is meditation upon your stainless feet,
producing wonder in the minds of the perfected ones?
May it be fitting for me from you. || 5 ||

"O Lord! When will my complete success be accomplished? [When] that very creeper of jewels—which is the contemplation, that is, the repeated gazing, upon Your stainless and pure feet, the rays of which consist of knowledge, action, and so forth—being adorned with various manifold splendors, shall grant all prosperity."
In the presence of perfected beings and yogis whose minds are disciplined, what kind of wonder does she produce? || 5 ||
O Lord, when shall I behold your stainless face,
from which flows an unprecedented flood of nectar?
Who immerses the entire universe without exception.

"Karhi" means: this is the utterance of one who remains in the state of emergence (vyutthāna). "O Lord, when shall I behold directly—that is, when shall I realize—your stainless face, which is the supreme form of peace?

It causes the entire universe—which consists of the worlds and their inhabitants, which is unprecedented and supramundane, and which is a flood of nectar and an expansion of bliss—to be submerged. || 6 ||
O Lord, when will your form, which rejoices as soon as it is meditated upon, fill [the world] with floods of supreme nectar through the liberation of non-differentiation from you?
They are always far removed from my manifestation.
"Merely thought of": liberation is indeed non-difference from You, which is the removal of the bondage of duality.
Its non-manifestation—that is, its failure to appear—is the cause of those distant, deep, and dense chasms consisting of longing.
When, at what time, will that which belongs to You arise merely by being thought of—blooming immediately after the moment of contemplation?
The agent, form (rūpa), should always fill and immerse [the self] with floods of supreme nectar and outpourings of bliss. || 7 ||
O Lord, my mind has not yet abandoned its fickleness despite its attachment to the unsurpassed flavor of You; when will this come to pass? May it happen soon! (8)
"Thine" (tvadīya): Thine unsurpassed rasa is the expansion of supreme consciousness; attachment to that is devotion to it.

By means of that, even with restlessness abandoned and emergence [from absorption] dissolved, the phrase "even now" indicates an intensity of longing—such as "when will it quickly happen?"—despite the fact that immersion has been tasted repeatedly. || 8 ||
May I never have to offer you anything that is dry or bitter at all times;
rather, may even pairs of opposites come to me as things obtained by being presented to you.

"Indeed! Having offered them up to you and attained them through their nature as pure consciousness, they have entered into you; thus, even upon emerging from that state, the savor of the impression of absorption has been acquired. Therefore, let all dualities—cold, heat, and the rest—descend at all times, however dry or bitter they may be."
Furthermore, because they are filled with the nectar of the touch of non-duality, [other things] consist mostly of what is coarse and unpleasant to the taste.
O Lord, may your pure rays of light come face to face with me, so that I may be cleansed of the darkness of afflictions of body and mind. (10)

"O Lord! [he says]. May the pure rays—the powers (śaktis)—intent on bestowing grace, emerge forth and manifest after submerging the appearance of the body and so forth; may they come face-to-face. By these [rays], let the darknesses—which are the very torments of body and mind—be completely wiped away and utterly destroyed. || 10 ||
O Lord, be gracious until those who obstruct my path—those thieves of virtue who steal away the ultimate truth—come under my control. (11)

"O Lord," [he said]. "Grace is as before. Those qualities which are the adversaries on your path—those very qualities such as *sattva* and the rest—are thieves who rob one of the ultimate reality (*paramārtha*), which is non-difference from consciousness (*cidabheda*); they seize it and render it incapable of being experienced."
"May they become submissive"—as it has been said: "The flow and outflow of qualities and so forth should not be obstacles for the Knower.

Here, the two verbal suffixes *loṭ* (imperative) and *liṅ* (optative), occurring together, convey a request characterized by a benediction (*āśis*), just as in the case of the imperative form "lunīhi" (cut!), which implies a mutual exchange of action; this should be remembered in other instances as well regarding the Lord.
When [the deity] is pleased, thieves become submissive; this worldly meaning is indeed clear. || 11 ||
O Lord, let my mind be quickly filled with the showers of the nectar of devotion to you, until all the essence-less latent impressions have been washed away by immersion. 12.

Regarding the phrase "tvadbhakti": the mind (*mānasa*) is also a lake (*saras*). When even a lake is filled with showers (*āsāra*), those who possess base (*asāra*)—that is, foul—impressions (*vāsanā*) float up and, having leaped out, they themselves dry up and emerge outside.
If devotion toward You exists even in the state of liberation, why indeed would it not exist for one who possesses the nature of a mortal?
Therefore, O Unborn One, place me upon the stage of accomplishment that is worthy of Your splendor. || 13 ||

Regarding the word *mokṣa*: the state of liberation (*mokṣadaśā*) is the state of Supreme Śiva-hood (*paramaśivatā*), the state of liberation while living (*jīvanmuktatā*), which is essentially what has been taught in the Tantras—as he himself stated: "Having attained that state, we have become firmly established and are as if liberated.
[The phrase] "those subject to mortality" refers to one whose true nature as the Self has not been recognized; [the state of liberation] is "conformable" to such a person.
As before, it is the ground of supreme accomplishment consisting of the immersion into the power of Rudra, because therein the state of being a servant to the Lord clearly manifests. || 13 ||
O Lord, do not think with arrogance that I am greedy for even a fragment of supernatural power;
I am emaciated by my devotion to you.
Liberation arises from the side of the powers beginning with *aṇimā*.

Regarding the word *siddhi*: with respect to the full accomplishment (*pūrṇasiddhi*) whose nature is immersion (*samāveśa*), the accomplishments such as *aṇimā* and so forth—which consist of duality—are but fragments of accomplishment.

Do not think yourself greedy for their attainment; that is to say, do not become conceited by considering me to be one who is greedy for fragments of accomplishment. Indeed, in the system of the Supreme Lord...

If one were to object, "In the scriptures it is heard that for practitioners, after the enjoyment of supernatural powers (siddhis), once those enjoyments have been experienced, they go to Śiva; therefore, your [teaching of] liberation through devotion seems dull," he states the following reasoning: "The liberation that follows immediately from the unfolding of the powers such as *aṇimā* occurs through the gateway of devotion to You."
In the presence of the bliss of immersion in you, [all else] is emaciated—that is, exceedingly small. || 14 ||
May the Blessed One be gracious to me, his servant; indeed, I ask for no more than this: that the Lord of the Three Worlds be a giver.
That which is not an object of sight for those like me. || 15 ||
Regarding the word "of the servant": it is only this much [that is attained], and not such results as *āṇimā* and so forth. [The phrase] "may he be pleased" (p.
154)—[referring to the one] for whom the three worlds are as before—does not mean that such an impossible fruit is similar to that [attained result]. Thus, it is not so.
This is because of the cognition: "The vision of those like me. || 15 ||
May the pair of your lotus feet forever blossom within my mind, which is filled with the nectar-essence of the remembrance of your form.
It was something surpassing the world, distilling an indescribable honey.
"From you"—[the meaning is: Your pair of lotus feet, having abandoned the expansion and contraction of dualistic distinctions as before, [emits] honey;

that honey is of the nature of supreme bliss (*paramānanda*), possesses a sweetness (*mādhurya*) transcending the world and being extraordinary (*alaukika*), and it flows from the lotus in the mind which is filled with rasa. || 16 ||
Let this father be my lord, or else Tryambaka; and let Bhavānī be my mother.
There is no second person here who belongs to me.
Thus indeed may I wander, most perfectly at peace. || 17 ||
"So be it. "Asau" (that one) refers to my Lord, the mass of consciousness (*cidghana*), who is my benefactor and progenitor, and who causes the manifestation of my subjectivity;

likewise, Tryambaka and Bhavānī, the Supreme Power (*parāśakti*), are my sovereign mother. For me, whose true nature as the Great Lord has been thus recognized, there is no second person whatsoever in this world.

By the rule "the sixth case [is used] for the remainder" (śeṣe ṣaṣṭhī), this much alone is sufficient; thus, being most fulfilled and exceedingly joyful, may I wander and dwell—may there be auspiciousness! || 17 ||
Thus ends the commentary on the nineteenth hymn, titled *Udyotana*, within the *Stotrāvalī* composed by the venerable teacher Utpaladeva, written by the venerable Kṣemarāja. 19.
Oṃ! To the Lord, the Lord of the three worlds,
white with ashes, three-eyed, and bearing the trident;
I bow to the one who wears the serpent as his sacred thread and has the crescent moon as his crest-ornament. || 1 ||

Oṃ Nātha. "The three worlds" is as before. "Bhūti" means the manifestation consisting of the universe; by that, "sita" means bound—this word *sita* being derived from the root *ṣiñ*, meaning "to bind. He is the bearer of the trident, which consists of the three eyes known as Will, Knowledge, and Action, and which is of the nature of blazing wisdom for the purpose of shattering duality. Upa...
By him, the expansions of the enjoyer (bhogin) have been brought near, specifically gathered, and withdrawn;

"vīta" is a usage of the root *vi-i* (to go away). The digit of the moon (*indukala*), which is the consciousness-power (*citiśakti*) that sustains the universe, is his crest (*śekhara*)—that is, his primary form.
Alternatively, the digit of the moon consists of the totality of all that is measurable, and it is the "crest" because it is the cause for the manifestation of absolute freedom (*svātantrya*).
"I bow to him whose ornaments are assumed for the sake of play"—this is as before; the meaning is clear according to the external sequence. || 1 ||
I bow to her who wears a white garment with a halo-like luster emanating from her own body,
and who possesses a shimmering garland of skulls.
[He is] the one whose ornaments are the imagined festival of the dance. || 2 ||
"I bow. His own body is a form consisting of consciousness (*cinmaya*); emerging from that, it is a throbbing halo of light, a mass of radiating rays.

He whose white, pure lower garment and upper shawl are thus [composed of light]—meaning, according to the principle that Śiva is of an expanding nature, he is eternally embraced by his own circle of powers (*svaśakticakra*).

In this festival of dance, He has fashioned an adornment—an external manifestation of the rising splendor of His own sovereign freedom—by means of a garland of skulls that is ever-expanding, consisting of the entire series of subjects from Sadāśiva down to the last individual soul (sakala), which, through its own self-application, blossoms, shines intensely, plays, and throbs; by this, the external sequence becomes clearly manifest. || 2 ||
I bow to those deities whose activity is like that of Hara and who are worthy of Hara.
The vital breaths of those who are the abodes of constant good fortune are always inclined toward Hari alone. || 3 ||

"I bow"—[meaning this: Those whose vital breaths (*prāṇas*) are "suited for Śiva," consisting of [the powers of] emanation, withdrawal, grace, and so forth; who are "solely devoted to Śiva," being savorers of the constant immersion (*samāveśa*) in Him; and therefore whose life-force is the "abode of good fortune" because it is desirable to the entire universe due to its being filled with supreme bliss. || 3 ||
This very thing is but another play of your sovereignty, Maheśvara, just as it is; for in these meritorious deeds accomplished by mere wish, [what need is there for further effort?]
I approach the supreme means through my own self.

Regarding the term "play" (*krīḍita*): this expression means that one perceives the world as a play through the expansion of *samāveśa* (immersive absorption). It is intended to demonstrate that this play is situated precisely behind—that is, upon—the very height of your state as Maheśvara, within sacrificial offerings (*avadāna*) that are accomplished by mere will and fashioned by mere desire.

In the wondrous deeds consisting of your fivefold activity, I myself personally obtain the means that is complete even in the face of the assault of my own power; by entering into you and seizing my own conscious power, when I act as the performer of the fivefold activity just like you, that is your "other" [nature].
The meaning is "play"; the particle *eva* is placed out of its logical order (*bhinnakrama*). || 4 ||
O Lord, while this play of destiny exists within your abode, which is honored by the entire universe,
how much could I possibly become?
Nor is there the arising of the flavor of bliss. || 5 ||

"Thy" (tvat): when this play of limitation occurs within that abode of thine, that majesty of thine which is worshipped by the universe and which is the self of the universe, it is "thine alone"— meaning not small, but rather abundant— conforming precisely to [the measure of] Thy own bliss.

"Everyone plays; for him whose universe is play, bliss is indeed limitless"—thus he expresses the praise of his own self as being His servant, and for this very reason, He addresses Him as "O Lord" (Nātha). || 5 ||
How could he not be fortunate, who is Hara, the beloved of Gaurī? And how could even Hara not be so, if [he is] not [the beloved of Gaurī]? What then?
The supreme beloved of Gaurī. || 6 ||
How so? He is "fortunate" (*subhaga*), meaning desirable to all; he is the "beloved of Gaurī," the Supreme Power (*parā śakti*), and thus desirable;

the meaning is that he is the Mass of Bliss (*ānandaghana*) embraced by the Supreme Goddess (*bhaṭṭārikā*). He is "Hara," captivating the heart through the wonder of total immersion (*samāveśa*), and the destroyer of the state of duality for the sake of the Supreme Power.
He is indeed most beloved. || 6 ||
For whom the root of one's own self is imperishable and consists of the nectar of meditation, the creeper of consciousness likewise takes on that same form.
Of that certain tree. || 7 ||

Regarding "meditation" (*dhyāna*): for one who possesses immersion (*samāveśa*), the root cause of his own self is the nectar of meditation, whose essential nature is the Lord Śiva— the very essence of the bliss of consciousness— recognized through the concealment of his own true form.

As it has been said: "There exists this Lord, or the progenitor," and so forth. Of that certain most rare and excellent tree which removes all torment, the creepers of consciousness—namely, the cognitions of blue, pleasure, and so on—are of such a nature that they consist entirely of the nectar of meditation, being eternal by virtue of their very form as consciousness. || 7 ||
At the moment when the itch of devotion is aroused, the Supreme Lord [manifests].
It becomes nothing more than the worship of a pillar made of a great touchstone. || 8 ||

Regarding the word "devotion" (*bhakti*): devotion is indeed attachment to the Blessed One, for it brings about a state of helplessness. When that [attachment] reaches its full bloom, worship—as previously determined—is the great pillar of the touchstone; it is a massive grinding-stone.
The meaning is that by quelling the itch of devotion, it becomes the cause for resting in one's own self, which is a mass of bliss.
To you who always delight in creation, who always sit in the bliss of maintenance,
and who always consume the three worlds—
Salutation to the satisfied Lord. || 9 ||

"Always. Thus, even in the realm of empirical transaction (*vyavahāra*), the Lord, entering the body and so forth, may by His will manifest externally that very flood of internal objects which is already shining [within]. According to this established principle, even as the Blessed One enters the body and so forth, at every moment—

Furthermore, the manner in which [the Self] acts as the cause of emanation and so forth, through the process of joining and separating the various infinite appearances of the grasped and the grasper, has been elaborated and determined by me in the *Spandasandoha*; therefore, that very work should be consulted. || 9 ||
Those who, having gone nowhere and having abandoned nothing, behold this very world as your abode— [to them belongs liberation].
Salutations again and again to those who are worthy of them. || 10 ||
"No," [he replied]. "Without going to such states as the single point (*ekānta*) or the twelve-point limit (*dvādaśānta*), nor to the other world,

but having abandoned enjoyments belonging to lower planes and this very body— which for the unawakened is considered something to be rejected— [I have come] to this, your abode, which is a mass of consciousness."

Salutations again and again to those fortunate ones who, possessed by the vision of the divine and great purpose, perceive [this]; by this repetition, their very status as knowers of the supreme reality is intimated. || 10 ||
For those enriched by the fortune of devotion,
what else remains to be prayed for? Or, for those impoverished of it, [what else is there]?
What else remains to be prayed for? || 11 ||
Regarding the word "devotion" (bhakti): "What else? means that since that which is to be attained has already been attained, there is indeed nothing else to be requested; "what else?
implies that since the ultimate reality (paramārtha) has not been secured, what is the use of anything else that is mostly insubstantial? || 11 ||
Even sufferings turn into happiness,
even poison turns into nectar,
and even cyclic existence turns into liberation.
Wherever there is a path, that belongs to Śaṅkara.

Regarding the "sufferings": even these three arise solely from the ascent of one's own power (*nijabala*), which is a mass of consciousness and bliss; this is the state of the path, denoted by the term *śāktapada*. || 12 ||
O Lord, for those who enjoy worldly existence, there is no suffering in the beginning, the middle, or the end; and yet, we [suffer].
How can it be said that we are sinking? || 13 ||

Regarding the word "mūle" (in the root): as before, this is a statement concerning one who remains in the state of emergence (*vyutthāna*). "In the root, in the middle, and at the end" refers to the arising, the expansion, and the repose of consciousness; we "sink," meaning we are overwhelmed by the state of emergence. || 13 ||
p.
160) By means of the yoga of knowledge and so forth, he ought to regard even others.
O Lord, you are the light only for those who are self-willed and for those who possess devotion.

Regarding the word "jñāna" (knowledge): O Lord, for some you manifest through means such as the yoga of knowledge and ritual action; however, for those devotees who are independent and require no external means, and who have attained Your majesty through immersion in You, You are eternally the very nature of light—this is the meaning. || 14 ||
For your devotees there are no afflictions, nor is there any anxiety regarding their own selves;
nevertheless, [the thought] "O Śiva" exists— this...
Whatever [arises] for them when they are directed toward the external world. || 15 ||
Regarding the phrase "of the devotees": *ārtayaḥ* refers to afflictions; *ādhyānam* is the contemplation [of You] with a longing for attainment.

[This occurs] even as You manifest as one's very own self (*svātmatayā*). Nevertheless, precisely because they are devotees, there arises something indescribable—manifesting the identity with supreme bliss and being without external cause. || 15 ||
I praise that which is the illumination of all appearances, which, although it is indeed permeated by reflective awareness (*vimarśa*), yet manifests as "I am this."
O Lord, that is Your power of action.

"Everything"—that which is "I am this," the entire universe, which is the constant illumination appearing as all things, the light of the Lord of the Universe—how can I praise that [Lord] who is enveloped and expanded by the *vimarśa* (reflective awareness) consisting of the wonder of supreme bliss?
O Lord, I praise Your two powers: the power of action (*kriyā-śakti*) and the power of lordship (*īśa-śakti*). As before. || 16 ||
All living beings without exception— even Brahmā, Indra, and Viṣṇu— exist [within it].
Therefore, O Lord, I bow to the universe which is composed of you, as it is being swallowed up [by you]. || 17 ||

"They exist" means as follows: let alone the well-known creators and sustainers such as Brahmā, Indra, and Viṣṇu—even those beginning with Rudra, and indeed all living beings without exception, these knowers of the field (kṣetrajñas), are always devouring their own objects of experience and remain intensely inclined toward them. || 17 ||
"O Lord, because of its connection with destruction,
everything other than me is entirely false;
it is thus that it is declared."
By you, through the play of withdrawal. || 18 ||

Regarding the word "sata" (of the existent): O Lord, it is said that by the very play of withdrawal (*saṃhāra*), everything from the level of Sadāśiva upwards—which, though not actually additional, appears as if additional because its own nature is projected outwards from the Supreme whose sole form is the intoxicated Consciousness—is false;
the meaning is that it does not exist separately. This is because, although it is not additional to the Existent (*sat*), it appears as if it were additional.

Because of the dissolution of that which appears [as an object], through its connection with the destruction [of duality], there remains a state of abiding within the very Self of Consciousness (cidātman) as something that has melted away.

As it has been said: "That which extends up to Sadāśiva," and so forth, ending with "endowed with destruction and origination"; likewise, "the state of being an effect is perishable therein," and so forth. || 18 ||
O bestower of boons, for those whose devotion is thick, even the inconceivable and all-wondrous thought merely by being meditated upon stands before them.
And they triumph over the state of being an agent. || 19 ||

"Merely by being meditated upon" means that even that essential nature which cannot be conceived by limited yogis stands before those whose wealth is devotion; it becomes manifest immediately after meditation.

This is the meaning: those devotees excel in relation to the agency of all wondrous thought; they alone are the instigators of extraordinary amazement and are preeminent in every respect—this is the meaning. || 19 ||
At night, the heroic warriors dance, their vital centers throbbing as if nourished by the sprinkling of the nectar of devotion to you.
He was emboldened by throngs of vetālas. || 20 ||

"Thine" (tāvaketi). The external meaning is clear. The "heroic folk" (*vīrajanaḥ*)—those who have torn asunder the great beast of saṃsāra, the world of devotees—dance even in the night, that is, in the midst of *māyā*, shining intensely through the expansion of consciousness (*cidvikāsa*).
How so? Because they are made blissful by the sprinkling of the wine of the aesthetic flavor of Thy devotion (*bhaktirasa*), as if by the sprinkling of the nectar of immersion into Thee.

The vital points (*marmamaṇḍala*) are gladdened by bliss; the noose consists of their accumulations, and through their throbbing relatives resembling the *āsana-mudrā*, and through hundreds of powers that follow the arising of visual conviction from the heart of the sacrificial animal (*paśu*) in the host of *vetālas*, [the yogin] is filled with enthusiasm, and thus the awakening of consciousness (*cid-abhyudaya*) is fully nourished.
May there be auspiciousness. || 20 ||
O Śambhu, by whichever limb of mine you have begun to take delight,
by that very limb this time has become endless.
May everything indeed become firmly established. || 21 ||

Regarding the word *ārabdhā*: although this verse appears as if it were not of [Vedic] origin (*anārṣa*) because an incomparable style is observed in certain places, it is nevertheless explained. By means of that very limb—which demonstrates the excellence of immersion into non-dual consciousness (*cidadvaya-samāveśa*)—and by which mode all [other] characteristics are unperceived, O Śambhu, your praise has been commenced.

Having made this entire time firm and unwavering in this manner for an infinite duration, he would "bhavipīṣṭa"—that is, he would attain [the goal]; "bhū" is the form of the root *āp* (to reach/attain). May there be auspiciousness! || 21 ||
Thus ends the twentieth commentary on the *Carvaṇāstotra* within the *Stotrāvalī* composed by the venerable teacher Utpaladeva, written by the illustrious Kṣemarāja. 20.
Oṃ tat sat! Destroy the afflictions, cause the heart-lotus to blossom, manifest your own vigor, and make your limbs dance;
O circle of moonbeams for the cakora-bird of the mind!
Having sipped water, properly sanctify this entire universe with nectar.
This series of utterances, having reached the path of hearing, shakes off the heat of worldly existence and instantly spreads an incomparable pervasion of supreme bliss;
thus, through devotion to the Lord Śambhu, the Supreme Being— [The remainder of the verse would complete this thought.]
This graceful commentary has been composed by us, who have been requested by those whose purposes have been fulfilled. || 2 ||
Throughout the three worlds, his fame has indeed been woven together by clear treatises and commentaries of incomparable nature;
therefore, [I bow] to the Guru, who is the very embodiment of the Supreme Lord.
Having heard this exposition, Kṣema composed [this work] for the sake of the next world. Om tat sat.
